name: Majapahit Empire
description: The Majapahit Empire emerged on the island of Java following the repulse of a Yuan Mongol expedition in 1293, rapidly expanding into a vast maritime realm across Southeast Asia. From its capital at Trowulan, the Hindu-Buddhist state exerted thalassocratic authority over commercial trade routes and numerous tributary domains throughout the Indonesian archipelago. The empire attained its cultural and geopolitical summit under King Hayam Wuruk and Prime Minister Gajah Mada before dynastic rivalries and the rise of Islamic coastal sultanates precipitated its decline. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Trowulan; Common languages: Old Javanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Thalassocratic mandala monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Singhasari Kingdom; Succeeded by: Demak Sultanate

name: Alaiye
label: anatolian beyliks
description: Alaiye was an Anatolian maritime principality founded along the southern Mediterranean coast following the collapse of Seljuq authority after the Battle of Kose Dag. Centred on the fortified port of Alanya, the beylik developed as a significant naval stronghold and commercial nexus under local Turkoman emirs. The state maintained strategic autonomy by navigating diplomatic tensions with neighbouring Cilician Armenia and the Karamanids until its eventual incorporation into the expanding Ottoman realm. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Alanya; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Beylik; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Free Imperial City of Leutkirch
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Leutkirch flourished as a self-governing urban republic within the Allgau region of southern Germany, possessing imperial immediacy under the Holy Roman Empire. The town secured extensive civic charters that allowed its burghers to manage local administration, judicial affairs and vibrant textile manufacturing independently of regional lords. Leutkirch retained its autonomous municipal status through religious upheavals and conflicts until mediatisation transferred the territory to Bavaria during the Napoleonic restructuring. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City; Capital: Leutkirch im Allgau; Common languages: Early Modern German and Swabian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Commune of Sassari
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Sassari governed northern Sardinia as an autonomous civic republic after shaking off Pisan dominance in the late thirteenth century. Operating under a comprehensive municipal code of statutes, the merchant oligarchy entered into an alliance with the Republic of Genoa to protect its maritime commerce and territorial autonomy. This period of municipal self-rule ended in the early fourteenth century when the Crown of Aragon launched its military campaign to conquer the island. \n\n Status: Autonomous commune; Capital: Sassari; Common languages: Sassarese, Sardinian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Oligarchic republic; Historical era: High to Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Giudicato of Torres; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sardinia

name: Commune of Terni
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Terni developed as an assertive self-governing city-state in southern Umbria, situated along the confluence of the Nera and Serra rivers. Governed by elected magistrates and guild councils, the municipal commonwealth fiercely defended its local jurisdiction against neighbouring communes and encroaching papal administrators. Although frequently convulsed by factional rivalries between Guelphs and Ghibellines, Terni preserved its civic liberties until gradual papal consolidation curtailed its independence during the sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous commune; Capital: Terni; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic commune; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Preceded by: Duchy of Spoleto; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Free Imperial City of Speyer
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Speyer functioned as a paramount urban centre of the Holy Roman Empire along the left bank of the Rhine. Possessing imperial immediacy, the prosperous city hosted numerous imperial diets and served as the initial seat of the Imperial Chamber Court, fostering a vibrant legal and commercial environment. Its long era of civic autonomy came under recurrent strain during regional conflicts and foreign incursions before the city was finally integrated into the Electorate of Bavaria. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City; Capital: Speyer; Common languages: Early Modern German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Bishopric of Speyer; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Imperial Abbey of Salem
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Abbey of Salem was a prominent Cistercian monastic principality situated near Lake Constance in southern Swabia. Holding imperial immediacy directly under the Holy Roman Emperor, the abbot exercised territorial jurisdiction over extensive rural estates, forests and agricultural communities. The monastic territory prospered through agricultural enterprise and cultural patronage until secularisation transferred its domains to the Margraviate of Baden in 1803. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey; Administrative seat: Salem; Common languages: German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical lordship; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Baden

name: Kampili Kingdom
description: The Kampili Kingdom was a short-lived Hindu polity established along the Tungabhadra River in northern Karnataka following the disruption of Seuna Yadava rule by northern invaders. Founded by Singeya Nayaka and governed from strong hill fortifications, the realm defended its independence against regional neighbours and incursions from the Delhi Sultanate. The kingdom was violently dismantled after a catastrophic siege by Tughlaq forces in the late 1320s, an event that directly catalysed the formation of the Vijayanagara Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kampili; Common languages: Kannada and Telugu; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Nayaka; Historical era: Medieval India; Preceded by: Seuna Yadava dynasty; Succeeded by: Delhi Sultanate

name: Bono Manso
label: akan states
description: Bono Manso was an influential Akan commercial state located in the forest-savanna transition zone of central Ghana. As the earliest documented centralised kingdom of the Bono people, it grew into a pivotal trading metropolis where merchants exchanged northern sub-Saharan commodities such as salt and textiles for indigenous gold, kola nuts and regional goods. The capital flourished for several centuries until military defeat and destruction by the expanding Asante Empire in the 1720s shifted regional authority southward to Techiman. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bono Manso; Common languages: Akan; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Bonohene; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: Techiman Kingdom

name: Signoria of Rimini
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Rimini was a prominent feudal state in the Romagna region of northern Italy, governed by the patrician House of Malatesta. Capitalising on strategic positioning along the Adriatic seaboard, the dynasty patronised Renaissance architecture, literature and military enterprise while steering the city through fierce regional wars. Malatesta dominion over Rimini persisted until the start of the sixteenth century, when Cesare Borgia overran the territory and brought it under direct papal governance. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Rimini; Common languages: Romagnol, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hereditary signoria; Ruling dynasty: House of Malatesta; Ruler title: Lord of Rimini; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Chiang Hung State
label: shan states
description: Chiang Hung State was a Tai Lu principality situated in the upland river basin of Xishuangbanna along the upper Mekong River. During this period, the realm operated as a subordinate vassal under the suzerainty of the Lan Na Kingdom while retaining local administrative customs under indigenous dynastic chieftains. Its mountain location enabled the court to facilitate cross-border trade between Yunnan and Southeast Asia despite enduring political pressure from both Burmese and imperial Chinese neighbours. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Chiang Lan; Common languages: Tai Lu; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal chiefdom; Ruler title: Chao Pha; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Cheli Chiefdom; Succeeded by: Lan Na Kingdom

name: Duchy of Saxe-Lauenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Lauenburg was an autonomous north German principality formed upon the late thirteenth-century partition of the older stem Duchy of Saxony. Ruled by an Ascanian ducal line from the island stronghold of Ratzeburg and the Elbe port of Lauenburg, the realm held imperial immediacy within the Lower Saxon Circle. The dukes retained their territorial integrity and traditional legal privileges through dynastic divisions until the extinction of the male Ascanian line in 1689 triggered a succession crisis. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Ratzeburg; Common languages: Middle Low German and Early Modern German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ascania; Ruler title: Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Duchy of Saxony; Succeeded by: Principality of Calenberg

name: Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg emerged as an imperial principality along the middle Elbe following the division of the historic Duchy of Saxony between rival Ascanian branches. Headquartered at Wittenberg, the dukes asserted their claim to the prestigious Saxon electoral voice, contesting rival claimants from Saxe-Lauenburg. Their political ascendancy was formally affirmed when Emperor Charles IV promulgated the Golden Bull of 1356, permanently establishing the duchy as the core of the Electorate of Saxony. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Wittenberg; Common languages: Middle Low German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ascania; Ruler title: Duke of Saxe-Wittenberg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Saxony; Succeeded by: Electorate of Saxony

name: Myinsaing Kingdom
description: The Myinsaing Kingdom arose in central Burma following the collapse of the Pagan Empire under Mongol pressure, ruled jointly by three warlord brothers based at Myinsaing, Mekkhaya and Pinle. The sibling regency successfully repelled a second Mongol invasion at the turn of the fourteenth century and reunified the agrarian heartland between Tagaung and Prome. Following the deaths of the elder brothers, internal dynastic competition dismantled the tripartite confederation and gave rise to the successor realms of Pinya and Sagaing. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Myinsaing; Common languages: Burmese, Shan and Mon; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and animism; Government: Tripartite monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Burmese warring states; Preceded by: Pagan Kingdom; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Pinya

name: Beylik of Karesi
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Karesi was a maritime Turkoman principality established in northwestern Anatolia along the Dardanelles and the southern shores of the Sea of Marmara. Emerging from the declining Seljuq Sultanate of Rum, the beylik maintained significant naval squadrons from Balikesir and Bergama, conducting extensive raids into Byzantine Thrace. Dynastic strife following the death of its founding emir weakened the principality, allowing the rising Ottoman dynasty to annex its fleet and territory during the mid-fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Balikesir; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Beylik; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Signoria of Oneglia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Oneglia was an autonomous maritime lordship positioned along the Ligurian coastline of northwestern Italy, held by the prominent Doria family. The dynasty governed the strategic harbour settlement and surrounding olive-producing hinterland under imperial immediacy, resisting encroachment from the neighbouring Republic of Genoa. Oneglia served as an important commercial and naval base for Doria enterprises until later dynastic transfers brought the territory under the authority of the House of Savoy. \n\n Status: Feudal lordship; Capital: Imperia; Common languages: Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal signoria; Ruling dynasty: House of Doria; Ruler title: Lord of Oneglia; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Savoy

name: Kingdom of Singapura
description: The Kingdom of Singapura was an influential Malay maritime trading polity established on the island of Temasek at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. According to regional traditions, the realm was founded by Sang Nila Utama and rapidly evolved into a thriving entrepot that connected Indian Ocean trade networks with the South China Sea. Archaeological findings on Fort Canning Hill confirm an active fourteenth-century mercantile centre that endured repeated regional invasions before succumbing to external attacks, after which its rulers established the Sultanate of Malacca. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Singapore; Common languages: Old Malay; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Thalassocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval Southeast Asia; Preceded by: Melayu Kingdom; Succeeded by: Malacca Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Poland
description: The Kingdom of Poland entered into a brief personal union with the Kingdom of Bohemia when King Wenceslaus II secured coronation at Gniezno in 1300. Operating from Krakow, the Bohemian monarch attempted to centralise royal administration across fragmented Polish duchies by introducing new administrative offices and stabilising regional coinage. This Bohemian union dissolved rapidly following the premature death of King Wenceslaus III in 1306, allowing Wladyslaw the Elbow-high to restore Piast rule and advance domestic reunification. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union; Capital: Krakow; Common languages: Old Polish and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Premyslid dynasty; Ruler title: King of Poland; Head of state: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Poland

name: Ajuran Sultanate
description: The Ajuran Sultanate was a powerful Somali Islamic empire that dominated trade, pastoral lands and river valleys throughout the Horn of Africa. Noted for its sophisticated hydraulic engineering, the state constructed extensive limestone wells and irrigation canals along the Shebelle and Jubba river basins to support agriculture and pastoralism. From administrative coastal seats like Mareeg and Merca, the sultanate maintained vibrant maritime commerce with Arabia, India and China while successfully resisting Portuguese naval assaults and inland migrations. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Mareeg; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Theocratic hereditary sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Mogadishu Sultanate; Succeeded by: Geledi Sultanate

name: Alitta
description: Alitta was an autonomous pre-colonial Bugis kingdom situated in the western peninsula of South Sulawesi. The polity operated an agrarian and riverine economy, maintaining an elected governing council that oversaw customary laws and local land cultivation. As one of the traditional component realms of the Ajatappareng confederation, Alitta coordinated mutual security and regional diplomacy with its neighbours until growing political dominance by Gowa restructured local power in the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Alitta; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Elective chieftaincy; Ruler title: Datu; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Gowa Sultanate

name: Ambohidratrimo Kingdom
description: The Ambohidratrimo Kingdom was an independent highland realm established in the central plateau of Madagascar, centred on one of the twelve sacred hills of Imerina. Governed by Vazimba and early Merina rulers, the hilltop citadel commanded fertile rice terraces and protected its inhabitants from regional competitors. The polity preserved its local sovereignty and ancestral spiritual traditions through dynastic alliances until broader political consolidation gradually integrated the chiefdom into the emerging Kingdom of Imerina. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ambohidratrimo; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Pre-colonial Madagascar; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Imerina

name: Commune of Fossombrone
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Fossombrone functioned as a self-governing city-state in the Metauro Valley of the Marche, situated along the ancient Roman Via Flaminia. Administered by municipal magistrates and civic councils, the town sustained an active regional commerce while fiercely preserving its autonomy against aggressive neighbouring baronies. During the fourteenth century, persistent regional conflict and military rivalries eventually forced the municipality under the hereditary lordship of the Malatesta and Montefeltro families. \n\n Status: Autonomous commune; Capital: Fossombrone; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic commune; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Spoleto; Succeeded by: Signoria of Fossombrone

name: County of Hohenwaldeck
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Hohenwaldeck was an autonomous alpine fief situated in the Upper Bavarian highlands around Lake Schliersee and Lake Tegernsee. Governed from the residential town of Miesbach and the ancient fortress of Hohenwaldeck, the counts exercised immediate imperial jurisdiction over local forestry, farming communities and regional pilgrimage routes. The territory preserved its separate noble standing within the Holy Roman Empire until the male line of the Waldeck family ended in the eighteenth century, leading to its reversion to the Electorate of Bavaria. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Miesbach; Common languages: Early Modern German and Bavarian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Waldeck; Ruler title: Count of Hohenwaldeck; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Dimasa Kingdom
description: The Dimasa Kingdom was an indigenous Tibeto-Burman monarchy that held sway over large areas of the Brahmaputra Valley and the North Cachar Hills in northeastern India. Headquartered at fortified riverine capitals such as Dimapur and Maibang, the Dimasa rulers erected distinctive monolithic architecture and cultivated rich wet-rice agriculture. The kingdom defended its borders against incursions from the neighbouring Ahom state and Koch kingdom until British colonial forces annexed the plains and hills during the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Maibang; Common languages: Dimasa; Religion: Hinduism and animism; Government: Tribal hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern Assam; Preceded by: Kamarupa Kingdom; Succeeded by: Colonial Assam

name: Free Imperial City of Wimpfen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Wimpfen was an autonomous urban enclave situated along the Neckar River in southwestern Germany, holding immediate status under the Holy Roman Emperor. Divided historically into a fortified hilltop settlement and a lower river town, the municipality developed thriving trade networks based on salt extraction, viticulture and river shipping. The city council maintained civic self-governance through extensive regional conflicts until secularisation and territorial reorganisation awarded the city to the Grand Duchy of Hesse in 1803. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City; Capital: Bad Wimpfen; Common languages: German and South Franconian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Hesse

name: Hadiya Sultanate
description: The Hadiya Sultanate was a prominent Muslim state located in the southwestern highlands of Ethiopia, south of the Awash River and Shewa. Inhabited primarily by Cushitic and Semitic communities, the realm commanded fertile agricultural plateaus and commanded formidable cavalry formations that dominated regional trade routes. Although frequently engaged in protracted border conflicts with the Christian Ethiopian Empire, Hadiya maintained its political independence and distinct Islamic culture until administrative incorporation into Abyssinia. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Hosanna; Common languages: Hadiyya, Silt'e and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruler title: Garad; Historical era: Medieval Horn of Africa; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Kingdom of Ardra
description: The Kingdom of Ardra was a coastal West African state founded by Aja migrants along the Bight of Benin in what is now southern Benin. Administered from its political and religious capital at Allada, the kingdom developed into a dominant commercial power by controlling trade routes connecting the Atlantic coast to the inland Yoruba states. Ardra held a pre-eminent role in diplomatic and commercial exchanges until the neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey launched an invasion and conquered Allada in 1724. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Allada; Common languages: Aja and Fon; Religion: Traditional Vodun religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: King of Ardra; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Dahomey

name: Kingdom of Dotawo
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: The Kingdom of Dotawo was one of the final Christian Nubian states to survive along the Nile in Lower Nubia between the first and second cataracts. Centred upon the fortified sandstone citadel of Jebel Adda, the realm preserved medieval Christian liturgy, Old Nubian literacy and royal court traditions long after the collapse of neighbouring Makuria. Surrounded by nomadic incursions and encroaching Islamic principalities, the isolated kingdom persisted through the fifteenth century before ultimately collapsing. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jebel Adda; Common languages: Old Nubian, Coptic and Greek; Religion: Coptic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Medieval Nubia; Preceded by: Kingdom of Makuria; Succeeded by: Funj Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Hormuz
description: The Kingdom of Hormuz was a wealthy maritime monarchy situated on the strategic island of Jarun at the entrance to the Persian Gulf. Founded by Arab and Persian merchant princes, the state controlled international maritime commerce connecting the Middle East, India and East Africa through its bustling emporium. Hormuz enjoyed extensive geopolitical autonomy until Portuguese naval forces under Afonso de Albuquerque arrived in 1507, compelling the king to acknowledge Portuguese suzerainty and pay annual tribute. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime kingdom; Capital: Hormuz; Common languages: Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Mercantile monarchy; Ruler title: King of Hormuz; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Salghurid Atabegs; Succeeded by: Portuguese Empire

name: Kingdom of Kutai Kartanegara
description: The Kingdom of Kutai Kartanegara was an established riverine monarchy situated along the lower and middle basins of the Mahakam River in eastern Borneo. Governed from its historic centre at Kutai Lama and later Tenggarong, the kingdom developed from early Hindu-Buddhist courtly traditions into a significant regional trade depot for forest products and rice. The realm maintained complete autonomy over its interior tributaries until the mid-seventeenth century, when expanded contact with Bugis migrants and European traders prompted structural political transitions. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tenggarong; Common languages: Kutai Malay; Religion: Hinduism and animism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Pre-colonial Southeast Asia; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara

name: Kingdom of Luwu
description: The Kingdom of Luwu was among the most ancient and venerated Bugis states on the island of Sulawesi, occupying the fertile coastal plains and mountain valleys around the Gulf of Boni. Centred at Malangke and later Palopo, the monarchy traced its origin to legendary ancestral figures recorded in the epic I La Galigo, possessing supreme spiritual prestige throughout the region. The kingdom drew substantial wealth from agriculture and interior iron ore deposits, maintaining its sovereign status until Dutch colonial forces subdued the realm in 1906. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Palopo; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Indigenous animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Datu; Historical era: Pre-colonial to Colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Lordship of Mülner
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Mulner was an autonomous noble dominion of the Holy Roman Empire held by the prominent patrician Mulner family of Zurich. Controlling extensive lands, mills and judicial jurisdictions around Inden and the Limmat basin, the lords exercised substantial political influence over regional commerce and urban governance. The family maintained sovereign feudal rights over their estates through the fourteenth century before civic expansion by the City of Zurich absorbed the lordship's privileges into its municipal territory. \n\n Status: Feudal lordship; Capital: Inden; Common languages: Middle High German and Alemannic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Mulner; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Canton of Zurich

name: Lordship of Rostock
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Rostock was a Baltic maritime fief within the Holy Roman Empire that came under the direct protection and overlordship of the Danish Crown in 1301. Following dynastic partitions among the House of Mecklenburg, Prince Nicholas placed his domain under Danish sovereignty to fend off aggressive territorial rivals in Werle and Mecklenburg. Danish garrison commanders exercised effective political and military administration over the town and surrounding ports until Denmark formally ceded the territory back to the Lord of Mecklenburg in 1323. \n\n Status: Vassal lordship; Capital: Rostock; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Head of state: King of Denmark; Ruler title: Lord of Rostock; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Rostock; Succeeded by: Duchy of Mecklenburg

name: Mbata Kingdom
description: The Mbata Kingdom was an influential Bantu kingdom situated in northern Angola, founded by the lineage of Sovereign Nsaku Ne Vunda. Operating with a developed agricultural base and hereditary provincial leadership, the state exercised considerable political authority along the Inkisi River basin. In the late fourteenth century, the ruler of Mbata concluded a dynastic alliance and political union with the neighbouring king of Mpemba Kasi, creating the foundational core of the unified Kingdom of Kongo. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mbanza Kongo; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Traditional Bukongo; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mani Mbata; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kongo

name: Mpemba Kasi
description: Mpemba Kasi was an ancient Bantu polity situated in the highlands of northern Angola south of the Congo River. Regarded in local oral history as the foundational cradle and mother of the Kongo nation, the kingdom possessed a well-organised system of clan settlements governed by a paramount ruler. In approximately 1375, King Nimi a Nzima negotiated a permanent dynastic alliance with the neighbouring realm of Mbata, formally uniting their lands to establish the Kingdom of Kongo. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mpemba Kasi; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Traditional Bukongo; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kongo

name: Ouargla
label: berber kingdoms
description: Ouargla was an autonomous Berber oasis kingdom and major caravan hub situated in the northern reaches of the Algerian Sahara Desert. Governed by local Ibadi and Sunni Zenata Berber lineages, the walled settlement prospered as a crucial trans-Saharan entrepot connecting sub-Saharan gold and ivory trails with Mediterranean coastal ports. The desert city-state maintained its political independence and lucrative commercial networks for centuries until expanding Ottoman regencies in Algiers extended their military influence across the southern oases. \n\n Status: Oasis kingdom; Capital: Ouargla; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Ibadi and Sunni Islam; Government: Mercantile chieftaincy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern; Preceded by: Zenata Berber confederation; Succeeded by: Ottoman Regency of Algiers

name: Oyo Empire
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: The Oyo Empire was a powerful Yoruba state in present-day southwestern Nigeria and eastern Benin, celebrated for its administrative sophistication and cavalry armies. Governed by the Alaafin from the historic capital of Oyo-Ile alongside the influential Oyo Mesi council of state, the empire established political hegemony across most of Yorubaland. The state controlled crucial inland trade routes and exacted tribute from neighbouring coastal kingdoms like Dahomey, maintaining enduring imperial strength until internal political fracturing invited northern incursions in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Oyo; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion and Islam; Government: Hereditary constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Alaafin; Legislature: Oyo Mesi and Ogboni; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: Ibadan Republic

name: Principality of Ustye
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Ustye was a small appanage principality situated along the upper Oka river basin in western Russia. Established during the fragmentation of the regional Chernigov and Smolensk dynastic networks, the realm was governed by a branch of the Rurikid dynasty based at the fortified settlement of Ustiva. The autonomous principality maintained local defence and agricultural production amid ongoing pressures from the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, which eventually absorbed the territory during its eastward expansion in the late fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Ustiva; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid dynasty; Ruler title: Kniaz; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Chernigov; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Rappang
description: Rappang was an autonomous Bugis principality situated in the inland agricultural plains of South Sulawesi, adjacent to Lake Tempe. The state maintained a prosperous economy supported by intensive wet-rice cultivation and regional overland trade routes connecting the western coast with the eastern gulf. As a charter member of the Ajatappareng confederation, Rappang closely coordinated diplomatic policy with its sister states until regional expansion by the Sultanate of Gowa subjugated the kingdom during the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Rappang; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Arung; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Gowa Sultanate

name: Sambuvaraya Dynasty
description: The Sambuvaraya Dynasty was a sovereign South Indian royal house that governed the historic Tondaimandalam region across northern Tamil Nadu. Taking advantage of the concurrent collapse of the Chola, Hoysala and Pandya realms, the chieftains established complete independence from their fortified hill capitals of Rajagambhiram and Padaividu. Rulers such as Venrumankonda and Rajanarayana Sambuvaraya issued royal records in their own regnal years until the expanding Vijayanagara Empire defeated and incorporated the principality in the late 1370s. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Padaividu; Common languages: Tamil; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sambuvaraya dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Medieval India; Preceded by: Pandyan Empire; Succeeded by: Vijayanagara Empire

name: Sarukhanids
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Sarukhanids were a Turkoman dynasty that founded an independent beylik in western Anatolia around the valley of the Gediz River. Established by Saruhan Bey in the wake of Byzantine retreat and Seljuq fragmentation, the principality ruled from Manisa and developed a formidable Aegean naval squadron that raided Christian shipping. The beylik maintained its commercial prosperity and regional autonomy until the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I annexed the domain, which was only briefly revived after Timur's invasion before permanent Ottoman absorption. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Manisa; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Beylik; Ruling dynasty: Saruhanids; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Sawitto
description: Sawitto was an independent Bugis kingdom positioned along the western coastal lowlands of South Sulawesi, centred near modern Pinrang. Benefiting from coastal maritime access and fertile river valleys, the realm engaged in thriving commerce and agricultural production alongside neighbouring inland kingdoms. Sawitto formed a core component of the Ajatappareng confederacy to balance against the growing power of southern rivals until military subjugation by the Sultanate of Gowa ended its autonomy in the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pinrang; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Datu; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Gowa Sultanate

name: Sidenreng
description: Sidenreng was a prominent inland Bugis state located around the extensive wetlands of Lake Sidenreng in southwestern Sulawesi. The kingdom derived substantial wealth from grain production, fishing and overland trading corridors linking the Makassar Strait with the Gulf of Boni. Serving as the primary political centre of the Ajatappareng confederation, Sidenreng maintained robust military alliances with its neighbours until southern conquests by the Sultanate of Gowa reduced the realm to vassalage in the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sidenreng; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Addatuang; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Gowa Sultanate

name: Signoria of Forlì
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Forlì was a fortified medieval state in the Romagna region of northern Italy, dominated by the Ordelaffi dynasty. The ruling family governed the commune with fierce independence, frequently siding with the Ghibelline imperial cause and resisting subjugation by the papacy. Through strategic alliances and defensive fortifications, the signoria maintained regional prominence until Cesare Borgia conquered the territory in 1500, leading to its permanent incorporation into the Papal States. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Forlì; Common languages: Romagnol, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Dynastic signoria; Ruling dynasty: House of Ordelaffi; Ruler title: Lord of Forlì; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Sultanate of Gowa
description: The Sultanate of Gowa was a pre-eminent Makassarese maritime state located in the southwestern peninsula of Sulawesi. Emerging from a confederation of local chiefdoms around Somba Opu, the monarchy developed into an expansive mercantile power that dominated trade routes across eastern Indonesia. Gowa established naval hegemony over neighbouring kingdoms and fostered international commerce with European and Asian merchants until Dutch East India Company forces curtailed its authority in the late seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Somba Opu; Common languages: Makassarese; Religion: Indigenous animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Maritime monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Suppa
description: Suppa was an autonomous Bugis coastal polity situated along the western littoral of South Sulawesi near the modern bay of Parepare. Engaging extensively in maritime commerce, fishing and agricultural production, the principality commanded key sea lanes between the Java Sea and the Moluccas. Suppa joined the Ajatappareng confederation alongside neighbouring realms to resist expansionist pressures from southern kingdoms, maintaining sovereign governance until military subjugation by Gowa in the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Parepare; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Datu; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Succeeded by: Gowa Sultanate

name: Tarascan State
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Tarascan State was a powerful pre-Columbian empire centred in the Lake Patzcuaro basin of Michoacan in western Mesoamerica. Ruled by the Irecha from the dynastic capitals of Patzcuaro and Tzintzuntzan, the Purepecha people created a highly centralised administration supported by sophisticated bronze metallurgy and defensive border garrisons. The realm successfully repulsed repeated invasion attempts by the neighbouring Aztec Empire, preserving complete political independence until submitting to Spanish conquistadors in the 1520s. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Patzcuaro; Common languages: Purepecha; Religion: Polytheism; Government: Theocratic absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Irecha; Historical era: Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica; Succeeded by: Viceroyalty of New Spain

name: Wulli
description: Wulli was an independent Mandinka kingdom established along the northern bank of the Gambia River in western West Africa. Governed by the Wali dynasty from the fortified capital of Medina, the realm occupied a crucial junction on trans-continental trade paths connecting the upper Niger basin with Atlantic trading stations. The kingdom prospered through the exchange of cotton, gold and agricultural goods, preserving its sovereign status until late nineteenth-century Anglo-French colonial demarcations partitioned the territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Medina; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Dynastic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wali dynasty; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: British Gambia Protectorate

name: Zichia
description: Zichia was an autonomous medieval Circassian kingdom occupying the northeastern coastline of the Black Sea and the fertile valleys of the Taman Peninsula. Centred upon the fortified trading emporium of Matrega, the realm sustained active commercial ties with Byzantine and Italian maritime merchants while maintaining local agrarian traditions. The kingdom defended its coastal independence against regional nomadic confederations and the Golden Horde until fifteenth-century political splintering reorganised the territory into sovereign Circassian aristocratic principalities. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Matrega; Common languages: Circassian; Religion: Khabzeism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Zygii; Succeeded by: Circassia

name: Kingdom of Hungary
description: The Kingdom of Hungary entered into a personal union with the Kingdom of Bohemia in 1301 when young Wenceslaus III of the Premyslid dynasty was crowned King Ladislaus at Székesfehérvár. Administered from Buda amidst the chaos following the extinction of the native Arpad line, royal authority struggled against powerful provincial oligarchs who exercised virtually independent regional dominion. The Bohemian union collapsed in 1305 when Wenceslaus renounced his claims to the Hungarian crown, paving the way for the Angevin dynasty to claim the vacant throne. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union; Capital: Buda; Common languages: Hungarian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Premyslid dynasty; Ruler title: King of Hungary; Head of state: Wenceslaus III of Bohemia; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hungary

name: Domain of Ugrin Csák
description: The Domain of Ugrin Csák was an autonomous oligarchic territory that emerged in the southern Pannonian region of Syrmia during the feudal anarchy following the death of King Andrew III. Governed from the river stronghold of Ilok by the powerful baron Ugrin Csák, the province functioned as a de facto independent state with its own administration and private baronial army. Ugrin utilised his domain to champion the Angevin pretender Charles Robert against rival claimants, and the territory was peacefully reintegrated into the royal domain upon Ugrin's death in 1311. \n\n Status: Autonomous baronial domain; Capital: Ilok; Common languages: Hungarian, Old Church Slavonic and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal oligarchy; Ruler title: Baron; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Hungary; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hungary

name: Free Imperial City of Donauwörth
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Donauwörth was an autonomous municipal republic situated at the strategic confluence of the Danube and Wornitz rivers in Bavarian Swabia. Holding imperial immediacy under the Holy Roman Empire, the city was governed by an independent town council that oversaw local justice, trade taxes and river transport. Donauworth leveraged its position on major east-west waterways to build a flourishing commercial community, maintaining civic liberties despite periodic territorial encirclement by the neighbouring Dukes of Bavaria. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City; Capital: Donauwörth; Common languages: Early Modern German and Swabian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Duchy of Bavaria

name: Duchy of Athens
label: frankokratia
description: The Duchy of Athens was a Frankish crusader principality encompassing Attica and Boeotia that fell under the dominion of the Catalan Company and the Crown of Aragon in the early fourteenth century. Ruled by Aragonese vicars-general from Athens and Thebes, the state operated as a feudal dependency of the Kingdom of Sicily while administering Catalan customary law. The Catalan dukes defended their Greek possessions against Byzantine revanchism and Latin rivals until the Florentine Acciaioli family seized control of the lordship in the late 1380s. \n\n Status: Feudal duchy in vassalage; Capital: Athens; Common languages: Catalan, French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke of Athens; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Athens; Succeeded by: Acciaioli Lordship of Athens

name: Kingdom of Naples
description: The Kingdom of Naples was established as an autonomous realm covering mainland southern Italy following the partition of the older Norman-Swabian Kingdom of Sicily under the Peace of Caltabellotta. Ruled by the Angevin dynasty from Naples, the monarchy maintained extensive administrative institutions, patronised university scholarship and engaged in vigorous Mediterranean diplomacy. Although troubled by dynastic rivalries within the royal house and intermittent conflicts with Aragonese Sicily, the kingdom preserved its sovereignty until Alfonso V of Aragon unified both realms in 1442. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Naples; Common languages: Neapolitan, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Anjou; Ruler title: King of Naples; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sicily; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon

name: Chiefdom of Shuidong
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Shuidong was an autonomous indigenous Tusi domain situated in the rugged highlands of modern Kaiyang County in Guizhou. Administered by the hereditary Song clan, the realm operated as an acknowledged vassal of imperial China while maintaining indigenous Bouyei and Hmong tribal governance. Regarded as one of the four great native chiefdoms of the region, Shuidong supplied troops and mineral revenue to the imperial court until direct imperial administration was imposed during the Ming dynasty. \n\n Status: Vassal native chiefdom; Capital: Guiyang; Common languages: Chinese, Bouyei and Hmong; Religion: Indigenous animism and Daoism; Government: Hereditary tribal chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Song clan; Ruler title: Tusi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ming Empire

name: County of Rolo
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Rolo was a diminutive independent feudal state situated in the Po Valley between the Duchies of Mantua and Modena. Governed under imperial immediacy by the noble Sessi family, the tiny county exercised autonomous judicial and fiscal prerogatives from its fortified castle at Rolo. The lordship survived for centuries as an imperial fief, resisting annexation by larger neighbouring principalities until the extinction of the male line in 1776 led to direct imperial administration and transfer to the Habsburgs. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Rolo; Common languages: Emilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Sessi; Ruler title: Count of Rolo; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Duchy of Mantua

name: Lordship of Styrum
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Styrum was an immediate feudal domain within the Holy Roman Empire located along the Ruhr River in Westphalia. Held by the Counts of Limburg-Styrum from their ancestral castle near Mulheim, the territory exercised autonomous territorial jurisdiction over surrounding estates without holding a formal seat in the Imperial Diet. The lords preserved their noble status and local commercial privileges through centuries of regional conflict until mediatisation absorbed the estate into the Grand Duchy of Berg during the Napoleonic era. \n\n Status: Immediate lordship; Capital: Mülheim an der Ruhr; Common languages: Middle Low German and Early Modern German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Limburg-Styrum; Ruler title: Lord of Styrum; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Berg

name: Ranpur State
description: Ranpur State was an autonomous Hindu princely domain situated in the thickly forested interior hills of Nayagarh in Odisha. Governed by an ancient indigenous royal dynasty from the residential township of Ranpur, the state asserted descent from early Odia rulers and exercised territorial authority over tribal and agricultural communities. The kingdom retained its traditional administrative customs and forest autonomy through shifting regional empires until entering subsidiary alliance relationships with British colonial authorities. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Ranpur; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ranpur royal family; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern India; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Beylik of Aydin
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Aydin was a powerful maritime Turkoman principality established in western Anatolia along the Aegean coastline and the fertile valley of the Buyuk Menderes. Founded by Aydinoglu Mehmed Bey, the emirate operated from Birgi and the port of Smyrna, becoming renowned for its daring naval corsair operations across the Aegean Sea under Umur Bey. The beylik challenged Byzantine, Genoese and Venetian fleets before internal disputes and the expanding power of the Ottoman Sultanate brought its territory under Ottoman sovereignty. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Birgi; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Beylik; Ruling dynasty: Aydinid dynasty; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Kakatiya Dynasty
description: The Kakatiya Dynasty ruled an extensive kingdom across the eastern Deccan from the grand granite citadel of Orugallu, modern Warangal. Following the devastating siege of their capital by the forces of Alauddin Khalji in 1310, King Prataparudra II was compelled to accept vassal status under the Delhi Sultanate and pay substantial annual tribute. The Kakatiya court maintained autonomous domestic administration over its Telugu territories during this tributary interval until a renewed invasion by the Tughlaq dynasty extinguished the state in the 1320s. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Warangal; Common languages: Telugu and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kakatiya dynasty; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Prataparudra II; Historical era: Medieval India; Succeeded by: Delhi Sultanate

name: Order of Saint John of Jerusalem
description: The Order of Saint John of Jerusalem was a sovereign Catholic military order that established an independent maritime principality on the island of Rhodes after being expelled from the Levant. Governed by an elected Grand Master and an international convent of knights, the order fortified Rhodes into an impregnable naval bastion that policed Aegean trade routes and raided Ottoman shipping. Following the epic 1522 siege and subsequent loss of Rhodes, the Hospitallers relocated their headquarters to Malta, ruling that archipelago until Napoleon's capture of the island in 1798. \n\n Status: Sovereign military order; Capital: Valletta; Common languages: Latin, French, Italian and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective ecclesiastical monarchy; Ruler title: Grand Master; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: French First Republic

name: Beyliks of Canik
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beyliks of Canik comprised a cluster of small autonomous Turkoman principalities that held power along the Black Sea coastline of northern Anatolia around the port of Samsun. Emerging in the borderlands between the declining Seljuq state and the Empire of Trebizond, these minor emirates were ruled by distinct dynastic families who derived revenue from forestry, agriculture and maritime trade. The principalities maintained fragile local independence through shifting alliances until the Ottoman Empire systematically conquered and annexed the region in the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality confederation; Capital: Samsun; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Beyliks; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Duchy of the Archipelago
label: frankokratia
description: The Duchy of the Archipelago was an insular crusader realm in the Aegean Sea that fell under the feudal overlordship of the Principality of Achaea in the early fourteenth century. Founded by Venetian patrician Marco Sanudo and headquartered at the castle of Naxos, the state held authority over most of the Cyclades islands. The ruling Catholic dynasty governed a predominantly Greek Orthodox population through feudal institutions while managing lucrative maritime trade networks until Ottoman naval expansion ended Latin lordship across the archipelago. \n\n Status: Vassal feudal duchy; Capital: Naxos; Common languages: Italian, Venetian and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Sanudo; Ruler title: Duke of the Archipelago; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Okolo-Ama
description: Okolo-Ama, historically recognised as the Kingdom of Bonny, was an influential Ijaw trading state situated in the Niger Delta of modern southern Nigeria. Governed by a paramount king alongside powerful merchant house heads, the kingdom capitalised on its network of tidal creeks to control inland transport and international trade. The city-state flourished as a prominent palm oil and mercantile depot during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries before entering a formal protectorate agreement with the British Empire in 1886. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bonny; Common languages: Ibani and Igbo; Religion: Traditional Ijaw religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Amanyanabo; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Principality of Wallachia
description: The Principality of Wallachia was an autonomous Romanian feudal realm established north of the Lower Danube and south of the Southern Carpathians. Consolidated under Prince Basarab I following his decisive victory over the Kingdom of Hungary at the Battle of Posada in 1330, the principality established administrative capitals at Curtea de Arges and Targoviste. Wallachia preserved its domestic institutions, Orthodox faith and territory through diplomacy and military defence against neighbouring powers before accepting Ottoman tributary status in the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Curtea de Arges; Common languages: Romanian, Old Church Slavonic and Latin; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Elective hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Basarab; Ruler title: Prince of Wallachia; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Banate of Severin; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Duchy of Mirandola
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Mirandola was a compact northern Italian state situated in the fertile lowlands of the Po Valley in Emilia, governed by the patrician House of Pico. Originating as an autonomous lordship under imperial immediacy, the state developed extensive agricultural estates, established its own mint and constructed formidable Renaissance fortifications around Mirandola. The dynasty ruled the principality until the War of the Spanish Succession, when Duke Francesco Maria was deposed and the territory was absorbed into the Duchy of Modena and Reggio. \n\n Status: Imperial duchy; Capital: Mirandola; Common languages: Emilian, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Pico; Ruler title: Duke of Mirandola; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Duchy of Modena and Reggio

name: Lordship of Argos and Nauplia
label: frankokratia
description: The Lordship of Argos and Nauplia was a Frankish feudal enclave established in the Argolid peninsula of the Peloponnese following the Fourth Crusade. Held as an autonomous fief by the French de la Roche and Brienne families, the lordship survived the Catalan conquest of Athens and maintained its dual administrative centres at the fortress towns of Argos and Nauplia. The lordship provided a vital maritime outlet for Latin interests in the Morea until the ruling Enghien dynasty sold the territories to the Republic of Venice in 1388. \n\n Status: Feudal lordship; Capital: Nafplio; Common languages: French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Brienne; Ruler title: Lord of Argos and Nauplia; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Achaea; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Shivpuri State
description: Shivpuri State was an independent Rajput principality established in western India during the early fourteenth century by Rao Lumbha of the Deora Chauhan clan. Centred upon the ancient settlements around Sirohi and the defensive slopes of Mount Abu, the kingdom maintained sovereignty through martial valour and strategic hill fortifications. The dynasty defended its borders against incursions from the Gujarat Sultanate and neighbouring Rajput clans, preserving its autonomy until political consolidation established the broader Sirohi Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sirohi; Common languages: Rajasthani; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Rajput monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Deora Chauhan dynasty; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: Medieval India; Succeeded by: Sirohi State

name: Kingdom of Pinya
description: The Kingdom of Pinya was an upper Burmese monarchy that controlled the central Irrawaddy heartland following the dissolution of the Myinsaing tripartite realm. Founded by King Thihathu, the court administered rich agricultural irrigation networks from Pinya while contending with secessionist rebellions and severe dynastic conflicts among royal heirs. The kingdom maintained fragile authority over central Myanmar until devastating raids by the northern Shan state of Maw dismantled its defences, enabling Thado Minbya to absorb its territories into the new Kingdom of Ava. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pinya; Common languages: Burmese, Mon and Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Myinsaing dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Burmese warring states; Preceded by: Myinsaing Kingdom; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Ava

name: Signoria of Carrara
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Carrara was a feudal lordship situated in northwestern Tuscany along the Carrione River, world-renowned for its extensive white marble quarries. Originally part of the Bishopric of Luni, the territory gained imperial immediacy and municipal autonomy before coming under the authority of prominent regional powers, including the Republic of Pisa and the Visconti of Milan. The lordship maintained its territorial identity and lucrative quarrying industry until being purchased by the Marquis of Massa in 1473, creating a lasting personal union between the two states. \n\n Status: Feudal lordship; Capital: Carrara; Common languages: Emilian, Tuscan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal signoria; Ruler title: Lord of Carrara; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Bishopric of Luni; Succeeded by: Duchy of Massa and Carrara

name: Signoria of Faenza
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Faenza was a prominent autonomous city-state situated in the Romagna along the Lamone River, governed by the patrician Manfredi family. Under Manfredi rule, the city developed into a flourishing cultural centre celebrated across Europe for its high-quality glazed ceramics and Renaissance arts. Faenza defended its civic liberties through volatile regional conflicts between rival signorie and encroaching papal armies until Cesare Borgia captured the city in 1501, bringing the domain under permanent papal control. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Faenza; Common languages: Romagnol, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Dynastic signoria; Ruling dynasty: Manfredi family; Ruler title: Lord of Faenza; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Kingdom of Chūzan
label: ryuku polities
description: The Kingdom of Chūzan was the central and most powerful of the three Okinawan kingdoms that divided the island during the Sanzan period. Headquartered at the formidable royal citadels of Urasoe and Shuri, the kingdom developed vibrant maritime diplomacy, sending regular tributary missions to Ming China and establishing emporia across Southeast Asia. Under the ambitious leadership of King Shō Hashi, Chūzan conquered Hokuzan in 1416 and Nanzan in 1429, successfully unifying the entire island chain into the Ryūkyū Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shuri; Common languages: Okinawan and Classical Chinese; Religion: Ryukyuan religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: First Sho dynasty; Ruler title: King of Chūzan; Historical era: Sanzan period; Succeeded by: Ryūkyū Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Nanzan
label: ryuku polities
description: The Kingdom of Nanzan was an autonomous southern Okinawan realm that controlled the southern peninsula of Okinawa Island during the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. Governed from the hilltop fortress of Nanzan Castle near Ozato, the kingdom was directed by a paramount chieftain whose retainers commanded local agricultural estates and coastal fisheries. Nanzan participated in regional maritime commerce and sent tributary trade missions to the Ming court until the forces of King Shō Hashi of Chūzan invaded and annexed the territory in 1429. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ozato; Common languages: Okinawan; Religion: Ryukyuan religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King of Nanzan; Historical era: Sanzan period; Succeeded by: Ryūkyū Kingdom

name: Principality of Piedmont
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Piedmont was an autonomous noble dominion of the Holy Roman Empire held by the cadet Savoy-Achaea branch of the House of Savoy. Centred upon the fortified regional seat of Fossano and the upper Po plains, the princes administered judicial and fiscal affairs independently of the main comital branch in Chambery. The principality pursued an active foreign policy in subalpine Italy until the extinction of the Savoy-Achaea lineage in 1418 allowed Duke Amadeus VIII of Savoy to reunite Piedmont with the ducal patrimony. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Fossano; Common languages: Piedmontese, Franco-Provençal and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Savoy-Achaea; Ruler title: Prince of Piedmont; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Savoy

name: Kingdom of Sagaing
description: The Kingdom of Sagaing was an independent Upper Burmese state founded in 1315 by Prince Saw Yun following a successful struggle for autonomy from his father, King Thihathu of Pinya. Governed from the fortified city of Sagaing on the western bank of the Irrawaddy, the realm maintained a separate administration and defended its territory through decades of fierce court intrigues and external warfare. Sagaing was finally overwhelmed and sacked by northern Shan invaders from Maw in 1364, paving the way for the unification of central Myanmar under Ava. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sagaing; Common languages: Burmese and Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Myinsaing dynasty; Ruler title: King of Sagaing; Historical era: Burmese warring states; Preceded by: Kingdom of Pinya; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Ava

name: Khorasan
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: Khorasan functioned as a distinct autonomous dominion across northeastern Iran and western Afghanistan under the Ilkhanid prince Yasa'ur during the early fourteenth century. Granted territorial governance amidst internal rivalries in the Mongol Ilkhanate, Yasa'ur established a de facto independent princely state from Herat, commanding powerful nomadic armies and exacting revenue from major caravan hubs. The prince's political ambitions sparked conflict with both the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id and the neighbouring Chagatai Khanate, which led to his military defeat and death in 1320. \n\n Status: Autonomous princely domain; Capital: Herat; Common languages: Persian and Middle Mongol; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal appanage; Ruling dynasty: Ilkhanid dynasty; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ilkhanate; Succeeded by: Kart Dynasty

name: Lordship of Werle-Goldberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Werle-Goldberg was an autonomous north German feudal principality created in 1316 through the partition of the lands of the House of Werle. Ruled by a branch of the Obotrite princely line from the residential town of Goldberg, the lordship held immediate status under the Holy Roman Empire, overseeing agrarian communities and regional market centres. The territory retained its independent judicial and dynastic identity until the death of its last ruling lord in 1374, whereupon the estates were peacefully reunited with Werle-Güstrow. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Goldberg; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Werle; Ruler title: Lord of Werle-Goldberg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Lordship of Werle; Succeeded by: Lordship of Werle-Güstrow

name: Kingdom of Wala
description: The Kingdom of Wala was an established sovereign monarchy located in the savannah region of northwestern Ghana, centred upon the ancient trading settlement of Wa. Inhabited by Wala and Dagaaba communities, the state was governed by the Wa Naa alongside an influential Muslim scholarly and clerical hierarchy headed by a royal imam. Wala prospered through its control over northern gold and kola nut caravan routes until late nineteenth-century regional warfare and subsequent British colonial expansion absorbed the kingdom into the Northern Territories. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wa; Common languages: Waale; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wa Naa; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Commune of San Benigno
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of San Benigno was an autonomous civic community situated in the Canavese district of Piedmont along the Malone River. Originating under the feudal and ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the renowned Benedictine Abbey of Fruttuaria, the commune gradually asserted municipal liberties and self-governing privileges for its burghers. name: Signoria of Padua
label: holy roman empire

name: Duchy of Neopatras

name: Signoria of Carpi
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Carpi was an autonomous feudal lordship situated in the Emilia region of northern Italy, governed by the Pio di Savoia family. Operating under imperial immediacy from the fortified Castello dei Pio, the dynasty promoted agricultural drainage, textile production and Renaissance artistic patronage. name: Kingdom of Hokuzan

From the impregnable cliffside citadel of Nakijin Castle, the Haniji dynasty directed local chieftains and conducted seafaring trade with Ming China and southern Japan. Hokuzan maintained strict territorial independence against its southern rivals until King Shō Hashi of Chūzan led an allied invasion in 1416, storming the mountain fortress and annexing the northern realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nakijin; Common languages: Kunigami and Okinawan; Religion: Ryukyuan religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Haniji dynasty; Ruler title: King of Hokuzan; Historical era: Sanzan period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Chūzan

name: Roman Empire

Establishing his separatist court at Didymoteicho and Adrianople, Andronikos mobilised aristocratic support and reduced tax burdens to challenge his grandfather, Emperor Andronikos II in Constantinople. name: County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos

name: Bastar State

name: Kingdom of Pinya

Ruled by the sons of founder Saw Yun from their palisaded capital at Sagaing, the kingdom successfully checked Pinya's expansionist ambitions while patronising Buddhist monastic institutions. name: Reddi Kingdom

Established by Prolaya Vema Reddi and governed from strong hill fortresses at Addanki and Kondaveedu, the monarchy spearheaded a cultural renaissance by patronising Telugu literature, reviving Vedic institutions and rebuilding temples. name: Signoria of Mantua

description: The Signoria of Mantua was an autonomous northern Italian principality governed by the patrician House of Gonzaga, who seized civic control of the commune in 1328. Operating under imperial investiture as imperial vicars, the Gonzaga developed Mantua into an impregnable marshland bastion and a renowned capital of Renaissance art, music and chivalric culture. name: County of Reuss
label: holy roman empire

Held by the ancient House of Reuss, whose male heirs were traditionally named Heinrich in honour of Emperor Henry VI, the dominion exercised sovereign territorial jurisdiction from residential seats like Greiz and Gera. name: Kingdom of Georgia

Based at the historic capital of Tbilisi, the monarch maintained nominal subordination to the Mongol court while quietly suppressing rebellious mountain nobles and reunifying eastern and western Georgian lands. George V leveraged the decline of central Ilkhanid authority in the 1330s to expel foreign garrisons, restore the royal treasury and re-establish an independent united Christian empire. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Tbilisi; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi dynasty; Ruler title: King of Georgia; Head of state: George V the Brilliant; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Signoria of Campo Ligure
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Campo Ligure was an autonomous imperial fief positioned in the Stura Valley of the Ligurian Apennines northwest of Genoa. Held by branches of the prominent Spinola patrician dynasty under imperial immediacy, the lordship controlled essential overland mountain passes connecting the Ligurian seaboard with the Po Valley. name: Tenkasi Pandyas

Compelled southward after the sacking of Madurai by northern armies, the kings were crowned at the Kasi Viswanathar temple and governed from the royal seat of Tenkasi. name: Signoria of Fermo
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Fermo was a powerful autonomous city-state located in the southern Marche overlooking the Adriatic coast. Governed by elected despots and hereditary dynasts, notably the da Mogliano and Euffreducci families, the signoria commanded extensive hill territories and defended its civic jurisdiction from encroaching papal authorities. Fermo was characterised by active agricultural trade, textile crafts and vigorous military defences until internal aristocratic strife enabled the Papal States to establish direct administrative rule in the sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Fermo; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Dynastic signoria; Ruler title: Lord of Fermo; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Balliol Loyalists
description: The Balliol Loyalists were an Anglo-Scottish armed faction that mounted a military campaign during the Second War of Scottish Independence to place Edward Balliol on the Scottish throne. Operating without a fixed capital as a mobile army, the claimants invaded Scotland in August 1332 and achieved a stunning victory at the Battle of Dupplin Moor, leading to Balliol's coronation at Scone. Their authority quickly unravelled within months as Bruce loyalists reorganised, ambushed Balliol's camp at Annan and drove him across the English border before the year's end. \n\n Status: Contested royalist faction; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Mobile royal camp; Common languages: Middle English, Scots and Anglo-Norman; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military claimant regency; Head of state: Edward Balliol; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

name: Commune of Spigno
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Spigno was an autonomous municipal and feudal state situated in the Bormida Valley of southern Piedmont. Originally governed under communal charters by local burghers, the town soon came under the hereditary lordship of the Del Carretto noble family, who governed the territory as an imperial fief. The lords constructed defensive castles and maintained local toll rights along regional transit routes until later dynastic transfers brought the lordship under the Asinari family and ultimately the House of Savoy. \n\n Status: Imperial fief; Capital: Spigno Monferrato; Common languages: Piedmontese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Del Carretto; Ruler title: Lord of Spigno; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Duchy of Savoy

name: Yatenga
description: Yatenga was an independent Mossi kingdom established in the northern plains of modern Burkina Faso around the upper White Volta basin. Founded by Yadega, a breakaway prince of the royal house of Tenkodogo, the state developed an efficient cavalry army and a centralised court headed by the Yatenga Naba at Ouahigouya. The kingdom maintained extensive agricultural settlements, successfully checked nomadic Tuareg incursions from the Sahel and preserved its traditional animist institutions until French colonial forces conquered the kingdom in 1895. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ouahigouya; Common languages: Mossi; Religion: Traditional Mossi religion and Islam; Government: Centralised monarchy; Ruler title: Yatenga Naba; Historical era: Pre-colonial West Africa; Succeeded by: French Upper Volta

name: Signoria of Sarzana
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Sarzana was a fortified feudal domain located at the boundary of eastern Liguria and Tuscany along the Magra River. Holding a key defensive position near the Gulf of La Spezia, the city was governed by autonomous dynasts and military captains who leveraged its strategic road network between Genoa, Pisa and Florence. Sarzana defended its civic liberties against competing Italian powers through alternating protectorates until the Republic of Genoa established permanent suzerainty over the city in the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Feudal signoria; Capital: La Spezia; Common languages: Ligurian, Tuscan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord of Sarzana; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Sultanate of Madurai
description: The Sultanate of Madurai, also recorded as the Ma'bar Sultanate, was an independent Islamic state established in Tamil Nadu when the provincial governor Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan seceded from the Delhi Sultanate in 1335. Operating from the historic temple city of Madurai, the sultans minted their own coinage and maintained a militarised administration over the surrounding southern plains. The sultanate engaged in protracted conflicts with the Hoysala Kingdom and local Hindu rulers until Kumara Kampana led Vijayanagara forces to conquer the city in the late 1370s. \n\n Status: Regional sultanate; Capital: Madurai; Common languages: Persian, Hindustani and Tamil; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ahsan Shahi dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan of Madurai; Historical era: Medieval India; Preceded by: Delhi Sultanate; Succeeded by: Vijayanagara Empire

name: Injuid Dynasty
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: The Injuid Dynasty was an autonomous Persian princely realm that governed the historical provinces of Fars and Isfahan following the disintegration of the Ilkhanate. Descended from the imperial estate administrator Sharaf al-Din Mahmud Shah, the Injuids ruled from Shiraz and Isfahan, heavily patronising classical Persian literature and fine arts at their royal court. The dynasty engaged in recurrent warfare with neighbouring atabegs and rivals until the rival Muzaffarids defeated and executed the last Injuid ruler, Abu Ishaq, in 1357. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shiraz; Common languages: Persian and Middle Mongol; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Injuid dynasty; Ruler title: Shah; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ilkhanate; Succeeded by: Muzaffarids

name: Jalayirid Sultanate
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: The Jalayirid Sultanate was an influential Mongol successor state that ruled Iraq and western Iran following the collapse of the Ilkhanate. Founded by Hasan Buzurg of the Jalayir tribe and governed primarily from Baghdad and Tabriz, the dynasty blended Turco-Mongol military prowess with Persian administrative and literary culture. The sultanate dominated regional trade and patronised groundbreaking developments in Persian miniature painting until devastating campaigns by Timur and conflicts with the Qara Qoyunlu brought about its collapse. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Baghdad; Common languages: Persian, Middle Mongol and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jalayirid dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ilkhanate; Succeeded by: Timurid Empire

name: Kart Dynasty
