description: The Kart Dynasty, also known as the Kartids, was an autonomous Sunni Muslim monarchy of Tajik origin that governed central Khorasan from the city of Herat. Having served as loyal vassals under the Ghurids and the Ilkhanate, the dynasty asserted full sovereignty under Malik Mu'izz al-Din Husayn following the collapse of central Mongol rule in the 1330s. The Kartid court transformed Herat into a radiant centre of Persian scholarship and architecture until Timur invaded the region in 1381, terminating the dynasty's rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Herat; Common languages: Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kart dynasty; Ruler title: Malik; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ilkhanate; Succeeded by: Timurid Empire

name: Mihrabanids

description: The Mihrabanids were an indigenous Persian Muslim dynasty that governed the arid frontier kingdom of Sistan from their capital at Zaranj. Re-establishing autonomous rule in the Helmand River basin amidst the decline of the Ilkhanate, the maliks exercised authority over vital oasis irrigation works and caravan routes between Iran and India. The dynasty preserved its local sovereignty and cultural autonomy through diplomatic accommodation with larger neighbours until being subdued during the conquests of Timur in the 1380s. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Zaranj; Common languages: Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mihrabanid dynasty; Ruler title: Malik; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ilkhanate; Succeeded by: Timurid Empire

name: Muzaffarids
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: The Muzaffarids were an influential Muslim dynasty that came to dominate central Persia, Fars and Iranian Azerbaijan following the fragmentation of the Ilkhanate. Founded by Mubariz al-Din Muhammad and ruled from the cultural capitals of Yazd, Kerman and Shiraz, the monarchy fostered an extraordinary flowering of Arabic and Persian literature, closely patronising poets such as Hafez. Governed through regional customary laws known as the Fors de Béarn, the principality flourished as a stable administrative and commercial sanctuary until entering a personal union with the Kingdom of Navarre. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Morlaàs; Common languages: Gascon and Basque; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Foix-Béarn; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 25 September 1347; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Navarre

name: Kingdom of Hungary (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Hungary maintained temporary military occupation administrations over captured foreign territories during offensive campaigns launched by the Angevins and King Matthias Corvinus. Notably including the Neapolitan expedition of Louis I in 1347 and later incursions into Moravia, Silesia and lower Austria, these martial zones were governed directly by appointed royal captains and garrison commanders. Established without a permanent civil seat, the occupations served to extract indemnity payments and project Hungarian royal power before being resolved by formal peace accords. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile royal military command; Common languages: Hungarian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Royal military administration; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Naples; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Naples

name: Bahmani Sultanate
description: The Bahmani Sultanate was the first independent Muslim empire on the Deccan Plateau of southern India, established in 1347 following the successful revolt of Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah against the Delhi Sultanate. Administered initially from Gulbarga and later from Bidar, the sultanate integrated Persian administrative models with local Deccani traditions and constructed impressive monumental fortresses and madrasas. Prolonged conflicts with the neighbouring Vijayanagara Empire and intractable factionalism between Deccani and immigrant Afaqi nobles eventually fractured the realm into the five Deccan Sultanates. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Gulbarga; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Deccani, Marathi, Kannada and Telugu; Religion: Sunni Islam and Shia Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bahmani dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Medieval India; Disestablished: 1528; Succeeded by: Deccan Sultanates

name: Menceyato of Tenerife
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Tenerife was a unified indigenous Guanche kingdom that exercised supreme authority across the entire island of Tenerife in the Canary archipelago. Governed by a paramount king known as the Mencey from the fertile valley of La Laguna, the society was structured around pastoral transhumance, clan councils and traditional stone-age craftsmanship. Following the death of the revered monarch Tinerfe the Great around the end of the fourteenth century, the realm was partitioned among his nine sons into rival independent menceyatos. \n\n Status: Native kingdom; Capital: San Cristóbal de La Laguna; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1348; Disestablished: 1401; Succeeded by: Tenerife Menceyatos

name: Moghulistan
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: Moghulistan was a Turco-Mongol khanate that emerged in the mid-fourteenth century across the eastern domains of the fractured Chagatai Khanate, encompassing the Ili basin, the Tian Shan mountains and the Tarim Basin. Founded under Tughluq Timur Khan, the state maintained nomadic steppe traditions while adopting Islam and establishing its administrative encampment near Almaliq. The khanate contended with relentless campaigns launched by Timur and suffered chronic internal strife between Chinggisid dynasts and powerful Dughlat emirs, eventually splintering into the regional khanates of Turpan and Yarkent. \n\n Status: Khanate; Capital: Almaliq; Common languages: Chagatai Turkic and Middle Mongol; Religion: Sunni Islam and Tengrism; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chagatai dynasty; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1348; Succeeded by: Turpan Khanate

name: Pagaruyung Kingdom
description: The Pagaruyung Kingdom was an ancient Minangkabau monarchy based in the fertile highlands of central Sumatra, founded by King Adityawarman in the mid-fourteenth century as a successor to Malayapura. Blending Buddhist-Hindu sacral authority with traditional matrilineal adat customs, the realm controlled vital gold mines and upland agricultural basins while projecting spiritual suzerainty across the island. The kingdom gradually embraced Islam in the sixteenth century, maintaining its venerable prestige until political turmoil during the Padri War precipitated Dutch colonial intervention. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Pagaruyung; Common languages: Minangkabau, Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja-Diraja; Historical era: Post-classical to Early Modern; Established: 1348; Disestablished: 1834; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Karauli State
description: Karauli State was a sovereign Rajput principality established in eastern Rajasthan within the cultural sphere of the Braj region. Founded in 1348 by Arjun Dev Pal of the ancient Jadaun Rajput clan, who claimed descent from Krishna, the state developed from a fortified bastion along the rocky banks of the Bhadravati River into an important religious and commercial centre. Karauli maintained its autonomy through shifting tributary relations with the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughals and the Marathas before concluding a protective alliance with the British in 1817. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Karauli; Common languages: Braj Bhasha and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadaun dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern India; Established: 1349; Disestablished: 1818

name: Lord Pskov
label: russian principalities
description: Lord Pskov was an autonomous medieval Russian merchant republic located on the southern shores of Lake Peipus and along the Velikaya River. Having achieved formal independence from the Novgorod Republic through the Treaty of Bolotovo in 1348, the city-state was governed by a popular assembly known as the veche, an elected posadnik and invited military princes. The republic developed an advanced judicial code and fortified its borders against the Livonian Order, flourishing as a sovereign trading power until gravitating toward Muscovite political protection. \n\n Status: Republic; Capital: Pskov; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Merchant republic; Legislature: Veche; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1348; Preceded by: Novgorod Republic; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Tlaxcala Confederacy
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Tlaxcala Confederacy was an independent Nahua republican alliance in the central Mexican highlands, composed of four allied city-states comprising Tepeticpac, Ocotelolco, Tizatlan and Quiahuiztlan. Completely encircled by the Aztec Empire, the confederacy resisted repeated imperial invasions during bitter Flower Wars and sustained its political liberty through a collective governing council of noble lords. In October 1519, following initial clashes, Tlaxcalan leadership formed a historic military alliance with Hernan Cortes that proved instrumental in the overthrow of Tenochtitlan. \n\n Status: Indigenous confederacy; Capital: Tlaxcala; Common languages: Classical Nahuatl and Otomi; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Aristocratic confederation; Ruler title: Tlatoani; Historical era: Mesoamerican Postclassic; Established: 1349; Disestablished: 1 October 1519; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Afrasiyab Dynasty
description: The Afrasiyab Dynasty was a local Shia Iranian ruling house that governed Tabaristan in the Caspian littoral province of Mazandaran following the overthrow of the Bavand dynasty in 1349. Established by Kiya Afrasiyab, the dynasty held fortresses across the forested slopes of the Alborz mountains and administered regional towns including Amol and Firuzkuh. The realm frequently clashed with rival sayyid movements, particularly the Marashis, before the dynasty was definitively extinguished during the northward consolidation of the Safavid Empire under Shah Ismail I. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Amol; Common languages: Mazanderani and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chalavi dynasty; Ruler title: Kiya; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1349; Disestablished: 1505; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: County of Waldeck
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Waldeck was an imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the hilly uplands between the Eder and Diemel rivers in present-day Hesse. Having secured imperial immediacy from Emperor Charles IV in 1349, the counts of the House of Waldeck governed their agrarian territory from the fortified ancestral seat of Waldeck Castle. The county maintained its autonomous standing across centuries of regional dynastic conflict, embraced the Protestant Reformation in the sixteenth century and established a new administrative capital at Arolsen. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Waldeck, later Arolsen; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Waldeck; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1350; Reorganised: 1693

name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
description: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was a powerful Siamese mandala monarchy founded in 1351 by King Uthong on an island at the confluence of the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak and Lopburi rivers. Developing from a regional trading polity into one of the paramount commercial and military empires of Southeast Asia, Ayutthaya subjugated Angkor, assimilated the northern kingdom of Sukhothai and engaged in extensive maritime commerce with Asia and Europe. The kingdom maintained remarkable cultural and political vitality until its capital was captured and destroyed by Burmese forces in 1767. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Ayutthaya; Common languages: Thai; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Uthong dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Post-classical to Early Modern; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 7 April 1767; Succeeded by: Thonburi Kingdom

name: Batibo
description: Batibo was an autonomous precolonial fondom situated in the Western Grassfields of modern Cameroon, serving as the political and spiritual heartland of the Moghamo-speaking Widikum people. Administered by a hereditary Fon supported by customary title societies and lineage elders, the state prospered along strategic trading paths linking the coastal forest belts with the western savannah. Batibo sustained its agrarian independence and indigenous cultural institutions for over five centuries until the progressive imposition of German colonial rule in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Batibo; Common languages: Moghamo; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Kamerun

name: Bima Kingdom
description: The Bima Kingdom was an influential pre-Islamic maritime principality located on the eastern peninsula of Sumbawa in the Lesser Sunda Islands. Governed by native rulers styled Sangaji from their port settlement at Bima Bay, the kingdom controlled vital shipping lanes and derived substantial revenue from the export of sappanwood, sandalwood, beeswax and island horses. The realm maintained political autonomy and cultural links with neighbouring Makassarese and Javanese kingdoms until 1621, when its monarch embraced Islam and transformed the polity into a sultanate. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Bima; Common languages: Bima; Religion: Animism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sangaji; Historical era: Pre-Islamic Indonesian era; Established: 1351; Reorganised: 1621; Succeeded by: Bima Sultanate

name: Dang
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Dang was an autonomous petty kingdom situated in the fertile inner Terai valley of southwestern Nepal, surrounded by the Mahabharata Range and the Siwalik Hills. Counted among the historic Baise and Chaubisi rajyas, the state was ruled by Khas-Rajput princes who fostered vibrant regional traditions and patronised holy pilgrimage centres associated with the Nath Hindu monastic movement. The kingdom maintained its separate identity and local feudal governance until it was conquered and integrated into a unified Nepal during the Gorkha expansion in the 1760s. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Dang; Common languages: Khas and Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern Nepal; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1761; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Dompu Kingdom
description: The Dompu Kingdom was an autonomous island principality situated in the central lowlands of Sumbawa in the Indonesian archipelago, bounded by Saleh Bay and Cempi Bay. Centred on the fertile inland basin around Dompu, the kingdom commanded rich agricultural lands and engaged in maritime commerce involving timber, horse breeding and regional spice transhipment. The realm guarded its sovereignty against expanding neighbouring powers such as Gowa and Bima before entering formal tributary relations with the Dutch East India Company at the turn of the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Dompu; Common languages: Bima and Dompu; Religion: Animism, later Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1700

name: Kingdom of Amber
description: The Kingdom of Amber was a prominent Rajput principality situated in the historical Dhundhar region of eastern Rajasthan, ruled by the Kachwaha Rajput clan from the fortified hillside citadel of Amber. Rising to immense influence during the sixteenth century, the kingdom forged strategic matrimonial and military alliances with the Mughal emperors, providing leading imperial commanders such as Raja Man Singh I. The state flourished culturally and commercially until 1727, when Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II established the planned city of Jaipur as the kingdom's new capital. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Amber; Common languages: Dhundari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kachwaha dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern India; Established: 1351; Reorganised: 1728; Succeeded by: Jaipur State

name: Nagar State
description: Nagar State was an independent mountain principality located in the Karakoram range of present-day Gilgit-Baltistan, nestled along the southern bank of the Hunza River. Governed by the Maglot dynasty with the title of Mir from the fortified capital of Nagarkhas, the Burusho state controlled difficult glacial valleys and maintained strategic trade connections across the alpine passes into Central Asia. Long engaged in traditional rivalry with the neighbouring kingdom of Hunza, Nagar retained complete sovereignty until its subjugation by British-led forces during the Hunza-Nagar Campaign of 1891. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Nagarkhas; Common languages: Burushaski and Shina; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Maglot dynasty; Ruler title: Mir; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern Central Asia; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1892

name: Oghara
description: Oghara was an autonomous precolonial Urhobo kingdom located in the western Niger Delta along the Ethiope River in modern southern Nigeria. Comprising allied settlements including Ogharefe and Oghareki, the polity was governed by a traditional monarch known as the Ovie together with a council of titled community elders. The kingdom developed a flourishing economy anchored in fishing, hunting, regional riverine commerce and palm cultivation, sustaining its sovereign independence until being incorporated into wider regional networks influenced by the expanding Kingdom of Benin. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Oghara-Efe; Common languages: Urhobo; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ovie; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1471; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Benin

name: Phaltan State
description: Phaltan State was an autonomous Maratha principality situated along the upper Banganga River basin in the Deccan plateau of western India. Founded by the Nimbalkar Maratha clan, the state governed its agrarian territories from the historic market and fortress town of Phaltan. The ruling family preserved remarkable local authority and military renown across centuries of political transformation under the Bahmanis, the Bijapur Sultanate and the Maratha Empire, maintaining unbroken dynastic autonomy until entering British paramountcy during the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Phaltan; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nimbalkar dynasty; Ruler title: Naik Nimbalkar; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern India; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1851

name: Principality of Konin
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Konin was a small medieval Russian appanage principality situated along the upper reaches of the Oka River basin. Emerging from the territorial fragmentation of the Upper Oka dynastic lands, the realm was governed by a cadet branch of the Rurikid house from its fortified seat at Koninskoe. The principality balanced cautiously between the growing territorial ambitions of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Grand Principality of Moscow before losing its separate political existence in the mid-fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Koninskoe; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1451; Historical region: Upper Oka

name: Principality of Mosalsk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Mosalsk was an autonomous feudal appanage in the upper Oka basin of western Rus, formed following the division of the Principality of Karachev. Ruled by the Princes Mosalsky, a branch of the Rurikid dynasty, the state held sway over the forested basin of the Mozhayka River from the fortified town of Mosalsk. Occupying a perilous frontier between rival eastern Slavic powers, the principality maintained sovereignty through the late fourteenth century before being absorbed into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Mosalsk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1401; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Obdorsk
label: yugra principalities;russian principalities
description: The Principality of Obdorsk was an indigenous Khanty state situated along the lower Ob River and the Arctic tundra of northwestern Siberia. Headed by native hereditary princes from the fortified settlement of Pulvonat-vosh, situated near modern Salekhard, the principality commanded lucrative trade in arctic furs, walrus ivory and fish across the polar Ural passes. The realm preserved complete autonomy through the medieval era, resisting Novgorod and early Muscovite expeditions until accepting tributary vassalage and administrative incorporation into the Russian Empire in the seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Indigenous principality; Capital: Pulvonat-vosh; Common languages: Khanty and Old East Slavic; Religion: Shamanism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1610; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia

name: Principality of Spazh
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Spazh was a minor feudal Russian realm established within the upper Oka river basin south of Kaluga. Formed as an appanage among the Upper Oka princes descended from the Chernigov branch of the Rurikids, the principality maintained its administrative stronghold at Spash. The rulers governed local agricultural communities and secured woodland trade corridors, retaining their autonomy until expanding Muscovite influence and Lithuanian border pressures led to the territory's absorption in the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Spash; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1451; Historical region: Upper Oka

name: Principality of Volkona
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Volkona was a medieval Russian appanage located in the upper Oka basin along the Volkona River near Kozelsk. Ruled by the Volkonsky branch of the Rurikid dynasty, the small realm originated from the fragmentation of the Grand Principality of Chernigov and maintained its fortified court at Volkona. The principality preserved independent local jurisdiction for over a century, navigating complex feudal loyalties between Lithuania and Moscow before being formally integrated into the centralised Muscovite state. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Volkona; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1471; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Sang Hyang Api
description: Sang Hyang Api was an autonomous island principality centred on the active volcanic island of Sangeang, situated northeast of Sumbawa in the Flores Sea. Attested in classical fourteenth-century Javanese chronicles such as the Nagarakretagama, the realm occupied a strategic maritime vantage along eastern Indonesian trade routes between Java and the Maluku Islands. Governed by local maritime chieftains, the island polity engaged in coastal trading, fishing and subsistence agriculture until being subordinated by regional sultanates and Dutch commercial dominance around 1700. \n\n Status: Maritime principality; Capital: Sangeang; Common languages: Bima; Religion: Animism and Hinduism; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1700; Historical region: Lesser Sunda Islands

name: Sape Kingdom
description: The Sape Kingdom was an independent coastal polity situated around Sape Bay at the eastern extremity of Sumbawa in the Lesser Sunda Islands. Guarding the vital Sape Strait that connected the Flores Sea with the Indian Ocean, the kingdom derived substantial wealth from maritime pilotage, provisioning trading fleets and exporting valuable local forest products. The kingdom governed its coastal and valley communities under traditional customary law until expanding Makassarese hegemony and Dutch trade restrictions absorbed the area into the Bima regional sphere. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Sape; Common languages: Bima; Religion: Animism, later Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Pre-colonial Indonesia; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1700; Succeeded by: Bima Sultanate

name: Sultanate of Kano
label: hausa states
description: The Sultanate of Kano was a powerful Hausa Islamic monarchy centred on the fortified commercial metropolis of Kano in northern Nigeria. Transitioning from traditional animist governance to an Islamic sultanate during the fourteenth-century reign of Sarki Yaji I, the state emerged as the premier mercantile, textile and craft emporium of the trans-Saharan trade network. Kano developed sophisticated bureaucratic and fiscal institutions that sustained its regional pre-eminence for centuries until the Fulani jihad led by Usman dan Fodio overthrew the dynasty in 1807. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Kano; Common languages: Hausa, Fulfulde and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sarki; Legislature: Taran Kano; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1351; Disestablished: 1808; Succeeded by: Kano Emirate

name: Free Imperial City of Dinkelsbühl
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Dinkelsbühl was an autonomous urban republic within the Holy Roman Empire, located along the Wörnitz River in Middle Franconia. Attaining imperial immediacy in 1351, the city was administered by a guild-dominated municipal council that oversaw robust cloth manufacturing and protected the settlement with an extensive ring of stone fortifications. Dinkelsbühl preserved its constitutional independence and civic liberties through centuries of regional warfare, including the Thirty Years' War, until mediatisation annexed the city to Bavaria in 1802. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Dinkelsbühl; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1352; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Marquisate of Bagnone
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Bagnone was an autonomous imperial fief situated in the Lunigiana region of northwestern Tuscany, nestled beneath the ridge of Monte Sillara along the Bagnone torrent. Governed by a branch of the Malaspina family following a dynastic partition in 1351, the marquisate controlled key upland tracks and levied tolls on traffic passing between the Tuscan coast and the Po Valley. The independent fief endured for a century until dynastic crises and economic pressures prompted its transfer to the Florentine Republic in 1452. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bagnone; Common languages: Italian and Tuscan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Malaspina; Ruler title: Marquess; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1352; Disestablished: 1452; Succeeded by: Republic of Florence

name: Marquisate of Treschietto
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Treschietto was a small imperial fief in the upper Lunigiana of northern Tuscany, situated along the Acquetta stream near the Apennine watershed. Established following the division of the Malaspina lands of Filattiera in 1351, the state was ruled by the Spino Fiorito branch of the Malaspina dynasty from their formidable stone castle perched above Treschietto. The marquisate maintained judicial immediacy and feudal prerogatives for nearly three centuries until the last marquis sold the territory to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in 1699. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Treschietto; Common languages: Italian and Tuscan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Malaspina; Ruler title: Marquess; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1352; Disestablished: 1699; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Tuscany

name: Samma Dynasty
description: The Samma Dynasty was a medieval Sindhi Muslim ruling house that governed Sindh from the mid-fourteenth century until the early sixteenth century. Establishing independent authority after overthrowing the Soomras and expelling the governors of the Delhi Sultanate, the rulers assumed the royal title of Jam and ruled from their illustrious capital at Thatta. The dynasty oversaw an era of agricultural prosperity, thriving Indian Ocean commerce and splendid architectural patronisation at Makli Hill, maintaining sovereignty until the kingdom was conquered by the Arghun dynasty in 1521. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Thatta; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Sindhi and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Samma dynasty; Ruler title: Jam; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1352; Disestablished: 1521; Succeeded by: Arghun dynasty

name: Bengal Sultanate
description: The Bengal Sultanate was a powerful and prosperous Islamic empire based in the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta of eastern South Asia. Founded by Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, who unified the regional divisions of Lakhnauti, Sonargaon and Satgaon, the sultanate maintained complete independence from Delhi and administered its wealthy realm from royal capitals at Pandua and Gaur. The state fostered maritime trade across the Indian Ocean, patronised both Bengali literature and Persian courtly culture, and remained a dominant regional power until its final conquest by Mughal armies under Akbar. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Gaur; Official languages: Bengali and Persian; Common languages: Bengali, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ilyas Shahi dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1353; Disestablished: 12 July 1576; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin was an imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the southwestern Baltic Sea littoral. Created following the territorial division of the House of Mecklenburg in 1352, the duchy was ruled by the Nikloting dynasty from its island palace at Schwerin and commanded extensive agricultural lands, inland waterways and coastal commerce. The state experienced recurring partitions and reunions with neighbouring Mecklenburg territories, successfully preserving its imperial immediacy until its elevation to a grand duchy at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Schwerin; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Mecklenburg; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Established: 1353; Reorganised: 14 June 1815; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin

name: Duchy of Mecklenburg-Stargard
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Mecklenburg-Stargard was a feudal principality of the Holy Roman Empire established in southeastern Mecklenburg through the dynastic partition of 1352. Governed by Duke John I and his successors from the high brick castle of Burg Stargard, the state encompassed the historical Lordship of Stargard, Sternberg and neighbouring borderlands adjacent to Brandenburg and Pomerania. The ducal house administered local agrarian estates and maintained internal peace until the death of Duke Ulrich II in 1471, whereupon the lands were reunited with Mecklenburg-Schwerin. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Burg Stargard; Common languages: Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Mecklenburg; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1353; Disestablished: 1472; Succeeded by: Duchy of Mecklenburg

name: Ramadanid Emirate
description: The Ramadanid Emirate was an autonomous Turkoman principality established in Cilicia following the collapse of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia in the mid-fourteenth century. Founded by Ramazan Bey of the Yüreğir Oghuz tribe and ruled from the historic city of Adana, the emirate operated under the suzerainty and military protection of the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo. Controlling the vital Cilician Gates and fertile agricultural plains, the dynasty governed the region autonomously until Ottoman victories over the Mamluks brought Cilicia under direct imperial Ottoman rule. \n\n Status: Protectorate; Capital: Adana; Common languages: Ottoman Turkish and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Ramadanid dynasty; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1353; Disestablished: 1516; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire during this brief period comprised the factional regime governed by Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos during the renewal of the Byzantine civil wars. Basing his military authority across loyal fortresses in Thrace and along the Dardanelles, Kantakouzenos struggled to maintain administrative control against his co-emperor John V Palaiologos while relying increasingly on Ottoman mercenary contingents. Following devastating earthquakes and the loss of Gallipoli to Turkish forces in 1354, Kantakouzenos was forced from power in Constantinople and retired to a monastery under the monastic name Joasaph. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Thracian mobile court; Common languages: Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Kantakouzenos dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1353; Disestablished: 1 April 1354

name: Kingdom of Lan Xang
description: The Kingdom of Lan Xang was a major Southeast Asian mandala monarchy founded in 1354 by King Fa Ngum, unifying disparate Lao river polities across the upper and middle Mekong basin. Governed initially from the royal seat at Luang Phrabang, the realm adopted Theravada Buddhism as its state religion and enshrined the sacred Phra Bang Buddha image as its national palladium. Lan Xang developed into a dominant trade and political power, maintaining regional integrity through shifting wars with Burma and Siam until dynastic partition fractured the state in 1707. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Luang Phrabang; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Khun Lo dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1354; Disestablished: 1708; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang

name: Oiniwar Dynasty
description: The Oiniwar Dynasty was an autonomous Maithil monarchy that ruled the historic Mithila region of northern Bihar from the mid-fourteenth century until the early sixteenth century. Established by Kameshwar Thakur following the decline of the Karnat dynasty, the kingdom governed fertile alluvial plains between the Himalayas and the Ganges from centres such as Madhubani and Sugauna. The court was celebrated as a premier centre of Sanskrit scholarship, Hindu jurisprudence and vernacular Maithili literature under the patronage of rulers like King Shiva Simha and the poet Vidyapati. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Madhubani; Common languages: Maithili and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Oiniwar dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1354; Disestablished: 1527; Succeeded by: Bengal Sultanate

name: Sultanate of Delhi (Military Occupation)
description: The Sultanate of Delhi maintained temporary military occupation zones across frontier regions during the early reign of Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq. Following military expeditions directed against breakaway sultanates in Bengal and insubordinate tributaries in eastern and southern India, imperial garrisons temporarily occupied critical river crossings and provincial forts without creating lasting civil administrations. Administered directly by appointed military governors, these garrisons extracted tribute and secured regional roads before formal treaties or logistical strains compelled the royal armies to withdraw to the Delhi heartland. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Imperial field command; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Hindustani and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military administration; Ruling dynasty: Tughlaq dynasty; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1354; Disestablished: 1371

name: Duchy of Luxembourg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Luxembourg was an important state of the Holy Roman Empire, elevated from a county in March 1354 by Emperor Charles IV in favour of his half-brother Wenceslaus I. Centred on the formidable cliff-top fortress of Luxembourg City, the duchy served as the ancestral base for the imperial House of Luxembourg, which simultaneously held the crowns of Bohemia, Germany and Hungary. The state exercised significant strategic influence across the Low Countries and the Meuse basin until financial indebtedness and dynastic exhaustion led to its cession to the Valois Dukes of Burgundy. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Luxembourg; Common languages: Luxembourgish, German and Old French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Luxembourg; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 13 March 1354; Succeeded by: Burgundian Netherlands

name: Duchy of Bar
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Bar was an autonomous principality straddling the borderlands of the Holy Roman Empire and the Kingdom of France, centred on the ducal castle of Bar-le-Duc along the Ornain River. Elevated from a county in 1354 by Emperor Charles IV for Robert I, the state occupied a delicate jurisdictional position, with western districts owing feudal homage to the French crown while eastern territories retained imperial immediacy. The duchy maintained robust independent governance and judicial institutions until entering a personal union with the neighbouring Duchy of Lorraine in 1420. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bar-le-Duc; Common languages: French and Lorrain; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Montbéliard; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1355; Reorganised: 1420; Succeeded by: Duchy of Lorraine

name: Free Imperial City of Munster
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Munster was an autonomous urban republic situated in the Fecht Valley of upper Alsace at the foot of the Vosges Mountains. Having originated around an ancient Benedictine abbey, the burghers obtained imperial immediacy and joined the Décapole league of Alsatian imperial cities in 1354 to safeguard their communal liberties. The town council governed local commerce, pastoral trade and wine production with complete civic independence until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 placed the Décapole cities under the sovereignty of the French Crown. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Munster; Common languages: Alsatian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Protestantism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1355; Disestablished: 24 October 1648; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Free Imperial City of Wissembourg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Wissembourg was an autonomous city-state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in northern Alsace along the Lauter River. Developing out of a secular dispute between the local urban commune and the wealthy Prince-Abbey of Wissembourg, the town secured imperial immediacy and became a prominent member of the Alsatian Décapole league in 1354. Governed by an elected magistrate and municipal council, Wissembourg thrived as a textile and viticultural centre until its autonomy was superseded by the Kingdom of France under the Peace of Westphalia. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Wissembourg; Common languages: Alsatian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1355; Disestablished: 17 May 1648; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Phagmodrupa Dynasty
description: The Phagmodrupa Dynasty was the pre-eminent ruling regime of Tibet from the mid-fourteenth century to the early seventeenth century, founded by Tai Situ Changchub Gyaltsen of the Lang clan. Overthrowing the Mongol-backed Sakya hegemony in 1354, the dynasty established its administrative capital at Nedong in the Yarlung Valley and enacted comprehensive legal, military and cultural reforms rooted in classical Tibetan traditions. The dynasty presided over a renaissance of Tibetan Buddhist learning and literature, retaining paramount authority until internal noble rivalries facilitated the rise of the Rinpungpa and Tsangpa dynasties. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Nedong; Common languages: Classical Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lang clan; Ruler title: Desi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1355; Disestablished: 1614; Succeeded by: Tsangpa Dynasty

name: Marquisate of Tresana
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Tresana was an independent imperial fief in the rugged Lunigiana region of northwestern Tuscany, nestled along the Osca torrent near the Magra River. Ruled by a branch of the Malaspina family from the commanding four-sided stone tower of Castello di Tresana, the small principality maintained territorial immediacy under the Holy Roman Empire. The marquisate preserved its feudal privileges, judiciary and border tolls amidst rivalries between Florence, Genoa and Milan until the arrival of revolutionary French armies led to its abolition in 1797. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Tresana; Common languages: Italian and Tuscan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Malaspina; Ruler title: Marquess; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1356; Disestablished: 17 October 1797

name: Principality of Mataranga
label: albanian principalities;serbian principalities
description: The Principality of Mataranga was a short-lived medieval Albanian realm established in the Myzeqe coastal plains between the Shkumbin and Seman rivers. Following the death of Serbian Emperor Stefan Dušan in 1355, the local lord Blasius Mataranga secured de facto sovereignty, bearing the Byzantine court dignity of sevastokrator and maintaining diplomatic ties with the Republic of Ragusa. Governed from the fortified seat of Pirgu, the principality controlled prosperous agrarian lowlands and lagoon fisheries until being partitioned by the neighbouring Thopia and Muzaka principalities in 1367. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Pirgu; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Mataranga family; Ruler title: Sevastokrator; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1356; Disestablished: 1368; Succeeded by: Principality of Albania

name: Principality of Valona
label: albanian principalities;serbian principalities
description: The Principality of Valona was an autonomous medieval state in southwestern Albania, encompassing the strategic coastline and hinterlands of Vlorë, Kaninë, Fier and Berat. Emerging as an independent lordship following the disintegration of the Serbian Empire in 1355, the state was ruled successively by the Asen dynasty and Balša II, who exploited maritime commerce along the Strait of Otranto. Maintaining diplomatic ties with Venice and Ragusa while patronising Orthodox foundations, the principality defended its shores against regional rivals until falling to the Ottoman Turks in 1417. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Vlorë; Common languages: Albanian, Medieval Greek and Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Asen dynasty; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1356; Disestablished: 1418; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Electorate of Saxony
label: holy roman empire
description: The Electorate of Saxony was a premier secular principality of the Holy Roman Empire, confirmed in its prince-electoral dignity by Emperor Charles IV through the Golden Bull of 1356. Initially governed by the House of Ascania from Wittenberg on the Elbe River, the electoral dignity and territories passed to the Margraves of Meissen from the House of Wettin in 1423. The electorate exercised decisive political influence within imperial councils, sustained prosperous silver mining in the Ore Mountains and remained a major European power until the dynastic Division of Leipzig in 1485. \n\n Status: Electorate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Wittenberg; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ascania, later House of Wettin; Ruler title: Prince-Elector; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 10 January 1356; Reorganised: 11 November 1485

name: Despotate of Dobruja
description: The Despotate of Dobruja was an autonomous medieval Bulgarian-Byzantine principality located in the coastal region between the lower Danube River and the Black Sea. Seceding from the Second Bulgarian Empire in the mid-fourteenth century under the magnate Balik and his brother Dobrotitsa, the realm established its maritime capitals at Karvuna and the fortified promontory of Kaliakra. The despotate fielded a formidable galley fleet, engaged in commercial rivalries with Genoa and Venice, and resisted expanding Ottoman armies until the definitive Turkish conquest of the fortress of Kaliakra. \n\n Status: Despotate; Capital: Kaliakra; Common languages: Middle Bulgarian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Terter dynasty cadet branch; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1357; Disestablished: 10 November 1444; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Duchy of Jülich
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Jülich was an autonomous territorial state of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Rur River between the Meuse and the Rhine. Elevated from a margraviate to a duchy by Emperor Charles IV in 1356, the realm was governed by the House of Jülich from its ancient fortified capital of Jülich. The dukes expanded their influence across the Rhineland through military campaigns, toll collection and regional matrimonial alliances, maintaining sovereign independence until the duchy amalgamated with the neighbouring County of Berg in 1423. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Jülich; Common languages: Middle Dutch and Ripuarian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Jülich; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1357; Disestablished: 1424; Succeeded by: United Duchies of Jülich-Berg

name: Empire of the Serbs and Greeks
description: The Empire of the Serbs and Greeks was a breakaway Balkan imperial realm centred in Thessaly and southern Epirus, established by Despot Simeon Uroš Nemanjić following the death of his half-brother Emperor Stefan Dušan. Proclaiming himself rival emperor in opposition to Stefan Uroš V, Simeon ruled from the fortified citadel of Trikala, governing a multi-ethnic populace of Greeks, Serbs, Albanians and Vlachs through a conciliatory Byzantine administrative style. Following Simeon's death in 1370, his son Jovan Uroš ruled briefly before abdicating to become a monk at Meteora. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Trikala; Common languages: Medieval Greek and Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nemanjić dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1357; Disestablished: 1372; Succeeded by: Despotate of Epirus

name: Lordship of Wiesensteig
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Wiesensteig was an autonomous imperial territory in Swabia, situated in the upper Fils valley amidst the steep terrain of the Swabian Jura. Ruled by the noble Counts of Helfenstein following a dynastic inheritance partition in 1356, the lordship was administered from the town of Wiesensteig and the commanding castle of Helfenstein. The state preserved its imperial immediacy and Catholic faith during the Reformation, maintaining autonomous feudal courts and forestry revenues until the extinction of the male Helfenstein line in 1627 led to its division. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Wiesensteig; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Helfenstein; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1357; Disestablished: 1643; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Tsardom of Vidin
description: The Tsardom of Vidin was an autonomous medieval Bulgarian state established along the southern bank of the Danube River in northwestern Bulgaria. Created when Tsar Ivan Alexander granted the western appanage to his eldest son Ivan Sratsimir, the realm seceded from the central court at Tarnovo and operated as an independent tsardom from the fortified fortress of Baba Vida in Vidin. The state controlled crucial river trade between the Balkans and Central Europe, surviving Hungarian occupation and Ottoman vassalage before being finally conquered by Ottoman forces following the Battle of Nicopolis. \n\n Status: Tsardom; Capital: Vidin; Common languages: Middle Bulgarian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shishman dynasty; Ruler title: Tsar; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1357; Disestablished: 1398; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Crown of Castile (Military Occupation)
description: The Crown of Castile instituted temporary military occupation zones across neighbouring Iberian territories during prolonged dynastic conflicts, notably the War of the Two Peters against the Crown of Aragon and campaigns against Portugal. Administered by royal field captains, adelantados and frontier garrisons, these occupied sectors lacked established civil councils and operated under strict martial law to secure strategic strongholds and extract resources. These wartime occupations terminated upon the cessation of hostilities through formal peace treaties, territorial exchanges or military retreats. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile royal army headquarters; Common languages: Old Spanish and Aragonese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Royal military administration; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Crown of Aragon; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon

name: Republic of Ragusa
label: maritime republics
description: The Republic of Ragusa was an autonomous aristocratic maritime republic centred on the fortified Adriatic port city of Dubrovnik in southern Dalmatia. Following the Treaty of Zadar in 1358, the republic threw off Venetian domination and accepted the nominal suzerainty and protection of King Louis I of Hungary while preserving absolute internal self-government. Governed by a Major Council, Senate and an elected Rector, Ragusa built an extensive merchant fleet, traded freely between Christian Europe and the Ottoman Balkans, and flourished as a beacon of diplomatic neutrality. \n\n Status: Client republic; Capital: Dubrovnik; Common languages: Ragusan Dalmatian, Old Croatian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Legislature: Major Council; Ruler title: Rector; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 18 February 1358; Disestablished: 1459

name: Despotate of Angelokastron and Lepanto
label: albanian principalities
description: The Despotate of Angelokastron and Lepanto was a short-lived medieval Albanian principality established across Aetolia and Acarnania in western Greece following the defeat of Nikephoros II Orsini at the Battle of Achelous in 1359. Founded by the Albanian chieftain Gjin Bua Shpata and formally recognised by Simeon Uroš, the state was administered from the fortified hill castle of Angelokastron and the port of Lepanto. The despotate defended its territory against rival Frankish and Greek dynasts until Shpata incorporated Arta into his realm, consolidating the lands into a unified state. \n\n Status: Despotate; Capital: Nafpaktos; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shpata family; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1359; Disestablished: 1375; Succeeded by: Despotate of Arta

name: Free Imperial City of Seltz
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Seltz was an autonomous municipal republic situated along the confluence of the Sauer and Rhine rivers in northern Alsace. Granted imperial immediacy by Emperor Charles IV in the 1350s, the town joined the Décapole league of Alsatian imperial cities in 1358 to safeguard its communal rights against the neighbouring Prince-Abbey of Seltz. The municipal council managed river trade and regional agrarian markets until financial indebtedness and imperial pawnings caused the city to lose its immediacy and pass under the control of the Electoral Palatinate in 1419. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Seltz; Common languages: Alsatian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1359; Disestablished: 1419; Succeeded by: Electoral Palatinate

name: Kingdom of Toungoo
description: The Kingdom of Toungoo during this initial era functioned as a tributary border principality in the middle Sittaung River valley of Lower Burma, subordinate to the Pinya Kingdom. Governed by hereditary local lords from the fortified settlement of Toungoo, the polity provided military levies and grain tribute to Pinya while maintaining effective domestic autonomy. Benefiting from an influx of Bamar refugees fleeing Shan incursions in the northern dry zone, Toungoo steadily strengthened its internal defences, emerging as a fully independent kingdom upon the fall of Pinya in 1364. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Toungoo; Common languages: Old Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Early Toungoo dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1359; Disestablished: 26 February 1364; Preceded by: Pinya Kingdom

name: Despotate of Arta
label: albanian principalities
description: The Despotate of Arta was an autonomous medieval Albanian principality established in southern Epirus following the victory of Albanian forces at the Battle of Achelous in 1359. Initially founded by Pjetër Losha and subsequently expanded under Gjin Bua Shpata, the despotate governed from the historic Epirote capital of Arta and controlled rich agricultural river valleys and trade along the Ambracian Gulf. The state defended its borders against the neighbouring rulers of Ioannina and the Frankish Counts of Cephalonia until falling to Carlo I Tocco in 1416. \n\n Status: Despotate; Capital: Arta; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Losha and Shpata clans; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 25 May 1359; Disestablished: 1417; Succeeded by: Despotate of Epirus

name: Marashis
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: The Marashis were an autonomous Iranian Twelver Shia sayyid dynasty that ruled the Caspian coastal province of Mazandaran from the mid-fourteenth century until the late sixteenth century. Established by Mir-i Buzurg, a charismatic dervish and sayyid leader who mobilised popular religious support against the rival Chalavi dynasty, the realm established administrative capitals at Amol and Sari. The dynasty maintained regional independence through astute guerrilla warfare in the dense northern forests, temporarily submitting to Timur before being permanently integrated into the centralised Safavid Empire by Shah Abbas I. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Amol, Sari; Common languages: Mazanderani and Persian; Religion: Twelver Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Marashi dynasty; Ruler title: Mir; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1360; Disestablished: 1597; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Principality of Moldavia
description: The Principality of Moldavia was an independent medieval state situated between the eastern Carpathian Mountains and the Dniester River in southeastern Europe. Founded when Voivode Bogdan I of Cuhea successfully threw off Hungarian suzerainty around 1359, the principality established its administrative capitals successively at Siret and Suceava. Moldavia developed robust commerce along the Black Sea trade route connecting Poland to Caffa, maintained flourishing Orthodox monasteries and defended its sovereign territory against Hungarian, Polish and Ottoman expansion under illustrious rulers such as Stephen the Great. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Suceava; Common languages: Romanian, Church Slavonic and Latin; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Bogdan-Mușat; Ruler title: Voivode; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1360; Disestablished: 1505

name: Yawnghwe State
label: shan states
description: Yawnghwe State was an autonomous Shan principality located in the southern Shan Hills of eastern Myanmar, encompassing the fertile basin of Inle Lake. Governed by a hereditary prince styled Saopha from the royal court at Nyaungshwe, the state controlled important regional trade routes connecting the central dry zone with the mountainous eastern plateau. Yawnghwe fostered distinctive agrarian practices including floating lake gardens while defending its territory against neighbouring Shan sawbwas until it accepted the imperial suzerainty of the expanding Toungoo Empire in 1558. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Nyaungshwe; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yawnghwe Saopha dynasty; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1360; Disestablished: 1558; Succeeded by: Toungoo Empire

name: Free Imperial City of Aalen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Aalen was an autonomous urban municipality of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Kocher River at the northern foot of the Swabian Jura. Elevated to imperial status under Emperor Charles IV in 1360, the city was governed by an independent town magistrate and council that fostered local timber processing, linen weaving and regional cattle trading. Aalen guarded its civic autonomy against the territorial ambitions of neighbouring Württemberg and the Prince-Provostry of Ellwangen until being mediatised into the Electorate of Württemberg in 1803. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Aalen; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1361; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Württemberg

name: Jolof Empire
description: The Jolof Empire was a major precolonial West African state established in the Sahelian savannah between the Senegal and Gambia rivers in modern Senegal. Founded by the legendary ruler Ndiadiane Ndiaye following the decline of local Mali imperial authority, the empire was governed by the Buur-ba Jolof from the capital of Linguère. The confederation encompassed several subordinate coastal and inland Wolof kingdoms, including Cayor, Baol, Waalo and Sine, thriving on trans-Saharan commerce, horse breeding and agriculture until fracturing into sovereign polities after the Battle of Danki in 1549. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Linguère; Common languages: Wolof, Serer and Fula; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ndiaye dynasty; Ruler title: Buur-ba Jolof; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1361; Disestablished: 1550

name: Principality of Mezetsk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Mezetsk was an autonomous Russian feudal appanage located in the upper Oka basin along the Serena River near modern Meshchovsk. Established following the division of the Principality of Karachev among Rurikid dynasts, the realm was governed by the Princes Mezetsky from their fortified river outpost. The small principality exercised independent judicial authority and guarded vital forested portages between the Dnieper and Oka systems until increasing political hegemony by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Moscow led to its absorption in the mid-fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Meshchovsk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1361; Disestablished: 1451; Historical region: Upper Oka

name: Sufids
description: The Sufids were an autonomous Turco-Mongol dynasty of the Qungrat clan that established an independent principality across Khwarezm in the lower Amu Darya delta. Founded by Husayn Sufi amidst the disintegration of Golden Horde authority in Central Asia, the state governed from the magnificent trading oasis of Konye-Urgench and dominated commercial caravan routes traversing the Aral Sea basin. The dynasty maintained defiant political independence for two decades, resisting expansionist pressures until the relentless campaigns of Timur captured and sacked their cities in the late 1370s. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Konye-Urgench; Common languages: Chagatai Turkic and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sufi dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1362; Disestablished: 1380; Succeeded by: Timurid Empire

name: Timurid Empire
description: The Timurid Empire was a vast Turco-Mongol imperial realm that dominated Greater Iran, Central Asia, Transoxiana and adjacent regions from the late fourteenth century to the early sixteenth century. Founded by the conqueror Timur, who established his imperial seat at Samarkand, the state combined Mongol military organisation with Islamic courtly governance and Persianate culture. The empire presided over a brilliant artistic, scientific and architectural renaissance under monarchs such as Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg before internal fragmentation and invasions by the Shaybanid Uzbeks extinguished the dynasty in 1507. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Samarkand, Herat; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Chagatai Turkic and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Timurid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1364; Disestablished: 1508; Succeeded by: Khanate of Bukhara

name: Kingdom of Ava
description: The Kingdom of Ava was the dominant Burmese monarchy that controlled upper Burma and the central dry zone from the mid-fourteenth century until the sixteenth century. Founded in 1364 by King Thado Minbya on an island formed by the Irrawaddy and Myitnge rivers, the kingdom reunited the fractured territories of Sagaing and Pinya and claimed ideological succession to Pagan. Ava developed rich irrigated agriculture in the Kyaukse plains, patronised classic Burmese literature and fought protracted wars against the Hanthawaddy Kingdom before falling to the Confederation of Shan States in 1527. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Ava; Common languages: Burmese and Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ava dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 26 February 1364; Disestablished: 15 March 1527; Succeeded by: Confederation of Shan States

name: Kingdom of Toungoo
description: The Kingdom of Toungoo was an independent Burmese state centred in the fertile valley of the Sittaung River in southern central Myanmar. Attaining full sovereignty under King Pyanchi I following the collapse of Pinya and Sagaing in 1364, the kingdom fortified its citadel at Toungoo and offered a secure refuge for Bamar scholars, artisans and soldiers fleeing northern turmoil. Although briefly brought into tributary ties with Ava, the resilient kingdom preserved its dynastic core, subsequently expanding in the sixteenth century under Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung to unify Burma into a formidable empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Toungoo; Common languages: Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Toungoo dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 26 February 1364; Disestablished: 1 April 1752; Succeeded by: Konbaung Dynasty

name: Chiefdom of Sinan
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Sinan was an autonomous indigenous Tusi principality located along the upper Wu River in eastern Guizhou province in southwestern China. Ruled by a cadet branch of the powerful Tian clan, the chiefdom declared its independence from the neighbouring Chiefdom of Sizhou in 1364, governing an ethnically diverse populace of Tujia, Miao and Gelao peoples. The hereditary chieftains exercised extensive feudal jurisdiction over local agriculture and trade routes until bitter feuding with Sizhou provoked imperial Ming military intervention, which resulted in the direct bureaucratic incorporation of both territories in 1413. \n\n Status: Indigenous chiefdom; Capital: Sinan; Common languages: Tujia, Miao and Southwestern Mandarin; Religion: Nuoism and Animism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Tian clan; Ruler title: Tusi Chieftain; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1365; Disestablished: 1415; Succeeded by: Ming Dynasty

name: Moghulistan (Military Occupation)
description: Moghulistan maintained a brief military occupation administration across Transoxiana following the decisive victory of Khan Ilyas Khoja at the Battle of the Mire in 1365. Forcing the retreat of Amir Husayn and Timur, Chagatai nomadic forces seized control of the agricultural hinterlands and advanced to besiege Samarkand. The occupying steppe armies established no permanent civilian institutions, ruling solely through military garrisons until an urban insurrection by the local Sarbadar movement, followed by a winter horse epidemic, compelled the nomadic invaders to abandon Transoxiana in 1366. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile cavalry encampment; Common languages: Chagatai Turkic and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Nomadic military administration; Ruling dynasty: Chagatai dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1365; Disestablished: 1366; Succeeded by: Chagatai Khanate

name: Principality of Bokhtyuga
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Bokhtyuga was an appanage state of north-eastern Rus, established in 1364 when it separated from the Principality of Rostov during the era of feudal fragmentation. Situated along the Bokhtyuga River near the upper Sukhona basin north of Vologda, the principality was held by a cadet branch of the Rostov Rurikid house. The princes governed local peasant settlements, timber harvesting and fishing rights along the riverways, maintaining autonomy until their lands were gradually bought up and incorporated into the expanding Grand Principality of Moscow in the 1420s. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Vologda; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1365; Disestablished: 1426; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Ustyug
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Ustyug was an autonomous medieval Russian principality located at the strategic confluence of the Sukhona and Yug rivers in northern Rus. Governed by a cadet line of Rurikid princes from the fortified settlement of Veliky Ustyug, the state controlled the primary waterways connecting central Russia with the fur-rich river networks of the Vychegda and Pechora. The principality successfully defended its commercial lifelines against rival Novgorod raids before dynastic agreements and sales gradually brought the entire territory under the direct suzerainty of the Grand Principality of Moscow. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Veliky Ustyug; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1365; Disestablished: 1426; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Free Imperial City of Isny
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Isny was an autonomous municipal republic of the Holy Roman Empire located in the rolling Allgäu region of southwestern Germany. Having purchased its civic freedom and imperial immediacy from the Counts of Montfort and Waldburg in 1365, the town was governed by an elected council of burghers and guild masters. Isny prospered through linen weaving, brass working and regional alpine cattle markets, maintaining its Protestant confession and urban independence until mediatisation transferred the city to the Counts of Quadt and subsequently to Württemberg in 1806. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Isny im Allgäu; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1366; Disestablished: 1807; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Württemberg

name: Princely County of Gorizia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Princely County of Gorizia was an autonomous feudal state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Isonzo valley between the Carnic Alps and the Adriatic Sea. Ruled by the noble Meinhardiner dynasty from their imposing castle above the town of Gorizia, the multilingual county commanded vital transit passes connecting the German lands with northern Italy and the Istrian coast. The counts maintained territorial autonomy amidst persistent pressure from the Republic of Venice and the House of Habsburg until the extinction of the line in 1500, whereupon the territory was inherited by Austria. \n\n Status: Princely County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Gorizia; Common languages: Slovene, Friulian, Italian and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Gorizia; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1366; Disestablished: 1501; Succeeded by: Archduchy of Austria

name: Principality of Shumorovo
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Shumorovo was a minor medieval Russian appanage principality situated along the Volga and Mologa river basins in north-eastern Rus. Originating as a partition of the Principality of Yaroslavl, the realm was governed by the Shumorovsky line of the Rurikid dynasty from the fortified settlement of Shumorovo. The princes derived revenues from woodland trapping, fisheries and river transportation, retaining their feudal court and domestic autonomy until the territorial consolidation of north-eastern Rus under Ivan III led to the realm's absorption into the Grand Principality of Moscow. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Shumorovo; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1366; Disestablished: 1426; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Realm of Negroponte
label: frankokratia
description: The Realm of Negroponte was a major maritime colonial dependency of the Republic of Venice, encompassing the entire Aegean island of Euboea and its surrounding coastal waters. Governed from the heavily fortified port city of Chalkis, known to the Latins as Negroponte, the colony was administered by a resident Venetian bailiff and served as the linchpin of Venetian naval and commercial power in the Levant. The island supported a flourishing mercantile and agricultural economy until an overwhelming Ottoman siege commanded by Sultan Mehmed II breached its walls in July 1470. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Chalkis; Official languages: Venetian; Common languages: Medieval Greek and Venetian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Colonial administration; Head of state: Bailiff of Negroponte; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1366; Disestablished: 1471; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Savoyard Crusaders
label: crusader states
description: The Savoyard Crusaders constituted an expeditionary Catholic military force organised by Count Amadeus VI of Savoy at the request of Pope Urban V to support the Byzantine Empire against regional foes. Arriving in the Aegean in 1366, the crusaders recaptured the strategic fortress of Gallipoli from the Ottoman Turks before sailing into the Black Sea to seize the fortified coastal ports of Mesembria and Sozopol from the Second Bulgarian Empire. Operating from their base at Nesebar, the crusaders governed captured strongholds under martial authority until handing them over to Emperor John V Palaiologos in 1367. \n\n Status: Crusader military expedition; Administrative seat: Nesebar; Common languages: Franco-Provençal, Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military expeditionary command; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1366; Disestablished: 1367; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Free Imperial City of Bremen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Bremen was an autonomous urban republic and leading member of the Hanseatic League, situated along the navigable lower reaches of the Weser River in northern Germany. Consolidating its civic independence from the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen in the fourteenth century, the city was governed by an elected senate and burgomasters who commanded extensive maritime trade with the North Sea and Baltic regions. Bremen stoutly defended its imperial immediacy during the Thirty Years' War and the Swedish Wars, preserving its constitutional autonomy until its incorporation into the Napoleonic Kingdom of Westphalia. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bremen; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Reformed Protestantism; Government: Imperial city republic; Legislature: Senate of Bremen; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1367; Disestablished: 1807; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Westphalia

name: League of God's House
label: holy roman empire
description: The League of God's House was an autonomous alpine confederation formed on 29 January 1367 in the Raetian valleys of modern Graubünden to resist the territorial ambitions of the Prince-Bishop of Chur and the House of Habsburg. Composed of communal jurisdictions representing the cathedral chapter, local ministerials and peasant valleys, the league established its deliberative assembly at Chur. The alliance coordinated common judicial, military and diplomatic policies with direct democracy in communal assemblies, eventually joining the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions to form the Three Leagues in 1471. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Chur; Common languages: Romansh and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal confederation; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 29 January 1367; Reorganised: 1472; Succeeded by: Three Leagues

name: Commune of Sanremo
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Sanremo was an autonomous municipal city-state located along the Riviera di Ponente in western Liguria. Having purchased its civic liberties from the Archbishop of Genoa and the Doria family in the mid-fourteenth century, the commune was administered by an elected council of burghers and consuls under its own local civic statutes. Sanremo thrived on coastal cabotage, citrus cultivation and olive oil production, tenaciously guarding its traditional municipal self-government and tax immunities against Genoese interference until the Republic of Genoa suppressed its privileges following an uprising in 1753. \n\n Status: Self-governing commune; Capital: Sanremo; Common languages: Ligurian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1368; Disestablished: 1749; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Principality of Albania
label: albanian principalities
description: The Principality of Albania was an autonomous medieval state established across central Albania by the noble Thopia dynasty, reaching the height of its power under Prince Karl Thopia.
