Seizing the strategic Adriatic port of Durrës from the Angevin Kingdom of Albania in 1368, the dynasty united the territories between the Mat and Shkumbin rivers and constructed the stronghold of Krujë. The principality engaged in dynamic maritime trade and diplomacy with Venice and the Papacy, maintaining its sovereign independence until mounting Ottoman incursions and Venetian annexations dissolved the realm in 1415. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Durrës; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Thopia dynasty; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1368; Disestablished: 1416; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Albania

name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania (Military Occupation)
description: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania maintained temporary military occupation zones across north-eastern Rus during the Lithuanian-Muscovite War of 1368 to 1372. Commanded by Grand Duke Algirdas in support of his ally Mikhail of Tver, Lithuanian cavalry contingents overran Muscovite frontier forts, devastated surrounding agricultural settlements and besieged the newly constructed stone Kremlin of Moscow. Operating without permanent civil administrative structures, these martial encampments served to exert coercive political pressure on Prince Dmitry Donskoy before concluding the Treaty of Lyubutsk, which re-established the balance of power along the frontier. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile grand ducal military encampment; Common languages: Lithuanian, Ruthenian and Old East Slavic; Religion: Baltic paganism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Military administration; Ruling dynasty: Gediminid dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 21 November 1368; Disestablished: 1372

name: Great Ming
description: The Great Ming was a powerful imperial dynasty of China founded in 1368 by the Hongwu Emperor following the expulsion of the Mongol-led Yuan court from the Central Plains. Administered initially from Nanjing and subsequently from Beijing, the empire established an efficient civil service examination system, constructed vast naval fleets under Zheng He and restored agricultural productivity across China proper. Ming authority sustained remarkable demographic and economic expansion and oversaw the reinforcement of the Great Wall, defending its realm until civil rebellions and the Manchu invasion established the Qing Dynasty in 1644. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Nanjing, Beijing; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Early Mandarin; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Zhu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1369; Disestablished: 1664; Succeeded by: Qing Dynasty

name: Sultanate of Brunei
description: The Sultanate of Brunei was an influential Malay maritime empire centred on the northern coast of Borneo, established in the late fourteenth century following the conversion of its founding monarch, Sultan Muhammad Shah, to Islam. Operating from successive riverine capitals at Kota Batu and Kampong Ayer, the sultanate achieved paramount naval and commercial hegemony across coastal Borneo, the Sulu Archipelago and the southern Philippines. Controlling valuable trade in camphor, pearls, sago and spices, Brunei preserved its sovereign independence until European colonial encroachment and the expansion of Sarawak reduced its borders in 1888. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Bandar Seri Begawan; Official languages: Brunei Malay; Common languages: Malay and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bolkiah dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Established: 1369; Disestablished: 17 September 1888; Succeeded by: British Protectorate of Brunei

name: Turpan Khanate
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Turpan Khanate was a Turco-Mongol Muslim state that ruled the fertile Turpan Depression and eastern Tarim Basin along the northern Silk Road in Central Asia. Emerging as the eastern division of Moghulistan under the descendants of Chagatai Khan, the khanate was governed from the ancient oasis city of Turpan. The state derived immense wealth from trans-continental caravan trade, engaged in recurring border conflicts and tributary diplomacy with the Ming Dynasty over control of Hami, and flourished as a bastion of Islamic culture before being conquered by the Yarkent Khanate in 1570. \n\n Status: Khanate; Capital: Turpan; Common languages: Chagatai Turkic and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chagatai dynasty; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1369; Disestablished: 1658; Succeeded by: Yarkent Khanate

name: Grand Duchy of Moscow (Military Occupation)
description: The Grand Duchy of Moscow maintained temporary military occupation administrations over contested border territories during recurring conflicts with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and neighbouring Rus principalities. Commanded by grand princely voivodes and boyar captains, these martial zones secured captured citadels, confiscated provincial revenues and fortified strategic frontier rivers along the upper Dnieper and Oka. The military administrations operated under emergency garrison law without permanent local civil assemblies, functioning until peace treaties, such as the truces of 1503 and 1522, formally incorporated the occupied territories into the centralised Russian state. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile voivode field command; Common languages: Old East Slavic and Russian; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Royal military administration; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1 April 1370; Disestablished: 1538

name: Kingdom of Poland
description: The Kingdom of Poland during this period was bound in a personal union with the Kingdom of Hungary following the death of Casimir III the Great in November 1370, when King Louis I of the Capetian House of Anjou inherited the Polish crown. Governed from the royal castle of Wawel in Kraków, often through the regency of Louis's mother Elizabeth of Poland, the kingdom witnessed important constitutional developments, notably the Privilege of Koszyce of 1374 granting fundamental rights to the nobility. The union concluded in 1384 when Louis's daughter Jadwiga was crowned Queen of Poland. \n\n Status: Personal union; Capital: Kraków; Common languages: Old Polish and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Capetian House of Anjou; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 17 November 1370; Disestablished: 16 November 1384; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Poland

name: Great Yuan
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Great Yuan, known retroactively in historiography as the Northern Yuan, was the imperial Mongol successor state that ruled the Mongolian Plateau following the loss of China proper to the Ming Dynasty in 1368. Governed by the Genghisid Borjigin clan from the ancestral capital of Karakorum, the state preserved imperial claims, traditional nomadic clan organisation and the legal code of the Yassa. The khagans fought repeated border wars against the Ming and reunified nomadic tribes under Dayan Khan, maintaining sovereign steppe autonomy until submitting to the Jurchen Later Jin dynasty in 1635. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Karakorum; Common languages: Middle Mongol; Religion: Tengrism, Shamanism and Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Nomadic imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Borjigin clan; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1371; Disestablished: 1636; Succeeded by: Later Jin

name: Palanpur State
description: Palanpur State was an autonomous principality situated in northern Gujarat, bordering the Aravalli Hills and the Thar Desert. Founded in the late fourteenth century by the Lohani Pashtun clan, who migrated from the Afghan frontier and established their seat at Palanpur, the state controlled important regional trading paths connecting Rajasthan with the Arabian Sea ports. The ruling dynasty maintained domestic independence through changing feudal allegiances to the Gujarat Sultanate, the Mughal Empire and the Marathas, preserving unbroken dynastic authority until concluding a subsidiary alliance treaty with the British East India Company in 1817. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Palanpur; Common languages: Gujarati and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lohani dynasty; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Medieval to Early Modern India; Established: 1371; Disestablished: 1821; Succeeded by: Palanpur Agency

name: County of Novellara
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Novellara was an autonomous imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the fertile lowlands of the Po Valley in Emilia. Established on 17 May 1371 when Feltrino Gonzaga retained Novellara and Bagnolo following the sale of Reggio Emilia to the Visconti, the territory was ruled by the cadet Gonzaga di Novellara line for over three centuries. The counts developed agricultural drainage systems, fortified the town with a stately moated castle and patronised Renaissance arts until the extinction of the male line in 1728 transferred the county to Modena. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Novellara; Common languages: Italian and Emilian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gonzaga di Novellara; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 17 May 1371; Disestablished: 10 December 1737; Succeeded by: Duchy of Modena and Reggio

name: Domain of Branković
label: serbian principalities
description: The Domain of Branković was an autonomous medieval Serbian principality that emerged in Kosovo and Metohija following the collapse of the Serbian Empire at the Battle of Maritsa in September 1371. Founded by the magnate Vuk Branković and administered from Pristina, the realm encompassed crucial commercial crossroads and wealthy silver-mining centres such as Trepča and Novo Brdo. Vuk participated prominently in the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and resisted Ottoman vassalage longer than many contemporary Serbian lords, before his sons eventually integrated their lands into the unified Serbian Despotate in 1412. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Pristina; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Branković dynasty; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 26 September 1371; Disestablished: 1413; Succeeded by: Serbian Despotate

name: Kingdom of Prilep
label: serbian principalities
description: The Kingdom of Prilep was an autonomous medieval state established in western Macedonia following the death of King Vukašin Mrnjavčević at the Battle of Maritsa in September 1371. Inherited by his son Prince Marko, who maintained the royal title of King of the Serbs, the realm was governed from the imposing clifftop fortress of Marko's Towers above Prilep. Marko ruled the Pelagonian lowlands with considerable local independence while navigating compulsory Ottoman vassal service, governing the realm until his death in battle at Rovine in 1395, after which the Ottomans directly annexed his territories. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Prilep; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mrnjavčević dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 26 September 1371; Disestablished: 1396; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Moravian Serbia
label: serbian principalities
description: Moravian Serbia was the premier Serbian principality to emerge following the dissolution of the Serbian Empire in September 1371, encompassing the fertile valleys of the Great, South and West Morava rivers. Governed by Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović from his fortified capital at Kruševac, the state developed extensive silver-mining revenues, fostered the Morava architectural school and united regional lords in common resistance to the Ottoman advance. The realm reached a dramatic climax at the Battle of Kosovo in June 1389, where Prince Lazar fell, after which his successors accepted Ottoman vassal status in 1390. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Kruševac; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lazarević dynasty; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 26 September 1371; Disestablished: 1390; Succeeded by: Serbian Despotate

name: Principality of Velbazhd
label: serbian principalities
description: The Principality of Velbazhd was an autonomous medieval state that emerged along the Upper Struma and Bregalnica river basins following the Battle of Maritsa in September 1371. Ruled jointly by the noble brothers Jovan and Konstantin Dragaš of the Dejanović dynasty, the realm was administered from the ancient fortress city of Velbazhd, modern Kyustendil. The princes governed extensive agrarian domains and patronised prominent Orthodox monasteries such as Poganovo and Osogovo, maintaining brief sovereign autonomy until overwhelming Ottoman military pressure compelled them to accept imperial Ottoman vassalage around 1374. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Kyustendil; Common languages: Old Serbian and Middle Bulgarian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dejanović dynasty; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 26 September 1371; Disestablished: 1374; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Principality of Zeta
label: serbian principalities
description: The Principality of Zeta was an autonomous medieval coastal realm situated across the limestone highlands and Adriatic coastline of modern Montenegro and northern Albania. Formed during the breakup of the Serbian Empire under the Balšić noble family, the principality established its primary administrative seats at Shkodër and Ulcinj. The Balšići maintained a powerful maritime fleet, controlled profitable Adriatic salt monopolies and vigorously defended their independence against rival Albanian lords, Venetian coastal ambitions and Ottoman incursions until the childless Prince Balša III bequeathed the realm to the Serbian Despotate in 1421. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Shkodër; Common languages: Old Serbian and Albanian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Balšić dynasty; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 26 September 1371; Disestablished: 28 April 1421; Succeeded by: Serbian Despotate

name: Vojinović Domain
label: serbian principalities
description: The Vojinović Domain was a powerful medieval Serbian regional principality that dominated the rugged highlands between the Drina River, the Lim valley and the Adriatic coast near Dubrovnik. Governed by the magnate Nikola Altomanović Vojinović from the clifftop fortress of Užice, the domain controlled vital silver transport routes and levied tribute on Ragusan merchants. Nikola's rapid expansion alarmed neighbouring rulers, prompting an allied coalition of Prince Lazar of Serbia and Ban Tvrtko I of Bosnia that besieged Užice and partitioned the territory in December 1373. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Užice; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: Vojinović family; Ruler title: Grand Župan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 26 September 1371; Disestablished: 1 December 1373; Succeeded by: Moravian Serbia

name: Chiefdom of Shuidong
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Shuidong was an autonomous indigenous Tusi principality situated in central Guizhou province in southwestern China, ruled by the hereditary Song clan from their seat in modern Kaiyang near Guiyang. Recognised as one of the Four Great Native Chiefdoms of Guizhou, the state acknowledged imperial suzerainty under the Ming Dynasty in 1372 while retaining full domestic authority over its Bouyei, Miao and Han inhabitants. The chiefdom maintained its autonomous governance for over two centuries until its involvement in the She-An Rebellion prompted direct annexation by the Ming Crown in 1630. \n\n Status: Vassal chiefdom; Capital: Guiyang; Common languages: Chinese, Bouyei and Miao; Religion: Nuoism and Animism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Song clan; Ruler title: Tusi Chieftain; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1372; Disestablished: 1631; Succeeded by: Ming Dynasty

name: Domain of Thessaly
description: The Domain of Thessaly was an autonomous feudal state established in central Greece following the division of the regional domains of the Despotate of Epirus and the Serbian Empire. Centred on the fortified upland town of Hypata, the realm controlled the fertile Spercheios river valley and the northern approaches to Boeotia amidst shifting rivalries among local Greek archons, Catalan mercenaries and Albanian chieftains. The domain maintained a precarious independence through defensive alliances and military garrisons until regional pressure from rival Epirote rulers and expanding Ottoman forces brought an end to local dynastic rule. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Hypata; Common languages: Medieval Greek and Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1372; Disestablished: 1383; Preceded by: Despotate of Epirus; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Free Imperial City of Heilbronn
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Heilbronn was an autonomous municipal republic of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Neckar River in northern Baden-Württemberg. Receiving its charter of imperial immediacy and a town constitution from Emperor Charles IV in 1371, the city was governed by an independent council representing merchant patricians and civic craft guilds. Heilbronn developed into a prominent trading emporium and viticultural hub along the Neckar navigation corridor, defending its communal liberties through the Reformation and the Thirty Years' War until its annexation to the Duchy of Württemberg during the mediatisation of 1802. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Heilbronn; Common languages: Swabian German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, later Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1372; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Württemberg

name: Principality of Gropaj
label: albanian principalities
description: The Principality of Gropaj was an autonomous medieval Albanian state that held territory around the mountain lakes of Ohrid and Prespa, encompassing the districts of Pogradec, Ohrid and Debar. Led by the magnate Andrea Gropa following the decline of Serbian imperial authority in 1371, the dynasty established its administrative seat at the fortified lakeside citadel of Ohrid. Allied with the Muzaka family against King Marko of Prilep, the Gropa rulers coined their own silver currency and patronised local Orthodox churches until Ottoman advances in Macedonia extinguished the independent lordship in the late fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Ohrid; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gropa family; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1372; Disestablished: 1396; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Chiefdom of Mu'ege
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Mu'ege, known in Chinese records as the Chiefdom of Shuixi, was an ancient Nasu Yi hereditary principality situated in the rugged mountain highlands of western Guizhou. Governed by the prestigious An clan from their seat at Dafang, the realm recognised the tributary suzerainty of the Ming Dynasty in 1373 while maintaining traditional Bimoist culture, customary Yi laws and clan armed levies. Ranked as one of the Four Great Native Chiefdoms of Guizhou, Mu'ege preserved substantial local authority across three centuries until being definitively suppressed and annexed by the Qing Dynasty in 1698. \n\n Status: Vassal chiefdom; Capital: Dafang; Common languages: Nasu Yi and Southwestern Mandarin; Religion: Bimoism and Buddhism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: An clan; Ruler title: Tusi Chieftain; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1373; Disestablished: 1699; Succeeded by: Qing Dynasty

name: Free Imperial City of Frankfurt am Main
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Frankfurt am Main was an autonomous urban republic situated along the Main River in Hesse, occupying a pre-eminent position within the Holy Roman Empire. Solidifying its constitutional independence as a free imperial city under Emperor Charles IV in the fourteenth century, the city was governed by an elected patrician Senate and served as the designated location for the election and coronation of German kings and emperors. Frankfurt flourished as Europe's premier commercial and financial fair metropolis until the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire led to its mediatisation in 1806. \n\n Status: Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Frankfurt am Main; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Imperial city republic; Legislature: Senate of Frankfurt; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 1373; Disestablished: 1807; Succeeded by: Principality of Aschaffenburg

name: Bulgarian Empire
description: The Bulgarian Empire during this concluding phase functioned as a constrained tributary vassal state of the Ottoman Empire, centred on the royal capital of Veliko Tarnovo in northern Bulgaria. Governed by Tsar Ivan Shishman after military setbacks forced him to accept the overlordship of Sultan Murad I in the 1370s, the rump state struggled to preserve its territorial integrity and Christian literary culture. Despite energetic defensive efforts and diplomatic overtures to neighbouring Christian rulers, Ottoman armies stormed Veliko Tarnovo in 1393, extinguishing the empire definitively in the aftermath of the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396. \n\n Status: Vassal empire; Capital: Veliko Tarnovo; Common languages: Middle Bulgarian; Religion: Bulgarian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shishman dynasty; Ruler title: Tsar; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1374; Disestablished: 1 November 1396; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Kara Koyunlu
description: Kara Koyunlu was a confederated Turkoman realm that dominated vast expanses of Armenia, Azerbaijan, northwestern Iran and eastern Anatolia. Governed by the Black Sheep tribal dynasty from capitals including Tabriz, the sultanate maintained Persian administrative traditions alongside fierce martial mobility. During its fourteenth- and fifteenth-century zenith, the state contested regional supremacy against the rival Aq Qoyunlu and the Timurids before succumbing to total conquest in 1468. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Tabriz; Official languages: Persian, Azerbaijani and Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Confederate monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kara Koyunlu; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Jalayirid Sultanate; Succeeded by: Aq Qoyunlu

name: Lordship of Werle-Güstrow-Goldberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Werle-Güstrow-Goldberg was an imperial estate in northeastern Germany established through successive partitions of the Obotrite patrimony of Mecklenburg. Administered from the residential town of Güstrow, the principality exercised territorial immediacy across fertile agrarian lands stretching towards Lake Müritz. name: Grand Duchy of Moscow
description: The Grand Duchy of Moscow was an expansive East Slavic principality that became the central unifier of the medieval Russian lands. Operating from its fortified kremlin in Moscow, the realm expanded steadily through diplomacy, dynastic purchases and military annexation of neighbouring princely territories. name: Guanartemate of Gran Canaria
label: guanche states
description: The Guanartemate of Gran Canaria was a sovereign indigenous polity that held unified jurisdiction over the entire volcanic island of Gran Canaria prior to European conquest. Ruled by an aboriginal high chieftain styled the guanarteme from the royal settlement of Galdar, the society developed sophisticated terrace agriculture, communal granaries and sacred judicial assemblies. The centralised monarchy eventually split into two rival chieftaincies around 1405, accelerating indigenous vulnerability before the Castilian conquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Galdar; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Guanarteme; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Guanartemate of Galdar

name: Kingdom of Kongo
description: The Kingdom of Kongo was an influential Central African realm centred along the fertile lower Congo River basin and the Atlantic littoral. Established through the unification of earlier regional chiefdoms, the state was governed by the elected manikongo from the administrative capital at Mbanza Kongo. name: Kingdom of Bosnia
description: The Kingdom of Bosnia was an independent South Slavic realm that arose from the earlier banate and expanded rapidly across the western Balkans under King Tvrtko I. Governed from the upland fortress capital of Bobovac, the monarchy prospered through rich silver mines, lively Adriatic maritime commerce and a distinctive feudal assembly of magnates. Despite prolonged religious friction between Roman Catholicism and the local Bosnian Church, the kingdom preserved its autonomy until the Ottoman conquest of 1463. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bobovac; Common languages: Old Bosnian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Bosnian Church; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kotromanić dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Banate of Bosnia; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Bosnia

name: Dullu
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Dullu was a mountainous Khas principality situated in the Karnali River basin of western Nepal, forming one of the prominent Baise Rajya chieftaincies. Ruling from the fortified hilltop seat of Dullu, its Hindu monarchs oversaw strategic trans-Himalayan trade paths and patronised distinctive stone inscriptions in early Khas script. name: Free Imperial City of Hamburg
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Free Imperial City of Hamburg was a prosperous maritime merchant republic located on the lower Elbe River estuary in northern Germany. As a leading participant in the Hanseatic League, the city possessed imperial immediacy that shielded its merchant oligarchs and grand burghers from regional feudal encroachment. Hamburg developed into an indispensable commercial emporium for North Sea shipping and Baltic exchange, maintaining its self-governing republican institutions until Napoleonic forces occupied the commune in 1811. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Hamburg; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Merchant republic; Legislature: Senate of Hamburg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Bouches-de-l'Elbe

name: Imperial Abbey of Zwiefalten
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Abbey of Zwiefalten was a self-governing Benedictine ecclesiastical territory situated in the Swabian Jura of southwestern Germany. Endowed with imperial immediacy, the monastic principality was ruled by its prince-abbot, who exercised secular justice and territorial sovereignty across neighbouring monastic lands and rural parishes. The abbey withstood the turbulence of the Protestant Reformation and the Thirty Years' War, flourishing into a celebrated baroque religious complex before undergoing secularisation and annexation to Württemberg in 1803. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey; Capital: Zwiefalten; Common languages: Early Modern German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Electorate of Württemberg

name: Imperial Bailiwick of Haguenau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Bailiwick of Haguenau was an immediate crown domain of the Holy Roman Empire located in northern Alsace. Headquartered in the fortified town of Haguenau, this provincial bailiwick administered the imperial estates and coordinated judicial protection for the surrounding Decapole cities under a resident imperial advocate. The bailiwick preserved crucial strategic river crossings and forested territories on behalf of the German monarch until administrative reorganisations transferred its direct jurisdiction during the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial bailiwick; Administrative seat: Haguenau; Common languages: German and Alsatian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Imperial administrative domain; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Landgraviate of Lower Alsace; Succeeded by: Electorate of the Palatinate

name: Lordship of Clermont
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Clermont was a strategic frontier fief situated in the Argonne region between the Kingdom of France and the Holy Roman Empire. Governed by feudal barons from the elevated stronghold of Clermont, the lordship controlled vital transit routes between Champagne and the Meuse valley. The territory navigated complex overlapping feudal allegiances to ensure its local autonomy, until intensifying royal centralisation and territorial consolidation brought the estate under the direct hegemony of the Duchy of Lorraine. \n\n Status: Feudal lordship; Capital: Clermont; Common languages: Old French and Middle French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal barony; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of Bar; Succeeded by: Duchy of Lorraine

name: Principality of Shuya
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Shuya was an East Slavic appanage state that broke away from the broader Suzdal territory in the upper Volga River drainage. Centred on the fortified commercial town of Shuya along the Teza River, the realm was governed by a cadet branch of the Rurikid dynasty known as the Shuysky princes. The small realm defended its agrarian core against regional skirmishes until mounting Muscovite pressure compelled its incorporation into the centralised Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1449. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Shuya; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Suzdal; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Sukhothai Kingdom
description: The Sukhothai Kingdom entered a protracted period of tributary vassalage under the southern Ayutthaya Kingdom during the late fourteenth century. Operating from its historic ceremonial capital of Sukhothai, the northern Siamese polity retained internal administrative customs and Buddhist monastic patronage under its local Phra Ruang rulers. However, sovereign authority and foreign diplomacy were firmly dictated by Ayutthaya kings, who ultimately dissolved the tributary arrangement and absorbed the territory into their administrative provinces in 1438. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Sukhothai; Common languages: Old Thai; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Tributary mandala monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Phra Ruang dynasty; Historical era: Post-classical; Preceded by: Sukhothai Kingdom (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Ayutthaya Kingdom

name: Republic of Genoa (Military Occupation)
description: The Republic of Genoa maintained temporary military occupation administrations over vital coastal bridgeheads during the War of Chioggia and regional Levant expeditions. Commanded directly by Genoese naval admirals without a permanent civilian capital, these expeditionary outposts mobilised garrisons, secured lagoon anchorages and intercepted Venetian maritime convoys. These fortified positions were maintained exclusively for strategic leverage during active campaigns, being evacuated or restored following the formal ratification of the Peace of Turin. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile fleet command; Official languages: Ligurian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Naval military administration; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Republic of Venice; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Beylik of Erzincan
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Erzincan was an autonomous Turkmen principality that controlled the strategic Upper Euphrates river valley in eastern Anatolia. Established by local emirs in the wake of Mongol Ilkhanid decline, the principality flourished under Emir Mutahharten, who adroitly balanced competing pressures from the neighbouring Black Sheep Turkomans, Trebizond and the Eretnids. Erzincan emerged as a thriving commercial crossroads for overland Silk Road caravans until Timur's campaigns and subsequent Qara Qoyunlu expansion overran the realm in 1411. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Erzincan; Common languages: Ottoman Turkish and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Eretnid State; Succeeded by: Kara Koyunlu

name: Bornu Empire
description: The Bornu Empire was a major Islamic realm in the Lake Chad basin, established when the ancient Sayfawa dynasty was driven southwest from Kanem by internal turmoil. Governed by monarchs styled mai from fortified court capitals, the state rebuilt its military supremacy, developed extensive horse cavalry forces and dominated trans-Saharan commercial routes in salt and textiles. Bornu sustained its independence for over five centuries until foreign invasions and European colonial expansion partitioned its ancestral heartland around 1900. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Kukawa; Common languages: Kanuri and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sayfawa dynasty; Ruler title: Mai; Historical era: Middle Ages to Modern; Preceded by: Kanem Empire; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Duchy of Berg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Berg was a prosperous territory of the Holy Roman Empire located on the right bank of the Rhine in Westphalia. Governed from the riverside residence of Düsseldorf, the duchy encompassed the historic Bergisches Land, benefiting from thriving iron manufacturing, river navigation and agrarian trade. The House of Jülich-Berg united the realm with neighbouring Rhenish duchies through strategic dynastic marriages, consolidating regional authority within the empire throughout the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: State of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Düsseldorf; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Jülich; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of Berg; Succeeded by: United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg

name: Emirate of Hakkari
label: kurdish principalities
description: The Emirate of Hakkari was an autonomous Kurdish principality situated in the rugged mountainous highlands between Lake Van and Lake Urmia. Governed by hereditary Kurdish emirs from the fortress town of Hakkâri, the principality retained substantial political independence amid regional conflicts between the Turkmen confederations, the Safavids and the Ottoman Empire. Hakkari sheltered diverse Kurdish tribes and Christian Assyrian communities under local customary law until Ottoman centralising drives suppressed the autonomous dynasty during the nineteenth-century Tanzimat reforms. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Hakkâri; Common languages: Kurdish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Kabare
description: Kabare was a prominent precolonial Shi kingdom situated in the fertile volcanic hills southwest of Lake Kivu in present-day eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Ruled by a sacred sovereign titled the mwami from royal residences near Bukavu, the kingdom developed an intricate clan-based social hierarchy supported by intensive banana cultivation, cattle husbandry and iron smelting. Kabare maintained stout political sovereignty against neighbouring lacustrine realms until Belgian colonial expeditions penetrated the eastern highland interior in late 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bukavu; Common languages: Mashi; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mwami; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Lord Pskov
label: russian principalities
description: Lord Pskov functioned as an autonomous aristocratic city-republic in northwestern Russia during its late fourteenth- and fifteenth-century phase of Muscovite suzerainty. Centred on the fortified riverside citadel of Pskov, the republic operated an elected veche popular assembly, adhered to its venerable judicial charter and defended the western frontier against Livonian incursions. While recognising the diplomatic supremacy and military guidance of the Grand Duke of Moscow, Pskov maintained internal self-governance until its formal territorial annexation by Moscow in 1510. \n\n Status: Vassal republic; Capital: Pskov; Common languages: Old East Slavic (Pskov dialect); Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Aristocratic republic; Legislature: Veche; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Novgorod Republic; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Kargolom
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Kargolom was a northern East Slavic feudal appanage established amidst the lakes and forests of the Onega River basin around Kargopol. Governed by a local branch of Rurikid princes, the small territory maintained internal autonomy by controlling hunting tracts, fur processing and freshwater transport corridors connecting central Rus with the White Sea coast. Kargolom preserved its precarious self-rule amidst regional rivalries until the growing power of the Muscovite grand princes compelled its peaceful absorption during the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Kargopol; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Beloozero; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Kem
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Kem was a secluded Rurikid appanage located in the subarctic wilderness of northern Rus along the waterways draining towards the White Sea. Administered from the river outpost of Kem, the principality's rulers collected tribute in furs, marine ivory and dried fish from dispersed Finno-Ugric and Slavic trappers. The domain functioned with relative domestic autonomy despite encroaching Novgorod trade interests, until Muscovite territorial expansion incorporated the distant northern march into the emerging Russian unified state in 1431. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Kem; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Beloozero; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Peremyshl
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Peremyshl was an Upper Oka principality in central Russia centred on the fortified town of Peremyshl along the Oka River. Ruled by a cadet branch of the Novosil Rurikid line, the principality held an important defensive frontier position against steppe nomadic raids while navigating conflicting diplomatic overtures from Lithuania and Moscow. The local dynasty preserved internal autonomy over its agrarian and riverine domain until the rapid expansion of Muscovite suzerainty incorporated the Upper Oka appanages in 1409. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Peremyshl; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Novosil; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Sheleshpan
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Sheleshpan was a minor East Slavic appanage in the Sheksna River basin, emerging from the fragmentation of the Beloozero princely house. Centred on the fortified settlement of Sheleshpanovo, the realm's rulers derived revenue from river commerce, forest hunting and traditional peasant husbandry. Despite their ancient Rurikid heritage, the princes possessed modest military resources and steadily gravitated into the political orbit of Moscow, which completed the annexation of the territory in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Sheleshpanovo; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Beloozero; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Kart Dynasty
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: The Kart Dynasty held vassal dominion over eastern Khurasan and the Hari River valley following Timur's invasion and pacification of the region in 1381. Ruling under strict Timurid oversight from the ancient cultural metropolis of Herat, the Tajik sovereigns collected taxes, repaired city fortifications and provided auxiliary troops to their imperial overlords. This dependent status persisted precariously until Timurid authorities systematically suppressed the dynastic family and incorporated the territory into the directly administered provinces of the Timurid Empire. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Herat; Common languages: Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kart dynasty; Ruler title: Malik; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kart Dynasty (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Timurid Empire

name: County of Castell'Ottieri
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Castell'Ottieri was a compact sovereign fief in southern Tuscany, situated near Mount Amiata in the valley of the Fiora River. Established by the aristocratic Ottieri family and governed from the fortified castle of Castell'Ottieri, the small county preserved its imperial immediacy through shrewd matrimonial alliances and treaties with neighbouring powers. The state successfully preserved its judicial independence against Sienese and Papal expansionism for over two centuries, until territorial sale transferred its sovereignty to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in 1617. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Castellottieri; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: Ottieri family; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Tuscany

name: Habsburg Domains
description: The Habsburg Domains comprised the extensive hereditary crown territories held by the Austrian House of Habsburg outside the formal perimeter of the Holy Roman Empire. Governed centrally from the imperial residence in Vienna, these heterogeneous lands encompassed Hungarian and Croatian frontier domains that required continuous military fortification against Ottoman expansion. The monarchy administered these peripheral lands through composite feudal arrangements and local royal diets, securing a crucial defensive perimeter that formed the foundation for the centralised Austrian Empire proclaimed in 1804. \n\n Status: Hereditary possession; Capital: Vienna; Common languages: German, Hungarian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Composite monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Habsburg; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Austrian Empire

name: Grand Duchy of Tver
label: russian principalities
description: The Grand Duchy of Tver was a powerful late medieval East Slavic principality situated along the upper reaches of the Volga River. Governed by ambitious Rurikid grand princes from the fortified capital of Tver, the realm was Moscow's primary geopolitical rival for leadership over the fragmented Russian principalities. Tver fostered sophisticated monastic culture, vibrant river commerce and independent foreign diplomacy, but internal dynastic division and repeated Muscovite military invasions eventually culminated in the complete conquest of the state by Ivan III in 1485. \n\n Status: Sovereign grand duchy; Capital: Tver; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Sultanate of Khandesh
description: The Sultanate of Khandesh was an independent Muslim realm that governed the fertile Tapti River valley in central western India. Founded by the Farooqi dynasty following secession from the Delhi Sultanate, the state flourished from its administrative capital at Burhanpur and the impregnable hilltop fortress of Asirgarh. Khandesh became renowned across the Deccan for fine textile manufacturing, cotton trade and cosmopolitan cultural patronage, maintaining its autonomy against neighbouring sultanates until Emperor Akbar's Mughal forces conquered the kingdom in 1601. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Burhanpur; Common languages: Persian, Marathi and Deccani; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Farooqi dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Delhi Sultanate; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Principality of Achaea
label: frankokratia
description: The Principality of Achaea functioned as a Frankish crusader state in the Peloponnese during its late medieval phase of feudal dependency under the Kingdom of Naples. Administered from the royal seat of Andravida, the principality's French and Italian chivalric rulers attempted to maintain their coastal possessions against Byzantine advances from the Despotate of the Morea. Weakened by chronic dynastic disputes and encroaching Ottoman fleets, the Latin lordship gradually disintegrated before being partitioned and annexed by the Byzantine Morea in 1432. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Andravida; Common languages: French and Medieval Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Prince of Achaea; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Achaea (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Despotate of the Morea

name: Ottoman Sultanate
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Ottoman Sultanate constituted a powerful transcontinental Islamic empire bridging southeastern Europe and northwestern Anatolia during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Headquartered at Edirne in Thrace, the sultanate commanded formidable Janissary infantry and Sipahi cavalry, conquering vast expanses of the Byzantine Empire and subjugating neighbouring Balkan kingdoms. Although shaken by defeat against Timur at Ankara in 1402, the centralised state quickly rebounded to establish undisputed regional dominance, culminating in the historic capture of Constantinople under Mehmed II in 1453. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Edirne; Official languages: Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ottoman dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ottoman Beylik; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Lordship of Biberstein
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Biberstein was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located in Lower Lusatia. Held by the noble House of Biberstein from their fortified baronial seat, the fief exercised judicial immediacy, collected customs duties on regional merchant roads and retained significant feudal privileges under Bohemian suzerainty. The lordship preserved its distinctive local liberties amid dynastic successions until changing territorial politics and family extinctions in the sixteenth century led to its absorption into the surrounding Margraviate of Brandenburg. \n\n Status: Imperial lordship; Capital: Biberstein; Common languages: German and Lower Sorbian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Biberstein; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Brandenburg

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
description: The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania formed a dynastic personal union in 1385 under the Union of Krewo following the marriage of Jogaila and Queen Jadwiga. Maintaining separate administrative bodies, chanceries and legal codes between Kraków and Vilnius, the dual monarchy successfully joined military strength to check the expansion of the Teutonic Knights. This formidable composite state extended from the Baltic Sea towards the Black Sea steppes, evolving steadily until formal institutional federation created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569. \n\n Status: Personal union; Administrative seat: Kraków and Vilnius; Common languages: Polish, Ruthenian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Dual monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jagiellonian dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Poland; Succeeded by: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth

name: Principality of Andoga
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Andoga was a northern East Slavic feudal appanage situated along the Andoga River in the Beloozero lake basin. Governed by a branch of the Beloozero Rurikid dynasty from the fortified outpost of Andozhsky Gorodok, the small realm derived its livelihood from fur trapping, inland fisheries and small-scale rye agriculture. The principality maintained local autonomy amidst inter-princely rivalries until the growing centralising power of the Grand Duchy of Moscow absorbed its territories during the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Andozhsky Gorodok; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Beloozero; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Beloye Selo
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Beloye Selo was an East Slavic appanage realm located within the forested northern borderlands of Beloozero. Administered by Rurikid princes from the lakeside stronghold of Belozersk, the principality exercised local jurisdiction over surrounding agrarian settlements, salt distribution and fur trapping outposts. Constrained by limited military resources, its ruling family maintained friendly relations with neighbouring northern principalities until diplomatic pressure and territorial purchases by the Grand Duchy of Moscow brought the appanage under direct Muscovite governance in 1471. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Belozersk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Beloozero; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Gjirokastër
label: albanian principalities
description: The Principality of Gjirokastër was an autonomous Albanian medieval realm in northern Epirus established by the aristocratic Zenebishi family. Centred on the hilltop citadel of Gjirokastër, the principality commanded the strategic valley of the Drino River and held extensive estates stretching towards the Ionian Sea. Prince Gjon Zenebishi defended the realm against the Despotate of Epirus and Angevin claims, maintaining independent governance until expanding Ottoman armies conquered the fortress in 1418 and incorporated the lands into the Sanjak of Albania. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Gjirokastër; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Zenebishi family; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Albania

name: Principality of Zahariaj
label: albanian principalities
description: The Principality of Zahariaj was a medieval Albanian feudal domain that held power across the lower Drin River valley and northern coastal lands around the fortress of Danjë. Led by the noble Zaharia family, the lordship defended its strategic castle against rival lords and maintained vital mercantile connections with the Republic of Ragusa and Venice. The realm sustained internal self-determination amidst fluctuating regional alliances until the assassination of Lekë Zaharia in 1444 precipitated Venetian intervention and the absorption of Danjë into the Venetian Stato da Màr. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Danjë; Common languages: Albanian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Zaharia family; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Principality of Dukagjini
label: albanian principalities
description: The Principality of Dukagjini was an autonomous northern Albanian realm established by the noble Dukagjini family across Upper Zadrima and western Kosovo. Governed from the historic administrative centre of Lezhë, the principality oversaw key trans-Balkan trading roads, regulated pastoral communities and promoted traditional customary law. Confronted with mounting Ottoman incursions, the dukes briefly ceded Lezhë to Venetian protection in 1393 before reclaiming regional power and eventually becoming foundational participants in the anti-Ottoman League of Lezhë under Skanderbeg in 1444. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Lezhë; Common languages: Albanian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Dukagjini family; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Zeta; Succeeded by: League of Lezhë

name: Principality of Smolensk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Smolensk was an important East Slavic march that operated under direct Lithuanian suzerainty during the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. Governed from the fortified city of Smolensk along the upper Dnieper River, the principality served as a vital buffer between the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Despite retaining its Rurikid princely dynasty and local Orthodox ecclesiastical structures, recurrent anti-Lithuanian uprisings prompted Grand Duke Vytautas to depose the local monarch and formally annex Smolensk in 1404. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Smolensk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Smolensk (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Kara Del
description: Kara Del was a sovereign Chagatayid Mongol kingdom centred on the oasis city of Kumul in the eastern Tarim Basin. Founded by Prince Gunashiri, a descendant of Chagatai Khan, the oasis state controlled vital arterial routes along the northern Silk Road through the Hami corridor. The kingdom supported caravan commerce, fostered Buddhist and Islamic cultural institutions and navigated complex diplomatic relations with the Northern Yuan before accepting tributary protectorate status under the Ming dynasty in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kumul; Common languages: Mongolian and Old Uyghur; Religion: Buddhism and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chagatayid dynasty; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Chagatai Khanate; Succeeded by: Kara Del (Ming Tributary)

name: Kingdom of Tlemcen
description: The Kingdom of Tlemcen functioned as a vassal state in northwestern Algeria during prolonged intervals of submission to the Marinid Sultanate of Fez. Governed by the Berber Zayyanid dynasty from their royal seat at Tlemcen, the kingdom oversaw prosperous trans-Saharan trading avenues connecting Mediterranean ports with the sub-Saharan interior. Although compelled to acknowledge Marinid suzerainty and pay annual tribute following punitive western campaigns, the Zayyanids maintained internal administrative autonomy, patronised Islamic scholarship and eventually restored full independence when Marinid dynastic authority fractured. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Tlemcen; Common languages: Berber and Maghrebi Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zayyanid dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tlemcen (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Tlemcen (Sovereign)

name: Principality of Kastrioti
label: albanian principalities
description: The Principality of Kastrioti was an independent northern Albanian realm founded by the noble Kastrioti family in the Mat and Dibra highlands. Operating from the fortified stronghold of Krujë, the principality commanded vital mountainous approaches between the Adriatic coast and the Balkan interior under Prince Gjon Kastrioti. The dynasty maintained diplomatic ties with Venice, Ragusa and the Kingdom of Naples while resisting early Ottoman incursions, providing the foundational territorial base for the celebrated resistance leader Skanderbeg during the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Krujë; Common languages: Albanian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Kastrioti family; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Serbian Empire; Succeeded by: League of Lezhë

name: Kingdom of Kaffa
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Kaffa was an independent monarchy situated in the densely forested highlands of southwestern Ethiopia along the Gojeb River. Governed by the Minjo dynasty from the royal residence at Bonga, the kingdom prospered through a rich agrarian economy featuring intensive terraced farming, wild coffee harvesting and lucrative trans-regional trade in gold and civet. Kaffa maintained formidable earthen defensive ramparts that preserved its distinct cultural traditions and territorial sovereignty for centuries until its conquest by Emperor Menelik II in 1897. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bonga; Common languages: Kafa; Religion: Traditional religion and Ethiopian Orthodoxy; Government: Divine monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Minjo dynasty; Ruler title: Tato; Historical era: Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Principality of Palekh
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Palekh was an East Slavic appanage realm located within the historical Vladimir-Suzdal territory of northeastern Rus. Governed by a cadet branch of the Rurikid house from the settlement of Palekh, the small state sustained an agrarian economy supplemented by craft production, regional river trading and forest harvesting. Despite political isolation, the princes defended their patrimony against neighbouring territorial squabbles until diplomatic pressure and centralising initiatives from the Grand Duchy of Moscow absorbed the fief in 1471. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Palekh; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Ryapolovo
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Ryapolovo was a minor East Slavic appanage in northeastern Rus, originating from the territorial divisions of the Starodub princely dynasty. Centred on the fortified settlement of Ryapolovo, the principality's rulers exercised jurisdiction over local peasant communes, woodland resources and small-scale transit trade. The Ryapolovsky princes maintained tenuous autonomy among competing regional lords until the inexorable territorial expansion of the Grand Duchy of Moscow incorporated their ancestral patrimony into the unified Russian state during the 1440s. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Ryapolovo; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Starodub; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Duchy of Cleves
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Cleves was an influential imperial principality situated along both banks of the Lower Rhine on the borderlands of Westphalia and the Low Countries. Elevated from a county in 1417 and ruled by the House of La Marck from the castle town of Kleve, the duchy prospered through intensive agricultural commerce, cloth weaving and river tolls. Dynastic unions with neighbouring Mark, Jülich and Berg forged a potent northwestern power bloc within the Holy Roman Empire throughout the late medieval era. \n\n Status: State of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Kleve; Common languages: Kleverlandish and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: House of La Marck; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: County of Cleves; Succeeded by: United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg

name: Kingdom of Great Joseon
description: The Kingdom of Great Joseon was a highly centralised Korean dynastic realm founded by King Taejo in 1392 following the overthrow of the Goryeo dynasty. Administered from the royal capital of Hanseong, the state entrenched Neo-Confucian governance, established an exemplary scholarly bureaucracy and oversaw major cultural flourishing, including the creation of the Hangul alphabet. Joseon guarded its territorial integrity between the Amnok and Tuman rivers, balancing formal tributary diplomacy with imperial China against strict internal administrative sovereignty for over five centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hanseong; Official languages: Middle Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Korean Confucianism and Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Yi; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Preceded by: Kingdom of Goryeo; Succeeded by: Korean Empire

name: Free Imperial City of Basel
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Basel was a self-governing city-state situated at the strategic bend of the Rhine River in northwestern Switzerland. Having secured municipal emancipation from the local prince-bishopric, the burghers enjoyed imperial immediacy that empowered their merchant guilds, city council and independent judiciary. Basel established itself as an intellectual and commercial crossroads of western Europe, hosting the Council of Basel and patronising humanism before formally severing ties with the Holy Roman Empire to join the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Basel; Common languages: Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban republic; Legislature: City Council of Basel; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Old Swiss Confederacy

name: Signoria of Perugia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Perugia was an autonomous central Italian city-state situated on a defensive hilltop overlooking the upper Tiber valley in Umbria. Governed intermittently by charismatic condottieri and rival patrician factions, including the Michelotti and the violent Baglioni family, the signoria maintained municipal self-determination despite persistent papal territorial claims. Perugia cultivated renowned Renaissance painters, humanistic scholarship and vibrant merchant commerce, sustaining its civic institutions until direct papal military intervention brought the city under papal administrative control in 1541. \n\n Status: Autonomous signoria; Capital: Perugia; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Signoria; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Preceded by: Commune of Perugia; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Duchy of Athens
label: frankokratia
description: The Duchy of Athens entered a period of Venetian protectorate administration in 1395 to counter imminent conquest by expanding Ottoman armies. While the Florentine Acciaioli family retained dynastic claims from the citadel of the Acropolis, Venetian podestàs and military garrisons directed coastal defence, urban fortifications and regional naval operations across Attica. This Venetian protective hegemony managed to preserve the Frankish crusader lordship against Turkish incursions for nearly a decade, until Antonio I Acciaioli recaptured Athens in 1403 and restored independent family lordship. \n\n Status: Protectorate; Capital: Athens; Common languages: Medieval Greek, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal duchy under protectorate; Ruling dynasty: Acciaioli family; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Athens (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Duchy of Athens (Sovereign)

name: Jaunpur Sultanate
description: The Jaunpur Sultanate was an independent Muslim realm established in the central Gangetic plains of northern India following the decline of the Tughlaq dynasty. Founded by the eunuch vizier Malik Sarwar and governed by the Sharqi dynasty from the grand capital of Jaunpur, the sultanate presided over a golden age of monumental Indo-Islamic architecture, fine arts and Persian scholarship. The Sharqi rulers vigorously defended their independence against Delhi while extending authority across Awadh and Bihar, before being defeated and annexed by the Lodi dynasty in 1494. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Jaunpur; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Hindustani and Awadhi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sharqi dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Delhi Sultanate; Succeeded by: Lodi dynasty

name: Kingdom of Bamum
description: The Kingdom of Bamum was a centralised precolonial state located in the volcanic Grassfields plateau of western Cameroon. Founded by King Nchare Yen and ruled from the fortified ancestral capital of Foumban, the kingdom developed a powerful dynastic administration supported by elite warrior societies, royal bronze casting and intensive highland agriculture. The Bamum monarchs continuously expanded territorial borders through coordinated military campaigns while defending their cultural sovereignty, remaining completely independent until German colonial forces occupied the region in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Foumban; Common languages: Bamum; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bamum dynasty; Ruler title: Mfon; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Nditam
description: Nditam was a sovereign precolonial Tikar chiefdom situated in the forested river basin of the Mbam-et-Kim region of central Cameroon. Governed by a traditional paramount ruler from the royal village settlement of Nditam, the polity maintained sacred ancestral rites, regulated regional hunting and farming lands, and controlled local trade routes. The chiefdom preserved its customary governance, communal solidarity and cultural autonomy through centuries of regional migrations until European colonial partitions integrated the Tikar kingdoms into the German Kamerun protectorate around 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign chiefdom; Capital: Nditam; Common languages: Tikar; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Pallavicino State
label: holy roman empire
description: The Pallavicino State was an autonomous feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in western Emilia between the Po River and the Apennines. Formed through the union of the marquisates of Busseto and Cortemaggiore, the estate was ruled by branches of the ancient Pallavicino dynasty as an immediate imperial fief. The small realm enjoyed judicial autonomy, minted its own currency and navigated intense rivalries between the Duchy of Milan and the Papacy until the Farnese dukes of Parma gradually annexed the territory in 1586. \n\n Status: Imperial fief; Capital: Busseto; Common languages: Emilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: House of Pallavicino; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Succeeded by: Duchy of Parma and Piacenza

name: Victual Brothers
description: The Victual Brothers formed a formidable maritime brotherhood of privateers and corsairs that established an autonomous piratical stronghold on the Baltic island of Gotland in 1395. Operating from the fortified port town of Visby, this self-governing guild of equal sharers plundered Scandinavian shipping lanes, interrupted Hanseatic trade networks and challenged Queen Margaret's northern hegemony. Their dominant maritime presence caused widespread economic disruption across the Baltic Sea until a powerful naval expedition dispatched by the Teutonic Order captured Gotland and dispersed the brotherhood in 1398. \n\n Status: Autonomous pirate confederacy; Capital: Visby; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Privateer brotherhood; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Crown of Sweden; Succeeded by: State of the Teutonic Order

name: Duchy of Milan
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Milan was an influential sovereign principality in northern Italy created in 1395 when Gian Galeazzo Visconti purchased the ducal title from Holy Roman Emperor Wenceslaus. Centred on the thriving metropolis of Milan, the duchy encompassed extensive agricultural lands across the Po Valley, fostering revolutionary hydraulic engineering, silk manufacturing and Renaissance cultural patronages. Governed successively by the Visconti and Sforza houses, Milan stood as a major European military and economic powerhouse until the Italian Wars transformed the state into a contested battlefield for foreign empires. \n\n Status: State of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Milan; Common languages: Lombard and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hereditary duchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Visconti; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Preceded by: Lordship of Milan; Succeeded by: Golden Ambrosian Republic

name: Grey League
label: holy roman empire
description: The Grey League was an autonomous alpine confederation established in 1395 across the Vorderrhein and Hinterrhein valleys of Raetia. Formed by local barons, the Abbot of Disentis and free peasant communities gathered at Trun, the league established mutual peace agreements and judicial independence to counteract the predatory power of feudal lords. Named after the simple homespun grey woollen cloaks of its members, the league governed through communal assemblies until federating with neighbouring Raetian leagues to establish the Three Leagues in 1471. \n\n Status: Autonomous confederation; Capital: Disentis; Common languages: Romansh and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Alpine federal republic; Legislature: League Assembly; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Disentis Abbey; Succeeded by: Three Leagues

name: Joint Ferrara and Venice Rule
label: holy roman empire
description: The Joint Ferrara and Venice Rule functioned as a bilateral administrative condominium over the contested Polesine di Rovigo territory along the lower Po River. Established following the Peace of Turin, this joint administration reconciled competing commercial interests between the House of Este in Ferrara and the Republic of Venice, ensuring regulated river navigation and shared customs revenues. Both powers maintained delegated magistrates and garrisons across the low-lying agricultural districts until shifting geopolitical tensions culminated in the Salt War of 1482, leading to outright Venetian annexation. \n\n Status: Condominium; Administrative seat: Ferrara; Common languages: Venetian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Bilateral condominium; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Ferrara; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Kathiri State of Seiyun in Hadhramaut
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Kathiri State of Seiyun in Hadhramaut was a sovereign South Arabian sultanate established in the late fourteenth century across the fertile Wadi Hadhramaut. Governed by the Banu Kathir tribe from their palatial desert capital at Seiyun, the sultanate commanded ancient frankincense routes, irrigated valley palm oases and overland trade leading toward Dhofar and the Arabian Sea. Despite recurrent tribal conflicts with rival Qu'aiti chieftains and mountain bedouin, the Kathiri state preserved its dynastic independence and traditional Islamic legal structures for centuries before entering the British protectorate framework in 1889. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Seiyun; Common languages: Arabic (Hadhrami dialect); Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Kathiri dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Preceded by: Rasulid dynasty; Succeeded by: Kathiri State of Seiyun (British Protectorate)

name: County of Vaduz
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Vaduz was an immediate territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Upper Rhine Valley between the Rhaetian Alps and the river plain. Ruled by the counts of Werdenberg-Sargans from the commanding hilltop fortress of Vaduz Castle, the county derived wealth from regional alpine cattle pastoralism, vineyard cultivation and transit tolls. The estate preserved its imperial immediacy through turbulent feudal successions and alpine skirmishes, forming an enduring political boundary that later became the core of the modern Principality of Liechtenstein upon consolidation in 1719. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Vaduz; Common languages: Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Werdenberg; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: County of Werdenberg; Succeeded by: Principality of Liechtenstein

name: Lordship of Berat
label: albanian principalities
description: The Lordship of Berat was an independent medieval Albanian principality that governed central and southern Albania alongside western Macedonia during the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. Centred on the imposing river fortress of Berat, the realm was directed by the noble Muzaka family, who patronised Orthodox monastic foundations and controlled fertile plains along the Devoll and Vjosa rivers. Despite resolute resistance under Prince Teodor II Muzaka against external encroachments, escalating Ottoman military campaigns broke the principality's defences and integrated the territory into the Sanjak of Albania in 1417. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Berat; Common languages: Albanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Muzaka family; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Albania; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Albania

name: Kalmar Union
description: The Kalmar Union was a grand northern personal union established in 1397 that united the three Scandinavian kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under a single monarch. Designed by Queen Margaret I and inaugurated with the coronation of Eric of Pomerania at Kalmar, the union preserved separate national laws, customary senates and royal privileges while pursuing unified foreign defence against Hanseatic commercial hegemony. Centred administratively at Copenhagen, the fragile union weathered recurrent Swedish noble rebellions until Gustav Vasa's successful war of liberation permanently dismantled Scandinavian unity in 1523. \n\n Status: Sovereign personal union; Capital: Copenhagen; Common languages: Old Danish, Old Swedish, Old Norwegian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective personal union; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Denmark; Succeeded by: Denmark-Norway

name: Marquisate of Balestrino
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Balestrino was a sovereign feudal estate of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Ligurian coastal mountains near Albenga. Administered by a cadet branch of the noble Del Carretto family from their fortified mountain castle at Balestrino, the marquisate commanded overland passes and controlled lucrative olive groves and chestnut forests. The rulers zealously defended their imperial immediacy against the territorial ambitions of the neighbouring Republic of Genoa, preserving self-governing feudal jurisdiction until Spanish Habsburg forces intervened in regional governance during the sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial marquisate; Capital: Balestrino; Common languages: Ligurian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Del Carretto family; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Marquisate of Balestrino (Spanish Feud)

name: Marquisate of Finale
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Finale was an independent maritime state of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the western Ligurian coast of Italy. Held for centuries by the senior branch of the Del Carretto dynasty from the coastal port and walled capital of Finale Ligure, the marquisate served as a crucial sovereign corridor between the Mediterranean and northern Italy.
