The marquisate maintained its independence against repeated naval blockades and military assaults by the Republic of Genoa, until dynastic insolvency and strategic diplomacy prompted its sale to the Spanish Crown in 1602. \n\n Status: March of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Finale Ligure; Common languages: Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Del Carretto family; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: March of Savona; Succeeded by: Spanish Empire

name: Marquisate of Zuccarello
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Zuccarello was a sovereign imperial fief established in western Liguria following the partition of the Clavesana patrimony in the late fourteenth century. Ruled by the Del Carretto family from the fortified valley settlement of Zuccarello, the small state guarded the strategic Neva River valley and exacted transit dues on merchants crossing into Piedmont. The marquisate preserved its autonomy through intricate balancing between Milan, Savoy and Genoa, sustaining its separate feudal status until political realignments and Habsburg diplomacy transferred the territory to Genoa in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial marquisate; Capital: Zuccarello; Common languages: Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Del Carretto family; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Principality of Ansbach
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Ansbach was an immediate imperial territory in Franconia created in 1398 from the southern partition of the Hohenzollern Burgraviate of Nuremberg. Governed from the residential palace in Ansbach, the principality encompassed prosperous agricultural plains, market towns and forest estates along the Franconian Rezat River. The margraves fostered legal reform, established Lutheran Protestantism during the Reformation and developed a professional bureaucracy, preserving their dynastic autonomy within the Franconian Circle until the last margrave abdicated and ceded the territory to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1791. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Ansbach; Common languages: East Franconian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Burgraviate of Nuremberg; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Principality of Bayreuth
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Bayreuth was a self-governing imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire formed from the northern division of the Burgraviate of Nuremberg in 1398. Known initially as Brandenburg-Kulmbach with its court at the Plassenburg fortress before establishing its capital at Bayreuth in 1604, the principality was ruled by Franconian Hohenzollern margraves. The territory expanded its agrarian wealth, promoted baroque urban architecture and patronised musical and academic institutions, retaining its sovereign status until dynastic treaties incorporated the margraviate into the Kingdom of Prussia alongside Ansbach in 1791. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bayreuth; Common languages: Upper Franconian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Burgraviate of Nuremberg; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Signoria of Piombino
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Piombino was an autonomous maritime state on the Tyrrhenian coast of Tuscany, formed in 1399 when Gherardo Appiani surrendered Pisa to Milan while retaining the coastal territory and Elba. Governed from the fortified port town of Piombino, the lordship profited from rich Elban iron mines, Mediterranean maritime trade and maritime customs revenues. The Appiani dynasty maintained their independence through strategic protectorates under Florence, Naples and the Holy Roman Empire, laying the institutional foundations that saw the state elevated to an imperial principality in 1594. \n\n Status: Sovereign lordship; Capital: Piombino; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: Appiani family; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Preceded by: Republic of Pisa; Succeeded by: Principality of Piombino

name: Principality of Yan
description: The Principality of Yan was a northern insurgent state established by Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, during the Jingnan civil war between 1399 and 1402. Operating from his northern military power base at Beiping, the prince mobilised veteran northern frontier cavalry and rebellious Ming garrison troops to challenge the centralising policies of his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor. After three years of intensive warfare across northern China, Zhu Di's armies broke imperial defences, captured the imperial capital of Nanjing and installed the prince as the Yongle Emperor of the unified Ming dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign rebel principality; Capital: Beijing; Common languages: Early Mandarin; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Military monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Zhu; Ruler title: Prince of Yan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ming Dynasty; Succeeded by: Ming Dynasty

name: Alliance of the Four Oirats
description: The Alliance of the Four Oirats was a powerful nomadic confederation of Western Mongol tribes that emerged on the upper Yenisei and Altai steppes around 1400. Formed by the Choros, Torghut, Dörbet and Khoshut clans following the disintegration of the Yuan dynasty, the confederacy challenged Eastern Mongol supremacy under rulers titled taishi. Governed through customary nomadic law and the Mongol-Oirat Code from nomadic encampments near Khovd, the confederacy expanded trade across Inner Asia and inflicted major defeats on Ming armies before eventually fracturing into the Dzungar and Kalmyk khanates. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: Khovd; Common languages: Oirat and Western Mongolic; Religion: Shamanism and Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Tribal confederacy; Ruler title: Taishi; Historical era: Postclassical to Early modern; Preceded by: Northern Yuan; Succeeded by: Dzungar Khanate

name: Đại Ngu
description: Đại Ngu was the official title of the Vietnamese kingdom under the short-lived Hồ dynasty, established in 1400 when the imperial regent Hồ Quý Ly deposed the Trần line. Centred on the massive stone citadel of Tây Đô in Thanh Hóa, the monarchy implemented far-reaching administrative, fiscal and agrarian reforms, including the introduction of paper currency and national civil service examinations. Despite concerted efforts to mobilise coastal defence against foreign aggression, internal political discontent facilitated the Chinese Ming invasion, which defeated the dynasty and established direct rule in 1407. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Tay Do; Official languages: Middle Vietnamese and Classical Chinese; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hồ dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Postclassical; Preceded by: Trần dynasty; Succeeded by: Ming Vietnam

name: Principality of Wales
description: The Principality of Wales was proclaimed in 1400 during the national Welsh uprising led by Owain Glyndŵr against English royal governance. Glyndŵr was declared Prince of Wales by Welsh nobles, mobilising guerrilla armies from mountain strongholds across Gwynedd and Powys and capturing key border fortresses. In 1404, Glyndŵr summoned a national parliament at Machynlleth, signed treaties with France and proposed independent universities and an autonomous Welsh church, sustaining de facto sovereignty until English blockades and attrition crushed the revolt around 1416. \n\n Status: Insurgent principality; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Machynlleth; Common languages: Middle Welsh and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince of Wales; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of England; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Jalayirid Sultanate
label: persia after the disintegration of the ilkhanate
description: The Jalayirid Sultanate operated as a subordinate vassal state under Timurid imperial overlordship following Timur's capture of Baghdad in 1400. Governed by Sultan Ahmad Jalayir from Mesopotamian strongholds, the Mongol Jalayir dynasty was forced to yield tribute and auxiliary military contingents while retaining limited local administrative authority over central and southern Iraq. The sultanate maintained Persian cultural patronages and Islamic scribal institutions amid ongoing regional wars, until violent confrontations with the expanding Black Sheep Turkomans permanently extinguished the dynasty and annexed Baghdad in 1432. \n\n Status: Vassal sultanate; Capital: Baghdad; Common languages: Persian, Arabic and Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jalayirid dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Jalayirid Sultanate (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Kara Koyunlu

name: Achiutla
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Achiutla was an independent Mixtec city-state and sacred ceremonial centre situated in the rugged highlands of the Mixteca Alta in modern Oaxaca, Mexico. Revered as the spiritual heart of the Mixtec civilisation, the realm was governed by hereditary caciques and high priests who performed sacred rituals in ancient mountain cave sanctuaries. Achiutla commanded rich agrarian valley terraces, patronised exquisite pictorial screenfold codices and maintained intricate trade alliances with neighbouring Mixtec kingdoms until Aztec military expansion subjugated the region in the late fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Achiutla; Common languages: Mixtec; Religion: Mixtec polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Cacique; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Succeeded by: Aztec Empire

name: Effutu
description: Effutu was an independent Guan coastal kingdom situated along the Gulf of Guinea in central modern Ghana. Ruled by traditional monarchs from the bustling coastal settlement of Winneba, the kingdom flourished through maritime fishing, salt extraction and extensive overland exchange of agricultural produce with forest societies. Effutu developed sophisticated religious institutions, including the celebrated annual deer-hunting festival of Aboakyer, preserving its indigenous political autonomy and coastal commercial influence against Fante and Ashanti encroachment until regional reorganisations transformed its governance in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Winneba; Common languages: Efutu and Guan; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Omanhene; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: Fante Confederacy

name: Ennarea
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: Ennarea was an independent kingdom in the Gibe River basin of southwestern Ethiopia, having achieved sovereignty following separation from the earlier Damot state. Governed by monarchs styled hinnare-tato from their fortified administrative seat at Yadare, the realm developed a thriving agrarian economy renowned for gold mining, cattle breeding and extensive long-distance trade. Ennarea maintained traditional Omotic religious and political institutions, maintaining internal autonomy despite tributary ties with the Ethiopian Empire until migratory pressure from expanding Oromo groups overwhelmed the kingdom around 1710. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yadare; Common languages: Gonga; Religion: Traditional religion and Ethiopian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Hinnare-tato; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Kingdom of Damot; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Limmu-Ennarea

name: Gondwana Kingdom
description: The Gondwana Kingdom, often known as Garha-Mandla, was a powerful indigenous Adivasi realm that dominated the rugged highlands and river basins of central India. Governed by hereditary Gond monarchs from fortress centres such as Jabalpur, the kingdom established an efficient administrative system supported by sophisticated irrigation tanks, extensive rice cultivation and forest trade. The dynasty zealously protected its cultural customs and territorial sovereignty against neighbouring regional sultanates, sustaining substantial independence until the Mughal Empire and subsequent Maratha expansions subdued the kingdom in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jabalpur; Common languages: Gondi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism and Gond animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rajgond dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Ijebu Kingdom
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: The Ijebu Kingdom was a prominent and highly organised Yoruba state situated in the forested coastal hinterland of southwestern Nigeria. Governed by a sacred monarch titled the awujale from the walled capital of Ijebu Ode, the kingdom operated through a sophisticated balance of power between the royal court and the Osugbo society of noble elders. Ijebu commanded lucrative commercial transit corridors connecting the Atlantic lagoon trade with inland Yoruba cities, maintaining strict political independence and defensive borders until British expeditionary forces conquered the state in 1892. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ijebu Ode; Common languages: Yoruba (Ijebu dialect); Religion: Yoruba religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Awujale; Historical era: Precolonial; Preceded by: Ife Empire; Succeeded by: Lagos Colony

name: Jambughoda State
description: Jambughoda State, historically designated as Narukot, was a sovereign Rajput principality established in eastern Gujarat near the Champaner hills during the late fourteenth century. Ruled by the Parmar clan of Rajputs from the capital town of Jambughoda, the principality commanded forested mountain passes populated predominantly by Naikda and Koli communities. The state maintained internal judicial self-governance and pastoral tribute collection, navigating regional overlordship from the Gujarat Sultanate and later the Marathas until formal treaties brought the realm into the British Raj's Baroda Agency in 1827. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Jambughoda; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Parmar dynasty; Ruler title: Thakor; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: Jambughoda State (British Protectorate)

name: Jehari
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Jehari was an independent Khas mountain principality situated in the rugged Bheri River watershed of western Nepal, constituting one of the historical Chaubisi Rajya petty states. Governed by hereditary Hindu chieftains from the hill fortress of Jehari, the realm oversaw mountain farming terraces, livestock grazing valleys and trans-Himalayan trade routes. The principality maintained local autonomy through shifting defensive alliances with neighbouring Baise and Chaubisi lords until the expanding Gorkha Kingdom annexed the territory into the unified Nepalese state during the unification wars of 1787. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Jehari; Common languages: Khas and Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Kakongo Kingdom
description: The Kakongo Kingdom was an autonomous Central African realm situated along the Atlantic coast north of the Congo River in modern Cabinda and the Republic of the Congo. Governed by hereditary monarchs from the royal capital of Kinguele, the state developed a flourishing maritime and riverine trade in raffia cloth, copper and agricultural products. Although maintaining close cultural, linguistic and periodic tributary ties with the neighbouring Kingdom of Kongo, Kakongo preserved its distinct dynastic sovereignty until European colonial powers partitioned the coast in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kinguele; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Bukongo; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial; Preceded by: Vungu Kingdom; Succeeded by: Portuguese Congo

name: Kalina
description: Kalina refers to the autonomous indigenous communities and maritime chieftaincies established by the Carib and Kalinago peoples across Guadeloupe and neighbouring islands in the eastern Caribbean. Free from centralised monarchical institutions, these seafaring islanders governed their settlements through hereditary war captains, councils of elders and collective assemblies. The Kalina maintained sophisticated oceanic canoe navigation, cassava agriculture and extensive inter-island exchange, defending their island homelands against rival groups until the arrival of Spanish and French colonial expeditions in the late fifteenth and seventeenth centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal society; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Carib and Island Carib; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Pre-Columbian; Succeeded by: Spanish Empire

name: Kingdom of Bone
description: The Kingdom of Bone was an influential Bugis state situated in the south-western peninsula of Sulawesi in maritime Southeast Asia. Governed by an elected monarch titled the arung mangkau from the inland capital of Watampone, the kingdom was organised around a powerful aristocratic council of seven noble lords known as the Ade Pitue. Bone developed sophisticated wet-rice agriculture, maritime commerce and legal codes, fiercely contesting regional hegemony against neighbouring Gowa before eventually becoming the dominant power of South Sulawesi throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Watampone; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Bugis animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Arung Mangkau; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Kingdom of Bunyoro
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Bunyoro, historically known as Bunyoro-Kitara, was a dominant precolonial empire in the African Great Lakes region of western Uganda. Ruled by the Babiito dynasty from royal palaces including Hoima, the kingdom held sway over extensive agricultural, pastoral and iron-working territories between Lake Victoria and Lake Albert. The realm was governed by a sacred monarch titled the omukama, whose armies expanded across central Uganda before internal fragmentation and prolonged military conflicts with expanding Buganda and British colonial forces eroded its power in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hoima; Common languages: Runyoro; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Babiito dynasty; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Precolonial; Preceded by: Empire of Kitara; Succeeded by: Uganda Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Loango
description: The Kingdom of Loango was a major coastal Bantu state that controlled the Atlantic littoral north of the Congo River in modern Congo, Gabon and Cabinda. Governed by monarchs styled the malooango from the walled capital of Bwali, the kingdom flourished through extensive ivory hunting, woven raffia cloth manufacture and regional trade in smelted copper. Loango achieved complete political emancipation from the Kingdom of Kongo, establishing a powerful commercial hegemony along the Central African coastline until European colonial expansion dissolved its sovereign administration in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bwali; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Bukongo; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Malooango; Historical era: Precolonial; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kongo; Succeeded by: French Congo

name: Kingdom of Rukum
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Rukum was an autonomous mountain principality situated in the high Himalayan valleys of the Rapti and Bheri watersheds in western Nepal. Functioning as one of the historical Chaubisi Rajya petty states, the kingdom was governed by Khas Hindu kings from the fortified hill settlement of Rukumkot. The realm derived wealth from upland pastoral grazing, copper mining and trans-Himalayan salt trade passing into Tibet. Rukum defended its rugged borders through shifting alliances until the centralising campaigns of the Gorkha Kingdom annexed the principality in 1787. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Rukumkot; Common languages: Khas and Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Kingdom of Wajoq
description: The Kingdom of Wajoq was an elective Bugis constitutional monarchy situated along the eastern plains of the South Sulawesi peninsula. Headquartered at the fortress settlement of Tosora, the realm was governed by an elected supreme ruler titled the arung matoa, who presided over a tripartite council of hereditary clan lords and civilian representatives. Wajoq developed extensive commercial ties, pioneered progressive written legal codes guaranteeing individual rights and rose to brief regional hegemony during the eighteenth century before succumbing to Dutch colonial pacification in 1906. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tosora; Common languages: Bugis; Religion: Bugis animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Elective constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Arung Matoa; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Preceded by: Cinnotabiq; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Laghouat
label: berber kingdoms
description: Laghouat was an independent Berber oasis principality located in the Amour Range of the Saharan Atlas in central Algeria. Governed by the Maghraoua tribal confederation from the fortified desert oasis of Laghouat, the state derived significant revenue from trans-Saharan camel caravans, extensive date palm cultivation and artisanal tapestry weaving. The community defended its desert trade crossroads against expanding Ottoman beyliks and rival nomadic confederacies, maintaining local tribal sovereignty until sustained French colonial sieges breached the town walls in 1852. \n\n Status: Sovereign oasis principality; Capital: Laghouat; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Tribal principality; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: French Algeria

name: Mamprusi Kingdom
description: The Mamprusi Kingdom was an ancient Gur state that dominated the savannah tablelands of northeastern Ghana and adjacent northern regions. Established by migrating royal warriors and administered from the sacred capital of Nalerigu, the kingdom was ruled by a revered sovereign titled the nayiri, who was ritually acknowledged as the elder sibling among northern voltaic monarchies. The state oversaw profitable trade routes linking the Sahelian kingdoms with southern forest goldfields, preserving its traditional court customs and territorial autonomy until British colonial annexation in 1899. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nalerigu; Common languages: Mampruli; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Nayiri; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: Northern Territories of the Gold Coast

name: Masina
description: Masina was a pastoral and agrarian kingdom established by Fulani clans within the fertile wetlands of the Inner Niger Delta in central Mali. Centred on the fortified settlement of Hamdallaye and earlier riverside capitals, the realm maintained a sophisticated pastoral economy sustained by seasonal livestock transhumance and flood-recession agriculture. The ruling ardo monarchs maintained local autonomy by carefully balancing alliances with neighbouring imperial powers such as Mali and Songhai, defending their grazing territories until the early nineteenth-century jihad transformed the state into the Massina Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hamdallaye; Common languages: Fula; Religion: Traditional religion and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ardo; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Massina Empire

name: Menceyato of Abona
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Abona was an independent Guanche kingdom situated across the arid volcanic slopes and southern coastlands of Tenerife. Ruled successively by the menceys Atguaxoña and Adxoña from the residential district of Abona, the realm relied on extensive goat pastoralism, coastal shellfish gathering and seasonal highland foraging. Abona avoided direct military entanglement during initial Castilian landings, adopting a cautious neutrality before ultimately submitting to the Crown of Castile following the pacification of the northern resistance kingdoms in late 1494. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Abona; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Adeje
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Adeje was a sovereign aboriginal polity situated in the southwestern volcanic district of Tenerife, encompassing the ancestral heartland of King Tinerfe the Great. Governed by menceys Pelinor and Sunta from the settlement of Adeje, the kingdom maintained abundant hillside springs, fertile grazing pastures and traditional stone dwelling hamlets. During the Spanish conquest under Alonso Fernández de Lugo, Adeje opted for peaceful diplomacy as one of the southern peace factions, preserving its local communities from devastation before formal integration into Castilian colonial administration. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Adeje; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Anaga
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Anaga was a fiercely independent Guanche realm encompassing the rugged, cloud-forested mountains and deep maritime ravines of northeastern Tenerife. Governed by Mencey Beneharo from the highland redoubt of Anaga, the society sustained an insular pastoral way of life and utilised steep volcanic cliffs for strategic collective defence. Anaga joined the northern confederation of resistance against Castilian conquistadors, waging guerrilla warfare across mountain defiles until catastrophic military defeats and European diseases forced its surviving leadership to surrender in December 1495. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Anaga; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Daute
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Daute was an autonomous aboriginal kingdom occupying the far northwestern promontory and rugged Teno massif of Tenerife. Ruled by the defiant menceys Cocanaymo and Romen from the coastal valley of Daute, the kingdom possessed rich volcanic terraces and natural cliffside fortifications. Firmly opposed to European colonisation, Daute committed its warrior contingents to the grand northern anti-Castilian alliance under Bencomo, sustaining fierce resistance throughout successive highland skirmishes until European firearms and cavalry forced its capitulation in the spring of 1494. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Daute; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Güímar
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Güímar was an influential Guanche realm situated across the sheltered southeastern valley of Tenerife. Governed by Mencey Añaterve from the royal settlement of Güímar, the kingdom was celebrated as the sacred site where the venerated image of the Virgin of Candelaria first appeared to indigenous goatherds. Having hosted early Franciscan missionaries under Friar Alfonso de Bolaños, Güímar allied with the Castilian forces of Alonso Fernández de Lugo as a peace faction, facilitating Spanish logistics during the final subjugation of the island. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Güímar; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Icode
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Icode was a sovereign Guanche kingdom situated on the fertile, pine-covered northern slopes of Tenerife beneath Mount Teide. Governed by Mencey Pelicar from the settlement of Icode, the realm prospered from perennial alpine streams, rich volcanic soil and abundant forest resources centred near its sacred ancient dragon tree. When Spanish forces invaded northern Tenerife, Icode allied with neighbouring kingdoms to defend indigenous autonomy, fighting tenaciously across difficult ravine terrain before Spanish cavalry superiority compelled the kingdom's formal surrender in late 1494. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Icode; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Tacoronte
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Tacoronte was a powerful northern Guanche kingdom situated in the fertile agrarian hills between the Cordillera Dorsal and the Atlantic coast. Ruled by Mencey Acaimo from the settlement of Tacoronte, the kingdom mobilised seasoned spearmen and stone throwers to defend its rich cereal fields and woodland pastures. Tacoronte formed a central component of the anti-Castilian war league, playing an instrumental role in the devastating ambush of Spanish troops at the First Battle of Acentejo before being subdued in May 1494. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tacoronte; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Taoro
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Taoro was the most prosperous and politically pre-eminent Guanche kingdom on Tenerife, commanding the fertile expanses of the Orotava Valley. Governed by the formidable Mencey Bencomo and his successor Bentor from the seat of Taoro, the realm organised the grand northern military coalition against the Castilian invasion. After inflicting a crushing defeat on the Spanish at the Barranco de Acentejo in 1494, Taoro's warriors were ultimately decimated by introduced epidemic diseases and cavalry assaults, leading Bentor to choose ritual suicide over surrender in 1496. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Taoro; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Menceyato of Tegueste
label: guanche states
description: The Menceyato of Tegueste was an autonomous Guanche kingdom situated in an upland valley basin between the Anaga mountain range and the northern coast of Tenerife. Ruled by Mencey Tegueste II from the valley settlement of Tegueste, the polity maintained rich livestock herds and closely integrated trade ties with adjacent northern communities. Staunchly committed to indigenous independence, Tegueste joined the northern resistance coalition under Taoro, fighting desperately against Alonso Fernández de Lugo's invading forces until Spanish victory at the battlefields of La Laguna dissolved the native monarchy. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tegueste; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Guanche polytheism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mencey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Tenerife; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Mong Lem State
label: shan states
description: Mong Lem State, known historically as Menglian, was an autonomous Tai Nüa principality situated in the rugged frontier mountains of southwestern Yunnan along the upper Salween watershed. Ruled by hereditary Shan saophas from the administrative seat of Menglian, the state governed ethnically diverse Dai, Lahu and Va communities under traditional customary law. The principality maintained local autonomy through adept tributary diplomacy with both the Chinese Ming and Qing courts and neighbouring Burmese kingdoms, preserving its traditional feudal institutions until twentieth-century administrative integration incorporated the region into modern China. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Menglian; Common languages: Tai Nüa and Southwest Mandarin; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and Animism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: Qing Dynasty

name: Mongyang State
label: shan states
description: Mongyang State, often referred to as Mohnyin, was an outlying Shan principality situated in the upper Ayeyarwady basin of modern northern Myanmar. Governed by ambitious Shan saophas from the fortified valley town of Mong Yang, the state developed formidable military strength through its control over fertile river valleys and inland trade routes. During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Mongyang played a decisive role in the Wars of the Shan States, repeatedly challenging the Burmese Kingdom of Ava until expanding Toungoo armies conquered the principality. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Mong Yang; Common languages: Shan and Old Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Toungoo dynasty

name: Nso
description: Nso was an independent precolonial kingdom situated in the rugged Bamenda Grassfields of northwestern Cameroon. Governed by a sacred paramount ruler titled the fon from the ancestral capital of Kumbo, the kingdom was structured around hereditary noble councils, warrior sodalities such as the Manjong, and the secretive Ngwerong regulatory society. The state established intensive terraced agriculture, developed distinctive beadwork and royal wood carving traditions, and vigorously maintained its political sovereignty against Fulani incursions until German military expeditions subdued the Grassfields in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kimbo; Common languages: Lamnso; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Nsundi Kingdom
description: The Nsundi Kingdom was an early Bantu realm situated along the Inkisi and lower Congo rivers in the modern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Governed by local monarchs from the royal settlement of Nsoundi, the polity controlled fertile riverine agriculture, iron-smelting furnaces and lucrative commercial crossings connecting the Atlantic hinterland. Through dynastic negotiations and military expansion during the fifteenth century, Nsundi was successfully integrated into the expanding Kingdom of Kongo, subsequently serving as the prestigious appanage province typically reserved for the royal heir apparent. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nsoundi; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Bukongo; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kongo

name: Ntem
description: Ntem was an independent precolonial forest chieftaincy located in the river basin of the Ntem and Campo drainage in southern Cameroon. Administered from the settlement of Ambam, the realm was organised through patrilineal clan councils and elders who coordinated forest agriculture, hunting reserves and regional palm oil exchange. The community preserved its customary judicial assemblies and spiritual rites amidst successive Bantu migrations, maintaining territorial independence until French and German colonial partition treaties divided the ancestral borderlands at the turn of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign chiefdom; Capital: Ambam; Common languages: Fang and Beti; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Principality of Kazym
label: yugra principalities
description: The Principality of Kazym was an indigenous Khanty state situated along the forested basin of the Kazym River in northwestern Siberia. Governed by hereditary native princes from fortified wooden settlements, the realm maintained a hunter-gatherer economy enriched by sable fur harvesting, sturgeon fishing and seasonal reindeer pastoralism. The princes performed ancestral shamanic rituals, collected tribute from river settlements and guarded regional waterways against neighbouring Siberian Tatars, preserving substantial self-governance until Tsarist Russian military expeditions established permanent Cossack forts and annexed the river basin in 1594. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Kazym; Common languages: Khanty; Religion: Shamanism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia

name: Principality of Kod
label: yugra principalities
description: The Principality of Kod, often designated as Koda, was a powerful Khanty state that dominated the waterways of the middle Ob River in northwestern Siberia. Governed by the indigenous Alachev dynasty from fortified river strongholds such as Shorkar, the principality maintained substantial military power through fleets of river war canoes and elite archers. Kod frequently allied with the Grand Duchy of Moscow against neighbouring rival principalities, enjoying significant internal autonomy and collecting furs until the expanding Russian state abolished the native dynasty and incorporated the territory in 1643. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Koda; Common languages: Khanty; Religion: Shamanism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Alachev; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia

name: Principality of Novlenskoye
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Novlenskoye was an East Slavic feudal appanage located across the upper Volga basin, created through the partition of ancestral princely patrimonies. Administered from the fortified settlement of Novlenskoe, the principality was ruled by a cadet branch of the Rurikid dynasty who oversaw local agrarian communes, forest hunting tracts and river transport dues. Constrained by limited military resources, its rulers pursued peaceful coexistence with neighbouring lords until diplomatic agreements and monetary purchases by the Grand Duchy of Moscow formally absorbed the principality in 1471. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Novlenskoe; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Yaroslavl; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Principality of Zaozerye
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Zaozerye was an independent East Slavic appanage realm located along the northern shores of Lake Kubenskoye in the Vologda region. Governed by local Rurikid princes from the lakeside settlement of Zaozerye, the territory prospered from productive freshwater fisheries, fur trading and grain farming along the Sukhona water route. The principality preserved its local administrative institutions and religious endowments throughout the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, until dynastic marriages and Muscovite political centralisation incorporated the domain into the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1448. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Zaozerye; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Yaroslavl; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Rajahnate of Cebu
label: barangay states
description: The Rajahnate of Cebu was an Indianised coastal mandala monarchy situated on the eastern littoral of Cebu in the central Philippine archipelago. Founded according to Visayan oral tradition by Sri Lumay, a prince of Chola and Sumatran descent, the polity was governed from the port settlement of Singhapala. The rajahnate flourished through maritime trade with Ming China, Champa and Malacca, commanding regional seafaring trade until Ferdinand Magellan made landfall in 1521, followed by Spanish conquest under Miguel López de Legazpi in 1565. \n\n Status: Sovereign rajahnate; Capital: Cebu; Common languages: Old Cebuano and Old Malay; Religion: Syncretic Hinduism, Buddhism and Animism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: Rajah; Historical era: Classical to Early modern; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of the Philippines

name: Shamkhalate of Tarki
label: caucasian khanates
description: The Shamkhalate of Tarki was a prominent Kumyk feudal state that held dominion across the eastern foothills and Caspian coastal plain of Dagestan. Headquartered at the fortified ancient mountain town of Tarki, the realm was led by an elected prince titled the shamkhal, who commanded feudal levies of horsemen and regulated major Silk Road transit passes. The state maintained a complex geopolitical balancing act between the Persian Safavids, the Ottoman Empire and Tsardom of Russia, asserting regional dominance in the North Caucasus before entering formal Ottoman vassalage in 1578. \n\n Status: Sovereign shamkhalate; Capital: Tarki; Common languages: Kumyk; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Shamkhal; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Golden Horde; Succeeded by: Shamkhalate of Tarki (Ottoman Vassal)

name: Sultanate of Malacca
description: The Sultanate of Malacca was a pre-eminent Malay maritime empire founded around 1400 by Parameswara along the strategic Strait of Malacca. Governed from the booming port capital of Melaka, the sultanate commanded international shipping between China, India and the Indonesian archipelago, establishing Classical Malay as the regional diplomatic lingua franca. Malacca became the premier Southeast Asian centre for Islamic dissemination, legal scholarship and maritime commerce, flourishing until Portuguese expeditionary forces under Afonso de Albuquerque conquered the royal citadel in 1511, scattering the dynasty into regional successor states. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Melaka; Official languages: Classical Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Postclassical to Early modern; Preceded by: Kingdom of Singapura; Succeeded by: Johor Sultanate

name: Tomaras of Gwalior
description: The Tomaras of Gwalior was an independent Rajput dynasty that ruled the strategic hill fortress and fertile surrounding plateau of Gwalior in central India. Having asserted autonomy following the disintegration of the Delhi Sultanate in the 1390s, the Tomara monarchs converted the sandstone citadel into a magnificent centre of classical Indian music, Sanskrit literature and Jain temple architecture. The dynasty successfully repelled repeated military sieges launched by the Sayyid and Lodi sultans of Delhi, maintaining its regal sovereignty until Ibrahim Lodi captured the fortress in 1518. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gwalior; Common languages: Sanskrit and Braj Bhasha; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tomara dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Delhi Sultanate; Succeeded by: Lodi dynasty

name: Tripura Kingdom
description: The Tripura Kingdom was an independent Tibeto-Burman realm that dominated the hilly tracts and lush river valleys of Northeast India along the Bengal frontier. Governed by the ancient Manikya dynasty from royal capitals at Udaipur and later Agartala, the kingdom developed a powerful military force that successfully checked Delhi and Bengal Sultanate incursions. The Manikya monarchs blended indigenous Tripuri customs with Sanskritic Hinduism, patronised Bengali literature and issued distinctive silver coinage, preserving their mountain sovereignty until British colonial suzerainty established a formal princely protectorate in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Agartala; Common languages: Kokborok and Bengali; Religion: Hinduism and Animism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Manikya dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: Tripura State (British Protectorate)

name: Uvwie
description: Uvwie was an autonomous Urhobo kingdom situated along the navigable Warri River basin in the western Niger Delta of modern southern Nigeria. Governed by a sacred monarch titled the ovie from the traditional political capital of Effurun, the state was administered through titled age-grade societies, ward councils and ancestral shrines. Uvwie prospered through extensive riverine canoe commerce, palm oil processing and agricultural production, jealously maintaining its distinct linguistic identity and political sovereignty against neighbouring Itsekiri and Benin pressures until British colonial penetration subjugated the delta in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Effurun; Common languages: Uvwie; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Ovie; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Yauri
description: Yauri was an independent Hausa kingdom and riverine emirate established along the Middle Niger River in modern northwestern Nigeria. Governed by traditional rulers styled the sarkin Yauri from the fortified walled capital of Bin Yauri, the kingdom developed a lucrative commercial economy based on river transport, dry-season onion farming and trans-Saharan trading connections. Yauri resisted military subjugation by larger neighbours such as the Songhai Empire and Kebbi, maintaining its territorial integrity and customary governance until the Fulani jihad of the early nineteenth century absorbed the state into the Sokoto Caliphate. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bin Yauri; Common languages: Hausa; Religion: Traditional religion and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sarkin Yauri; Historical era: Precolonial; Succeeded by: Sokoto Caliphate

name: Kingdom of Cusco
description: The Kingdom of Cusco was an Andean monarchy founded by the Quechua-speaking Inca people within the fertile upland valley of Cusco in southern Peru. Governed by sacred monarchs titled the Sapa Inca from their stone palace capital, the state functioned as a regional city-state surrounded by competing warlike confederations such as the Chancas and Lupacas. Cusco developed sophisticated stone masonry, terraced mountain maize cultivation and civic canal systems, laying the socio-political and military foundations that allowed Pachacuti to transform the kingdom into the continent-spanning Inca Empire after 1438. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cusco; Common languages: Quechua, Aymara and Puquina; Religion: Inca polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hanan Cusco; Ruler title: Sapa Inca; Historical era: Pre-Columbian; Preceded by: Killke culture; Succeeded by: Inca Empire

name: Signoria of Bologna
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Bologna was an autonomous city-state in Emilia-Romagna that flourished under the aristocratic ascendancy of the Bentivoglio family. Governed from the family palazzo in Bologna, the signoria maintained municipal republican forms alongside de facto princely dynastic rule, patronising celebrated Renaissance painters, humanist scholars and the historic university. The Bentivoglio lords deftly balanced competing diplomatic pressures from Venice, Florence and Milan to safeguard their local sovereignty, until the military campaigns of Pope Julius II stormed the city in 1506 and incorporated Bologna directly into the Papal States. \n\n Status: Autonomous signoria; Capital: Bologna; Common languages: Bolognese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Signoria; Ruling dynasty: Bentivoglio family; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Renaissance; Preceded by: Commune of Bologna; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Sultanate of Malwa
description: The Sultanate of Malwa was an independent Muslim state established in central India in 1401 when the Afghan governor Dilawar Khan Ghuri declared sovereignty following Timur's sack of Delhi. Ruling from the fortified provincial centres of Dhar and later the impregnable plateau fortress of Mandu, the sultanate oversaw prosperous cotton agricultural plains and major trade routes across the Vindhya Range. Malwa developed distinctive architectural styles characterised by lofty sandstone mosques and royal palaces, engaging in protracted wars with Gujarat, Mewar and the Bahmanis before being annexed by Akbar's Mughal forces in 1562. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Mandu; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Malvi and Hindustani; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ghurid and Khalji dynasties; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Delhi Sultanate; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Swiss Associate Territories
label: holy roman empire
description: The Swiss Associate Territories encompassed a diverse network of sovereign states, urban republics and monastic estates linked to the Old Swiss Confederacy through formal perpetual alliances. Without a centralised administrative capital, these associated lands included the Republic of the Valais, the Three Leagues, the Imperial Abbey of Saint Gall and the city of Biel. These territories maintained internal self-governance, independent courts and municipal armies while coordinating common military defence and foreign policy through the federal Tagsatzung diet, preserving their unique status until the French Revolutionary invasions dismantled the old confederate order in 1798. \n\n Status: Confederated associate territories; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Reformed Protestantism; Government: Confederal association; Legislature: Tagsatzung; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Succeeded by: Helvetic Republic

name: Hanthawaddy Kingdom (Military Occupation)
label: mon kingdoms
description: The Hanthawaddy Kingdom maintained an extensive military occupation over contested Upper Burmese territories during the protracted Forty Years' War against the Kingdom of Ava. Commanded directly by King Razadarit from fortified river encampments without a civilian capital, Mon expeditionary forces seized fortified towns along the Ayeyarwady River and garrisoned captured agricultural districts. These frontline garrisons enforced martial administration, collected logistics tribute and maintained forward blockade cordons until reciprocal military exhaustion and peace settlements concluded active hostilities between the Mon and Burmese crowns. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Royal army field headquarters; Common languages: Mon and Old Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military occupation administration; Historical era: Warring states; Preceded by: Kingdom of Ava; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Ava

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania maintained joint military occupation administrations over captured frontier zones during active campaigns against Muscovite, Teutonic and Moldavian forces. Administered directly by crown hetmans and field starosts from fortified forward camps without a civilian seat, these martial zones secured lines of communication and enforced logistical requisitioning. These military occupation commands operated exclusively during wartime operations, being demobilised or converted into permanent voivodeships following the conclusion of formal border truces and territorial treaties. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Expeditionary military command; Common languages: Polish, Ruthenian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Succeeded by: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth

name: Serbian Despotate
description: The Serbian Despotate was an autonomous South Slavic realm that arose from the remnants of Moravian Serbia under Despot Stefan Lazarević. Governed from the fortified river capitals of Belgrade and Smederevo, the despotate enjoyed a notable economic and cultural renaissance, propelled by prosperous silver mining at Novo Brdo and refined Byzantine-Slavic literary patronage. Navigating perilous diplomatic waters between Hungarian protection and Ottoman vassalage, the despotate mounted fierce military defence until Sultan Mehmed II stormed the final citadel of Smederevo in 1459, extinguishing medieval Serbian sovereignty. \n\n Status: Sovereign despotate; Capital: Belgrade; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lazarević and Branković dynasties; Ruler title: Despot; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Moravian Serbia; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Smederevo

name: Ottoman Sultanate
label: ottoman interregnum
description: The Ottoman Sultanate under Prince Süleyman Çelebi constituted the European half of the divided Ottoman realm during the chaotic Ottoman Interregnum. Operating from the royal administrative capital of Edirne in Thrace, Süleyman governed the core Balkan provinces of Rumelia, commanding veteran Janissary regiments and signing diplomatic treaties with the Byzantine Empire and Venice. His court patronised classical Ottoman poetry and sustained regional trade, but escalating military conflicts against his rival brothers culminating in Musa Çelebi's European invasion brought about Süleyman's overthrow and death in 1411. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Edirne; Official languages: Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ottoman dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ottoman Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Ottoman Sultanate
label: ottoman interregnum
description: The Ottoman Sultanate under Prince Mehmed Çelebi was an autonomous rival faction established during the civil war of the Ottoman Interregnum following Sultan Bayezid I's capture at Ankara. Governed from the mountainous stronghold of Amasya in northern Anatolia, Mehmed consolidated control over the province of Rûm, rallied loyal Turkmen cavalry and defeated rival princely brothers across central Anatolia. Demonstrating exceptional strategic and diplomatic acumen, Mehmed progressively conquered the remaining splinter domains, defeated Musa Çelebi in 1413 and reunited the entire Ottoman realm as Sultan Mehmed I. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Amasya; Official languages: Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ottoman dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ottoman Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Kingdom of Georgia
description: The Kingdom of Georgia functioned as a tributary vassal state under Timurid imperial overlordship during the early fifteenth century following Timur's devastating Caucasian invasions. Governed by the Bagrationi dynasty from the ancient capital of Tbilisi, the Christian monarchy was compelled to pay annual tribute and provide auxiliary forces to the Timurid court while jealously maintaining its internal governance and Orthodox church liturgy. King George VII rebuilt devastated towns and fortified mountain defiles, successfully reclaiming full royal sovereignty as soon as Timur's death in 1405 precipitated the fracture of Timurid imperial control. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Tbilisi; Common languages: Middle Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Georgia (Sovereign); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia (Sovereign)

name: Eastern Court
description: The Eastern Court, known historically as the Kedhaton Wetan, was a breakaway Javanese royal realm centred at Blambangan during the Regreg civil war within the Majapahit Empire. Led by Prince Bhre Wirabhumi in open defiance of the Western Court of Wikramawardhana, the court established separate sovereign administration across eastern Java and Bali between 1405 and 1406. The bitter dynastic conflict depleted the empire's financial resources and naval supremacy before royal forces captured the eastern redoubt, beheaded Wirabhumi and reunified the fractured realm, leaving Majapahit permanently weakened. \n\n Status: Sovereign rebel realm; Capital: Blambangan; Common languages: Old Javanese; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Rajasa; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Postclassical; Preceded by: Majapahit Empire; Succeeded by: Majapahit Empire

name: Jumla
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Jumla was a prominent Khas mountain kingdom situated in the Sinja Valley of the Karnali basin in northwestern Nepal. Serving as the primary successor to the ancient Khasa Malla Empire, the kingdom was governed by Hindu monarchs from the high-altitude fortress town of Jumla. The state served as the cradle of the early Khas language, maintained extensive livestock grazing on alpine plateaus and regulated profitable trans-Himalayan trade routes into western Tibet until the military expansion of the Gorkha Kingdom conquered the realm in 1788. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jumla; Common languages: Khas and Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Preceded by: Khasa Kingdom; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Sultanate of Sulu
description: The Sultanate of Sulu was an Islamic maritime realm that operated as a tributary vassal under the Sultanate of Brunei following its foundation in the Sulu Archipelago. Governed by Sultan Sharif ul-Hashim from the port capital of Jolo and royal residences at Buansa, the state commanded lucrative maritime trade in pearls, sea cucumber and bird nests across the Sulu and Celebes seas. While acknowledging Bruneian suzerainty and participating in regional trade networks, the Tausug sultans steadily consolidated power through the Ruma Bechara noble council, ultimately achieving full sovereignty by 1578. \n\n Status: Vassal sultanate; Capital: Jolo; Common languages: Tausug, Sama and Classical Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruling dynasty: House of Hashim; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Postclassical to Early modern; Preceded by: Precolonial barangays; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Sulu (Sovereign)

name: Kingdom of Gáldar
label: guanche states
description: The Kingdom of Gáldar was an indigenous Canarian realm that governed the northern and western portions of Gran Canaria throughout the fifteenth century. Formed following the political partition of the island after the death of ruler Artemi Semidán, the polity was administered by hereditary chieftains known as guanartemes from their seat at Gáldar. The society maintained ancestral pastoral traditions and fortified hilltop granaries while defending its independence against European maritime raids. Its sovereign existence terminated in 1483 following sustained military campaigns by the Crown of Castile. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Gáldar; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Traditional Guanche religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1405; Disestablished: 1483; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Kingdom of Telde
label: guanche states
description: The Kingdom of Telde was an aboriginal Guanche domain occupying the eastern and southern districts of Gran Canaria during the fifteenth century. Established alongside its sibling realm of Gáldar after the division of the island, Telde was governed by a guanarteme supported by a council of noble elders and religious leaders. The population engaged in barley cultivation, goat pastoralism and coastal fishing, resisting repeated Castilian landing expeditions across several decades. The kingdom fell on 29 April 1483 when Castilian troops decisively subdued the island and incorporated its territory into the Spanish Crown. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Telde; Common languages: Guanche; Religion: Traditional Guanche religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1405; Disestablished: 29 April 1483; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Siberian Khanate
description: The Siberian Khanate was a western Siberian Turco-Mongol realm established following the progressive disintegration of the Golden Horde. Governed alternately by Shaybanid and Taibugid dynasties from fortified capitals at Chimgi-Tura and Qashliq, it constituted the northernmost Islamic monarchy in Eurasia. The khanate collected fur tributes from native Khanty, Mansi and Selkup communities while fostering riverine trade along the Tobol and Irtysh basins. Russian Cossack incursions led by Yermak Timofeyevich in the 1580s triggered prolonged warfare that concluded with the realm's definitive absorption into the Tsardom of Russia before 1600. \n\n Status: Khanate; Capital: Qashliq; Common languages: Siberian Tatar, Khanty and Mansi; Religion: Sunni Islam and Shamanism; Government: Khanate; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Golden Horde; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia; Ruler title: Khan

name: Great Ming (Military Occupation)
description: Great Ming under military occupation designated the temporary imperial garrison regime imposed across northern Vietnam during the campaigns of the Yongle Emperor. Following the invasion launched in late 1406 against the Hồ dynasty, Ming expeditionary generals established martial control over river strongholds along the Red River valley. The occupation authorities suppressed local resistance, commandeered regional grain stores and requisitioned timber before organising the conquered territory into the formal province of Jiaozhi. Continued unrest and renewed insurgent operations in 1411 necessitated further mobile military governance to preserve imperial outposts. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile expeditionary headquarters; Common languages: Literary Chinese and Middle Vietnamese; Religion: Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Early modern; Ruler title: Emperor; Preceded by: Hồ dynasty; Succeeded by: Ming dynasty

name: Caboloan
label: barangay states
description: Caboloan was a sovereign precolonial coastal principality established across the fertile Agno River basin in west-central Luzon. Headquartered at Binalatongan, the polity flourished under local hereditary monarchs who coordinated maritime exchange with Ming dynasty merchants and regional Southeast Asian ports. Its economy relied on wet-rice agriculture, river trade, gold panning and deer-hide exportation across extensive commercial networks. Sovereign governance persisted until the late sixteenth century, when Spanish colonial expeditions from Manila subjugated the region and integrated it into the Captaincy General of the Philippines. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Binalatongan; Common languages: Pangasinan; Religion: Animism; Government: Petty monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1406; Disestablished: 1577; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of the Philippines

name: Gujarat Sultanate
description: The Gujarat Sultanate was a powerful late medieval Islamic maritime monarchy encompassing western India around the Gulf of Khambhat. Founded by Muzaffar Shah I following the decline of Delhi authority, the realm established its permanent royal capital at Ahmedabad under Ahmad Shah I in 1411. The sultanate prospered through Indian Ocean commercial routes, exporting textiles, indigo and spices while maintaining a formidable navy along the Arabian Sea. Despite Portuguese naval incursions and brief Mughal interventions, the state preserved its independence until its eventual conquest by Emperor Akbar in 1573. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Ahmedabad; Common languages: Gujarati and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1407; Disestablished: 1573; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire; Currency: Taka

name: Marquisate of Rocchetta-Suvero
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Rocchetta-Suvero was a diminutive imperial fief located in the rugged Vara valley of eastern Liguria. Governed by a cadet branch of the Malaspina dynasty, the lordship maintained immediate vassalage to the Holy Roman Empire, shielding its autonomy amidst the expansionist ambitions of Genoa and neighbouring Tuscan princes. The marquisate derived revenue from river tolls, chestnut farming and mountain transit dues linking the Lunigiana to coastal ports. Its sovereign jurisdiction survived until the Napoleonic restructuring of northern Italy dismantled imperial feudal enclaves in 1797. \n\n Status: Imperial fief; Capital: Rocchetta di Vara; Common languages: Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina; Historical era: Early modern; Disestablished: 1797; Succeeded by: Ligurian Republic

name: Duchy of Latera
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Latera was an autonomous aristocratic enclave located in the volcanic uplands of northern Lazio near Lake Bolsena. Bestowed upon a cadet branch of the Farnese family in 1408, the fief exercised judicial autonomy and imperial privileges separate from direct Papal administration. The dukes governed from their fortified stone palazzo in Latera, overseeing agricultural estates, vineyards and thermal springs across the surrounding caldera. The separate existence of the lordship concluded in February 1668 when the male dynastic line failed and its territory reverted to the Apostolic Camera. \n\n Status: Fief of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Latera; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: Farnese; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 6 November 1408; Disestablished: 18 February 1668; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Kingdom of Kotte
description: The Kingdom of Kotte was the pre-eminent Sinhalese state in southwestern Sri Lanka during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Founded by Parakramabahu VI with its royal seat at the fortified city of Kotte, the monarchy temporarily unified the entire island after subduing northern principalities and tributary chiefdoms. The realm supported Theravada Buddhist institutions, patronised classical Sinhala literature and controlled lucrative coastal cinnamon trade routes along the Indian Ocean. Internal dynastic partitions in the sixteenth century weakened the kingdom, allowing Portuguese colonial influence to expand until Kotte was ultimately absorbed by European authorities. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kotte; Common languages: Sinhalese and Tamil; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1412; Disestablished: 1597; Ruler title: King; Preceded by: Kingdom of Gampola

name: Principality of Prozorov
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Prozorov was a minor Rus appanage principality situated along the upper Volga drainage in north-eastern Russia. Arising from a territorial partition of the Yaroslavl dynastic patrimony in the early fifteenth century, the principality was ruled by Rurikid princes from the fortified settlement of Prozorovo. Its rulers administered local agrarian communities, maintained forest hunting grounds and collected riverine tolls while balancing relations with neighbouring princes. The autonomous domain was absorbed around 1461 during the territorial consolidation campaigns orchestrated by the Grand Principality of Moscow. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Prozorovo; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1409; Disestablished: 1461; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Sit
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Sit was a small north-eastern Russian feudal domain established along the banks of the Sit River. Formed through the division of the Mologa princely estate among Rurikid heirs, the polity was governed from its central seat at Sit. The princes oversaw rural hamlets, collected tribute in grain and timber and provided military contingents under regional alliances with larger Rus polities. Moscow's aggressive absorption of regional appanages brought an end to Sit's separate political existence in 1461, transforming its dynastic masters into service boyars of the Muscovite court. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Sit; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1409; Disestablished: 1461; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Kingdom of Sicily
description: The Kingdom of Sicily functioned as an insular crown possession of the Crown of Aragon throughout much of the fifteenth century. Administered from Palermo by appointed viceroys following the dynastic succession of Ferdinand I of Trastámara, the realm retained its traditional Sicilian parliament and legal customs. The island played an indispensable role in western Mediterranean naval logistics, supplying grain, silk and maritime levies to sustain Aragonese imperial ambitions across Italy. This administrative phase concluded in January 1479 when the union of the Aragonese and Castilian crowns created the unified Spanish monarchy. \n\n Status: Possession of the Crown of Aragon; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Sicilian, Latin and Catalan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy under viceroy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sicily (autonomous); Succeeded by: Spanish Monarchy; Currency: Sicilian piastra

name: Principality of Romodanovo
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Romodanovo was a compact north-eastern Rus feudal realm created out of the partition of the Starodub patrimony along the Klyazma basin. Governed by Rurikid princes from the township of Romodanovo, the principality commanded agrarian tracts, hunting woodlands and local trade routes. The ruling lineage maintained autonomous domestic authority while rendering military assistance during regional conflicts among Vladimir-Suzdal successor states. By the 1440s, mounting Muscovite pressure compelled the princes to cede their sovereign independence and enter the service nobility of the Grand Prince of Moscow. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Romodanovo; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1411; Disestablished: 1441; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Ukhtoma
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Ukhtoma was a northern Rus appanage principality formed through the division of the Beloozero princely inheritance. Centred on the settlement of Ukhtoma along the river of the same name, the polity was governed by Rurikid princes who exercised local administrative and judicial prerogatives. The inhabitants sustained their livelihood through hunting, fur trapping, lake fishing and small-scale rye farming across boreal forests. The principality lost its sovereign autonomy around 1451 when the Grand Principality of Moscow absorbed the Beloozero borderlands into its centralising state apparatus. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Ukhtoma; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1411; Disestablished: 1451; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Vadbola
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Vadbola was an appanage state established in the lake-rich Beloozero region of northern Russia. Originating from the fragmentation of the Belozersk patrimonial territories among Rurikid siblings, the realm took its name from the Vadbola River where its administrative court resided. Its rulers supervised riverine commerce, collected pelt dues from forest trappers and maintained defensive posts against northern raiders. Sovereign rule terminated in 1451 when the burgeoning authority of Moscow extinguished local appanage independence, assimilating the Vadbolsky princes into the Muscovite boyar aristocracy. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Vadbola; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1411; Disestablished: 1451; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Electorate of Brandenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Electorate of Brandenburg was a major northern German principality and electoral state within the Holy Roman Empire. Entrusted to the House of Hohenzollern by Emperor Sigismund in the 1410s, the margraves transferred their governmental seat to Berlin, pacifying unruly robber barons and establishing centralised administration. The electorate held an esteemed vote in imperial elections and expanded its influence across Pomerania, Lusatia and the Neumark while embracing the Protestant Reformation during the sixteenth century. Its territorial power increased dramatically upon securing the hereditary inheritance of the Duchy of Prussia in 1618. \n\n Status: Electorate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Berlin; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, then Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Hohenzollern; Historical era: Early modern; Ruler title: Prince-Elector; Succeeded by: Brandenburg-Prussia

name: Ottoman Sultanate
label: ottoman interregnum
description: The Ottoman Sultanate under Prince Musa Çelebi formed the Rumelian fraction of the fragmented Ottoman realm during the final phase of the Ottoman Interregnum. Operating from the imperial capital of Edirne, Musa governed the Balkan provinces, rallying frontier gazis, nomadic cavalry and commoners through egalitarian social rhetoric. His uncompromising policies and raids into neighbouring Byzantine and Serbian lands provoked a coalition between Christian princes and his brother Mehmed. The faction collapsed on 5 July 1413 following Musa's defeat and death at the Battle of Çamurlu, enabling Mehmed I to reunify the empire. \n\n Status: Contested sultanate; Capital: Edirne; Official languages: Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1412; Disestablished: 5 July 1413; Preceded by: Ottoman Interregnum; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Signoria of Desana
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Desana was an independent imperial lordship situated in Piedmont near Vercelli. Enfeoffed under the direct jurisdiction of the Holy Roman Empire, the territory constituted a sovereign enclave surrounded by the expanding dominions of the Duchy of Savoy. The signoria was ruled by the patrician Tizzoni family, who fortified the central castle, drained local marshlands for rice and grain farming and operated an active monetary mint. This feudal arrangement persisted until 1511, when the fief was elevated to a formal imperial county under continued Tizzoni dynastic leadership. \n\n Status: Imperial signoria; Capital: Desana; Common languages: Piedmontese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: Tizzoni; Historical era: Renaissance; Established: 1411; Reorganised: 1511; Succeeded by: County of Desana

name: Bushahr State
description: Bushahr State was a prominent Rajput hill kingdom located along the upper Sutlej River valley in the western Himalayas. Governed by the local royal dynasty from its ancestral court at Sarahan near the historic Bhimakali temple, the kingdom commanded vital trans-Himalayan trade routes linking the Punjab plains with Tibet. Its merchants traded wool, pashmina, borax and timber while paying close attention to mountain border defences. The realm retained independent authority across several centuries until nineteenth-century Gorkha invasions briefly interrupted its sovereignty prior to its re-establishment under British paramountcy. \n\n Status: Princely kingdom; Capital: Sarahan; Common languages: Western Pahari and Kinnauri; Religion: Hinduism and Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bushahr dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Ruler title: Raja; Succeeded by: British Raj

name: Kingdom of Arakan
description: The Kingdom of Arakan during the 1410s existed as a dependent vassal state subject to the Hanthawaddy Kingdom of Lower Burma. Caught in the destructive crossfire of the Forty Years' War between Ava and Pegu, the Arakanese capital of Launggyet was captured by Mon expeditionary armies dispatched by King Razadarit. Mon governors and pro-Hanthawaddy puppets governed the coastal realm, exacting annual tribute while garrisoning key ports along the Bay of Bengal.
