Hanthawaddy suzerainty was eventually shaken off following the death of Razadarit, allowing rival powers and local princes to contest regional supremacy. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Launggyet; Common languages: Arakanese and Mon; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Launggyet dynasty; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Mrauk U; Ruler title: King

name: Kingdom of Ava (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Ava under military occupation comprised operational frontline territories held under martial control by Upper Burmese royal field armies. During intense military campaigns down the Irrawaddy river basin, King Minkhaung I and subsequent Ava monarchs established armed garrisons and temporary stockades to subjugate defiant border lords. The occupying garrisons requisitioned riverboats, collected forced grain levies and enforced curfews over rebellious townships without establishing formal civil administration. name: Uzbek Khanate

name: Kingdom of Arakan
description: The Kingdom of Arakan in the mid-fifteenth century was a coastal Buddhist monarchy that functioned as a tributary protectorate of the Bengal Sultanate. Restored to his ancestral throne with Bengali military assistance in 1430, King Min Saw Mon established a new royal capital at the inland river fortress of Mrauk U. Although culturally and religiously Buddhist, the Arakanese court adopted Persianate courtly etiquette, struck silver dinga coins bearing Islamic titles and paid tribute to the sultans in Gaur. This tributary relationship shielded the realm from Burmese aggression until Arakanese monarchs gradually consolidated independent maritime power. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal kingdom; Capital: Mrauk U; Common languages: Arakanese and Bengali; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mrauk U dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1430; Ruler title: King; Currency: Silver dinga

name: Kingdom of Mutapa
description: The Kingdom of Mutapa was a major precolonial Shona empire situated across the northern Zimbabwean plateau and the middle Zambezi River basin. Founded around 1430 by King Nyatsimba Mutota after migrating from Great Zimbabwe, the monarchy ruled from stone-built capitals including Zvongombe. The sovereigns, styled Mwenemutapa, oversaw productive goldfields and copper mines, exchanging precious metals and ivory with Swahili and Portuguese merchants along the Indian Ocean coast. Mutapa commanded formidable provincial armies and spiritual authority across southern Africa until European interventions and regional rebellions gradually fragmented the empire in the seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Zvongombe; Common languages: Shona; Religion: Shona traditional religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mutapa; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1430; Ruler title: Mwenemutapa; Preceded by: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe

name: Songhai Empire
description: The Songhai Empire was the dominant imperial power of the western Sahel during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Centred along the Niger River bend with its imperial capital at Gao, the state eclipsed the declining Mali Empire through the military campaigns of Sonni Ali and Askia Muhammad. The empire encompassed vital commercial metropolises including Timbuktu and Djenné, fostering renowned centres of Islamic jurisprudence, trans-Saharan caravan trade and gold and salt distribution. Songhai's imperial hegemony ended abruptly on 13 March 1591 following its decisive defeat by gunpowder-armed Moroccan forces at the Battle of Tondibi. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Gao; Common languages: Songhai, Arabic and Manding; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional religions; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sonni and Askia dynasties; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1430; Disestablished: 13 March 1591; Succeeded by: Pashalik of Timbuktu

name: Kingdom of Cambodia
description: The Kingdom of Cambodia during its Post-Angkor era was a sovereign Theravada Buddhist monarchy established in southern Indochina. Following the abandonment of Angkor in the early 1430s due to Siamese pressure, King Ponhea Yat relocated the royal court to Phnom Penh and later Lovek. The kingdom reoriented its economy toward maritime river commerce along the Mekong and Tonlé Sap, trading spices, timber and rice with Asian merchants. Sovereign Cambodian authority endured until February 1594, when Siamese armies captured Lovek and reduced the kingdom to tributary status. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Phnom Penh and Lovek; Common languages: Middle Khmer; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Varman dynasty; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1431; Disestablished: 1 February 1594; Preceded by: Khmer Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Cambodia (Siamese vassal)

name: Mahra Sultanate
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Mahra Sultanate was an autonomous coastal monarchy situated in eastern Yemen and extending across the island of Socotra. Governed by the hereditary Banu Afrar dynasty from coastal capitals at Shihr and Qishn, the sultanate was predominantly inhabited by Mehri-speaking pastoralists and fishermen. The realm profited from frankincense harvesting, date cultivation and seasonal maritime trade across the Arabian Sea to India and East Africa. The sultanate maintained its independent political existence despite Portuguese raids and regional rivalries until concluding formal protectorate treaties with the British Empire in the late 1880s. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Qishn; Common languages: Mehri and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Afrar; Historical era: Early modern to late modern; Established: 1432; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Marquisate of Mantua
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Mantua was an illustrious sovereign principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in south-eastern Lombardy. Elevated from a lordship in September 1433 by Emperor Sigismund for Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, the state was ruled from its fortified island city surrounded by the Mincio lakes. The Gonzaga court emerged as one of the pre-eminent cultural centres of the Italian Renaissance, commissioning masterworks from Andrea Mantegna and establishing an influential diplomatic presence across Europe. The marquisate maintained its sovereign standing until April 1530, when Emperor Charles V elevated the territory into the Duchy of Mantua. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Mantua; Common languages: Lombard, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Gonzaga; Historical era: Renaissance; Established: 22 September 1433; Disestablished: 1530; Succeeded by: Duchy of Mantua

name: Timbuktu
label: tuareg polities
description: Timbuktu functioned as an independent desert city-state during the mid-fifteenth century following its liberation from declining Malian imperial rule. Captured around 1433 by Maghsharen Tuareg warriors led by Chief Akil Ag Malwal, the city was governed through collaboration between nomadic Tuareg leaders and urban Sanhaja Muslim scholars. Timbuktu thrived as an international entrepôt along trans-Saharan caravan arteries, exchanging Saharan rock salt for sub-Saharan gold and housing prestigious Islamic academies and book collections. Autonomous Tuareg control ended in January 1468 when Emperor Sonni Ali stormed the city and incorporated it into the Songhai Empire. \n\n Status: Autonomous city-state; Capital: Timbuktu; Common languages: Tamasheq, Songhai and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Nomadic-scholastic council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1433; Disestablished: 1468; Preceded by: Mali Empire; Succeeded by: Songhai Empire

name: Gajapati Kingdom
description: The Gajapati Kingdom was a major Hindu imperial power that dominated eastern India from the coastal plains of Odisha. Founded in 1434 by Emperor Kapilendra Deva following the demise of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the empire governed from its capital at Cuttack. At its zenith, the realm extended along the Bay of Bengal from the Ganges delta to southern India, clashing with the Vijayanagara Empire and Deccan sultanates. The Gajapati monarchs were celebrated patrons of Lord Jagannath of Puri, ruling until internal usurpations brought the dynasty to an end in 1541. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Cuttack; Common languages: Odia and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Suryavamsha; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1434; Disestablished: 1541; Preceded by: Eastern Ganga dynasty; Succeeded by: Bhoi dynasty; Ruler title: Gajapati

name: Lunavada State
description: Lunavada State was a sovereign Rajput principality established in the Rewa Kantha hilly tracts of eastern Gujarat. Founded in 1434 by Rana Bhim Singh, a scion of the Solanki Rajput dynasty, the realm took its name from its fortified administrative capital at Lunavada. The rulers maintained strategic autonomy amidst the shifting power balances of western India, defending their forested hill tracts against the sultans of Ahmedabad and later Maratha tax collectors. The principality preserved its sovereign existence until 1826, when it entered into treaty relations with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Lunavada; Common languages: Gujarati and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Solanki Rajput; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1434; Disestablished: 1826; Succeeded by: British East India Company; Ruler title: Rana

name: Duchy of Saint Sava
label: serbian principalities
description: The Duchy of Saint Sava was a late medieval South Slavic state encompassing modern Herzegovina, southern Dalmatia and northern Montenegro. Consolidated by the Kosača noble family, the polity achieved formal prominence in 1448 when Stjepan Vukčić Kosača adopted the prestigious title of Duke of Saint Sava, from which the regional name Herzegovina derived. The dukes administered their realm from mountain strongholds at Blagaj and Mostar, balancing diplomatic ties with Venice, the Kingdom of Bosnia and Hungary. The independent duchy was systematically overrun and conquered by invading Ottoman armies between 1481 and 1483. \n\n Status: Feudal duchy; Capital: Mostar and Blagaj; Common languages: Serbo-Croatian; Religion: Serbian Orthodoxy, Bosnian Church and Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kosača; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1448; Disestablished: 1483; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Herzegovina

name: Khanchi
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Khanchi was an autonomous hill principality established in the Gandaki River basin of western Nepal. Established in 1435 by Raja Hang Vir Singh as one of the historic Chaubisi Rajya petty kingdoms, the polity was governed by Khas Kshatriya monarchs from their ridge-top fortress at Khanchi. The state drew revenue from terrace farming, mountain pass tolls and pastoralism, maintaining intricate diplomatic ties and defensive alliances with neighbouring hill states. Khanchi retained its sovereign independence for more than three centuries until the expanding Gorkha Kingdom annexed the territory in 1786 during the unification of Nepal. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Khanchi; Common languages: Khas and Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1435; Disestablished: 1786; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal; Ruler title: Raja

name: Rinpungpa Dynasty
description: The Rinpungpa Dynasty was a powerful feudal regime that held hegemony over Western Tibet and the Tsang region during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Originating from Rinpung Castle in the Yarlung Tsangpo Valley, the noble house eclipsed the weakening Phagmodrupa dynasty to govern substantial parts of Ü-Tsang from their stronghold at Shigatse. The Rinpungpa rulers were devoted patrons of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, engaging in bitter sectarian rivalries against the emerging Gelug sect supported by Lhasa authorities. Their regional supremacy waned after 1512, concluding with their overthrow by the Tsangpa dynasty in 1565. \n\n Status: Feudal kingdom; Capital: Rinpung and Shigatse; Common languages: Classical Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Theocratic feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rinpungpa; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1435; Disestablished: 1565; Succeeded by: Tsangpa dynasty

name: League of the Ten Jurisdictions
label: holy roman empire
description: The League of the Ten Jurisdictions was an autonomous Alpine republican confederation founded in the valleys of modern Graubünden, Switzerland. Formed on 30 April 1436 following the extinction of the Counts of Toggenburg, the ten member communities convened at Davos to establish mutual defence and judicial solidarity. The league was created to prevent the House of Habsburg from imposing feudal authority, relying on communal councils and citizen assemblies. In 1471, the league joined the Grey League and the League of God's House, creating the permanent Free State of the Three Leagues. \n\n Status: Republican confederation; Capital: Davos; Common languages: Romansh and Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 30 April 1436; Reorganised: 1471; Succeeded by: Three Leagues

name: Parbat
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Parbat was an autonomous Himalayan principality located in the rugged Kali Gandaki gorge of western Nepal. Counting among the most powerful of the Chaubisi Rajya petty states, the kingdom was governed by Khas Kshatriya monarchs from their capital at Beni. The polity acquired considerable wealth through trans-Himalayan trade between Tibet and India as well as extensive copper and iron mining throughout its mountain valleys. Parbat preserved its sovereign existence through strong hill fortifications until 25 September 1786, when military forces of the Gorkha Kingdom annexed the principality into the unified Kingdom of Nepal. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Beni; Common languages: Nepali and Magar; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1437; Disestablished: 25 September 1786; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal; Ruler title: Raja

name: Alirajpur State
description: Alirajpur State was an autonomous Rajput principality established in the hilly tribal borderlands of south-western Madhya Pradesh. Founded in 1437 by Raja Anand Deo of the Rathore clan, the monarchy had its royal headquarters at the town of Alirajpur near the Narmada River. The state governed an ethnically diverse domain dominated by Bhil communities, deriving income from forest produce, transit levies and traditional agricultural settlements. Alirajpur preserved its sovereign independence against neighbouring sultanates and Maratha warlords until 1819, when it entered into subsidiary treaty relations with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Alirajpur; Common languages: Malvi, Bhili and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rathore Rajput; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1437; Disestablished: 1819; Succeeded by: British East India Company; Ruler title: Raja

name: Negara Daha
description: Negara Daha was a classical Hindu-Buddhist kingdom situated along the river networks of southern Kalimantan on the island of Borneo. Succeeding the earlier realm of Negara Dipa, the state maintained its royal court in the interior Hulu Sungai region with administrative centres near Marabahan. The kingdom engaged in riverine commerce, exporting rattan, wax, dammar resin and gold while sustaining wet-rice cultivation along fertile floodplains. Dynastic succession disputes culminated in September 1526 when Prince Samudera secured military assistance from Demak, converted to Islam and transformed the realm into the Sultanate of Banjar. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Marabahan; Common languages: Banjar and Old Javanese; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1438; Disestablished: 24 September 1526; Preceded by: Negara Dipa; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Banjar

name: Inca Empire
description: The Inca Empire, known natively as Tawantinsuyu, was the largest pre-Columbian imperial state in South America. Expanding rapidly from the Kingdom of Cusco following the accession of Pachacuti in 1438, the empire united diverse Andean cultures across present-day Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. Administration relied on a massive paved road network, stone storehouses, quipu record-keeping and state-organised mit'a labour service overseen by the divine Sapa Inca. The sovereign empire disintegrated in August 1533 following a destructive civil war and the capture and execution of Emperor Atahualpa by Spanish conquistadores. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Cusco; Official languages: Classical Quechua; Religion: Inca religion; Government: Divine absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hanan Cusco; Historical era: Pre-Columbian; Established: 1438; Disestablished: 29 August 1533; Succeeded by: New Castile; Ruler title: Sapa Inca

name: Kingdom of Hungary
description: The Kingdom of Hungary entered a personal union with the Kingdom of Poland between 1440 and 1444 under King Władysław III. Crowned Ulászló I at Székesfehérvár after a contested succession against Ladislaus the Posthumous, the monarch governed from Buda. The union coordinated Central European resources to confront the escalating expansion of the Ottoman Empire across the Danube frontier, supported by general John Hunyadi. This dynastic partnership abruptly concluded on 10 November 1444 when the king perished fighting Ottoman forces at the Battle of Varna. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union; Capital: Buda; Common languages: Hungarian, Latin and Polish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jagiellonian; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 17 July 1440; Disestablished: 10 November 1444; Ruler title: King

name: Kingdom of Lo
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Lo was an autonomous Tibetic realm situated in the arid high-altitude plateau of Upper Mustang in northern Nepal. Founded by King Ame Pal, who established the walled capital of Lo Manthang in the 1440s, the kingdom controlled the strategic Kali Gandaki salt route connecting the Tibetan plateau with the Indian lowlands. The society preserved Tibetan Buddhist culture, Sakya monastic institutions and decorated cliff-side cave retreats while levying duties on pack caravans. The kingdom maintained sovereign independence across centuries of mountain isolation until accepting tributary subordination to the Gorkha Kingdom in 1789. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lo Manthang; Common languages: Standard Tibetan and Seke; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bista; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1440; Disestablished: 1789; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal; Ruler title: Gyelpo

name: Republic of Cospaia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Republic of Cospaia was a sovereign microstate situated in northern Umbria between Tuscany and the Papal States. Accidentally created on 1 March 1441 when a papal treaty misidentified a local boundary stream, the hamlet operated as a stateless republic without formal taxes, courts or armies. The population was governed by a council of family heads, using their independent frontier status to pioneer tobacco cultivation and cross-border trade. Cospaia enjoyed nearly four centuries of peaceful liberty until its territory was partitioned between Tuscany and the Papal States on 26 June 1826. \n\n Status: Autonomous microstate; Capital: Cospaia; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Stateless republic; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1 March 1441; Disestablished: 26 June 1826; Succeeded by: Papal States and Grand Duchy of Tuscany; Currency: None (Italian and Papal coins used)

name: Kowoj State
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Kowoj State was an autonomous Late Postclassic Maya polity situated in the central Petén lakes region of northern Guatemala. Established around 1441 by Maya migrants who fled the collapse of Mayapán in the Yucatán, the polity established fortified insular centres at Topoxte and Zacpetén. Archaeological excavations distinguish Kowoj settlements by their characteristic C-shaped plaza assemblages and tandem-plan elite residential compounds. The kingdom engaged in fierce regional rivalries against the neighbouring Itzá Maya while defending its territory against Spanish incursions until colonial armies subdued the Petén Basin in 1698. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Topoxte; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 1441; Disestablished: 1698; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Marquisate of Massa
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Massa was an independent imperial fief located along the Tyrrhenian seaboard of north-western Tuscany. Governed by the Malaspina dynasty from the fortified Rocca Malaspina in Massa, the marquisate commanded valuable agricultural coastal plains and the rich marble quarries of the Apuan Alps. The rulers maintained diplomatic equilibrium among Florence, Genoa and Milan while exercising complete territorial sovereignty under imperial immediacy. In 1553, marriage united the ruling house with the Genoese Cybo family, forming the Cybo-Malaspina line that governed the marquisate until Emperor Leopold I raised it to a principality in 1664. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Massa; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina and Cybo-Malaspina; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1442; Disestablished: 1664; Succeeded by: Principality of Massa

name: Kingdom of Naples
description: The Kingdom of Naples was an Italian monarchy integrated directly into the dominions of the Crown of Aragon between 1442 and 1458. Following a campaign against René of Anjou, King Alfonso V entered Naples on 2 June 1442, reuniting southern Italy with Sicily under Aragonese rule. Alfonso made Naples the administrative and intellectual centre of his Mediterranean empire, reforming taxation, patronising humanist scholars and rebuilding the Castel Nuovo. Direct crown possession concluded upon Alfonso's death in June 1458, when the Neapolitan throne passed separately to his son Ferrante. \n\n Status: Possession of the Crown of Aragon; Capital: Naples; Common languages: Neapolitan, Latin, Italian and Catalan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Trastámara; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Renaissance; Established: 2 June 1442; Disestablished: 27 June 1458; Preceded by: Kingdom of Naples (Angevin); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Naples (independent)

name: Kingdom of Hungary, Kingdom of Poland and Despotate of Serbia (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Hungary, Kingdom of Poland and Despotate of Serbia under military occupation denoted the operational theatre held by Christian coalition armies during the Balkan Long Campaign. Commanded by King Władysław III, voivode John Hunyadi and Despot Đurađ Branković, allied forces crossed the Danube in late 1443, liberating Niš and advancing into Ottoman-controlled Sofia. Allied officers administered temporary martial requisition zones to supply wintering cavalry, secure river crossings and recruit local Christian irregulars. This allied military occupation ended in January 1444 when heavy blizzards and tactical stalemate compelled the expeditionary forces to withdraw northward. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile crusade military headquarters; Common languages: Hungarian, Polish, Serbian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Allied military administration; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 5 November 1443; Disestablished: 25 January 1444; Preceded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Duchy of Urbino
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Urbino was a sovereign Renaissance principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the northern Marche. Elevated from a county in 1443 by Pope Eugene IV for Oddantonio da Montefeltro, the duchy attained international renown under Duke Federico da Montefeltro, who constructed the monumental Ducal Palace and assembled one of Europe's greatest humanist libraries. The duchy passed to the della Rovere family in 1508, with its ducal court relocating to coastal Pesaro in 1523. Independent dynastic rule ended in 1631 following the death of Francesco Maria II, when the Papal States annexed the realm. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Urbino and Pesaro; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: Montefeltro and Della Rovere; Historical era: Renaissance to Early modern; Established: 1443; Disestablished: 1631; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Kingdom of Kozhikode
description: The Kingdom of Kozhikode during the mid-fifteenth century functioned as an autonomous tributary state subject to the Vijayanagara Empire. Subordinated following military expeditions led by Emperor Deva Raya II into northern Malabar, the hereditary monarchs, styled the Zamorins, remitted annual tribute to Hampi. Kozhikode nonetheless retained substantial internal autonomy, thriving as the premier spice emporium on the Arabian Sea where Arab, Persian and Chinese merchants traded black pepper. The kingdom gradually threw off Vijayanagara overlordship around the end of the fifteenth century prior to Portuguese naval confrontations. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal kingdom; Capital: Kozhikode; Common languages: Malayalam and Arabic; Religion: Hinduism and Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nediyiruppu Swaroopam; Historical era: Medieval India; Ruler title: Zamorin; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kozhikode (sovereign); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kozhikode (sovereign)

name: Nandapur Kingdom
description: The Nandapur Kingdom was a sovereign Hindu hill realm established in 1443 across the Eastern Ghats highlands of southern Odisha and northern Andhra. Founded by King Vinayak Dev of the Suryavanshi dynasty, the state ruled from its fortified jungle capital at Nandapur before dynastic descendants relocated the court to Jeypore. The kings held sway over local Adivasi tribal communities, extracting forest produce, timber and iron ore while securing mountain passes between the Deccan and the coastal plains. The realm preserved sovereign independence across multiple centuries until mid-eighteenth-century conflicts subordinated the dynasty to regional powers. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nandapur and Jeypore; Common languages: Odia and Telugu; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Suryavanshi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1443; Disestablished: 1751; Succeeded by: Jeypore Estate; Ruler title: Raja

name: Tahirids
description: The Tahirids were an Arab Muslim dynasty that governed Yemen between 1454 and 1517 following the collapse of the Rasulid Sultanate. Originating from the highland district of Rada'a, the Banu Tahir sultans established administrative seats at Zabid and Juban, quickly extending their sovereignty across the Tihama coastal plain, Aden and Sanaa. The realm prospered through Red Sea maritime trade and Indian Ocean spice traffic, using customs revenues to build magnificent mosques, aqueducts and religious colleges. Sovereign Tahirid rule ended abruptly in 1517 when Mamluk expeditionary forces from Egypt invaded Yemen with firearms, deposing the dynasty. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Zabid and Rada'a; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Banu Tahir; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1454; Disestablished: 1517; Preceded by: Rasulid dynasty; Succeeded by: Yemen Eyalet

name: Venad Kingdom
description: The Venad Kingdom was a southern Indian principality at the tip of the Malabar coast that acknowledged tributary vassalage to the Vijayanagara Empire during the mid-fifteenth century. Following the southern military expeditions of Emperor Deva Raya II, the ruling Kulasekhara dynasty in Kollam and Padmanabhapuram was obligated to remit regular tributes to the imperial treasury. The kingdom nonetheless maintained internal self-governance, profiting from coastal pepper plantations, coconut cultivation and maritime trade with Arab merchants across the Indian Ocean. The rulers threw off imperial vassalage around 1500, reasserting full independence before the subsequent emergence of Travancore. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal kingdom; Capital: Padmanabhapuram and Kollam; Common languages: Malayalam and Tamil; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kulasekhara; Historical era: Medieval India; Preceded by: Venad Kingdom (sovereign); Succeeded by: Venad Kingdom (sovereign)

name: League of Lezhë
label: albanian principalities
description: The League of Lezhë was an autonomous military and political confederation of Albanian princes established on 2 March 1444 in the Venetian-held town of Lezhë. Unified under the supreme military command of Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg, the alliance brought together rival noble clans, including the Arianiti, Dukagjini and Thopia, to mount common defence against the Ottoman Empire. From his mountain stronghold at Krujë, Skanderbeg mobilised disciplined citizen militias and guerrilla units, repelling multiple imperial Ottoman invasions across more than two decades. The unified league began to unravel after Skanderbeg's death in 1468, eventually fragmenting under renewed Ottoman pressure. \n\n Status: Military confederation; Capital: Lezhë and Krujë; Common languages: Albanian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Aristocratic confederation; Head of state: Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 2 March 1444; Disestablished: 1469; Preceded by: Albanian principalities

name: Duchy of Athens
label: frankokratia
description: The Duchy of Athens was a Crusader state in Attica and Boeotia that functioned as a tributary vassal of the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea during the mid-fifteenth century. Ruled by Duke Nerio II Acciaioli from the Acropolis in Athens, the duchy was forced to accept Byzantine suzerainty following military campaigns led by Despot Constantine Palaiologos. The territory supported a population of Greek and Italian inhabitants, sustaining agricultural estates and Aegean commerce. Moreote vassalage collapsed in the 1450s as Ottoman armies intervened, culminating in the final Ottoman conquest of Athens in 1458. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal duchy; Capital: Athens; Common languages: Greek, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Greek Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Acciaioli; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1458; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire; Ruler title: Duke

name: Gorée
description: Gorée functioned as an overseas Portuguese maritime trading station and naval anchorage situated off the Cap-Vert peninsula of Senegal. Acquired during the Atlantic voyages of explorer Dinis Dias in the mid-1440s, the small rocky island served as a secure staging post for caravel navigation along the West African coast. The Portuguese constructed a fortified factory, a Catholic chapel and maritime storehouses, trading European manufactures for gold dust, hides and enslaved captives from the mainland Wolof kingdoms. Portuguese colonial control persisted until 1617, when the Dutch West India Company seized the island. \n\n Status: Portuguese colony; Capital: Gorée; Common languages: Portuguese and Wolof; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial trading post; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1445; Disestablished: 1617; Succeeded by: Dutch West India Company

name: Arguin
label: european enclaves in north africa before 1830
description: Arguin was a pioneering Portuguese island fortress and commercial factory situated in the shallow Bay of Arguin off the Mauritanian coast. Established under the direction of Prince Henry the Navigator in 1445, the fortified outpost formed Portugal's earliest permanent overseas trade station along the African Atlantic seaboard. Portuguese factors maintained diplomatic treaties with local nomadic Sanhaja Berber chieftains, bartering horses, Moroccan textiles and wheat for Saharan gold dust, gum arabic and captives. The fortified station remained an essential crown possession until Dutch expeditionary forces captured the garrison in 1634. \n\n Status: Portuguese colony; Capital: Arguin; Common languages: Portuguese and Berber; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial military factory; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1446; Disestablished: 1634; Succeeded by: Dutch West India Company

name: Khanate of Kazan
description: The Khanate of Kazan was a prominent Muslim Tatar state situated along the Middle Volga on the territories of former Volga Bulgaria. Established in the 1440s by Ulugh Muhammad and his son Maxmud following the fragmentation of the Golden Horde, the realm was governed from the citadel of Kazan. The khanate commanded lucrative river trade between Muscovy, Central Asia and Siberia, while exercising authority over ethnically diverse Tatar, Chuvash, Mari and Bashkir populations. name: Umatwara State

Founded in the mid-fifteenth century by the Umath clan of Paramara Rajputs, the state established its administrative capital at Rajgarh. name: Sultanate of Agadez
label: hausa states;tuareg polities;berber kingdoms

Founded in the fifteenth century when disparate Tuareg confederations selected a shared sovereign, titled the Amenukal, the sultanate established its political and religious seat at Agadez. The city flourished as a pivotal trans-Saharan caravan terminus, coordinating camel traffic, bilma salt distribution and Islamic scholarly exchanges between North Africa and the Hausa kingdoms. name: Bajura
label: nepal petty kingdoms

The polity supported its mountain population through terrace farming, transhumant pastoralism and trans-Himalayan barter trade linking Tibetan wool markets with the sub-Himalayan valleys. Bajura preserved its sovereign independence through natural mountain ramparts for more than three centuries until 1 September 1791, when Gorkhali armies annexed the territory into the expanding Kingdom of Nepal. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Bajura; Common languages: Doteli, Khas and Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1451; Disestablished: 1 September 1791; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal; Ruler title: Raja

name: Gyaaman
description: Gyaaman was a sovereign precolonial Akan kingdom located in the forest-savannah transitional borderland of modern Ghana and Ivory Coast. Founded in the fifteenth century by the Aduana clan from Dormaa, the state established its primary commercial and administrative headquarters at Bonduku. The kingdom commanded rich gold deposits, flourishing through kola nut trade, metalworking and intercultural diplomacy connecting Akan states with Mande and Dyula merchants. name: Iroquois Confederacy

Established under the Great Law of Peace by the Peacemaker and Hiawatha, the union united five nations—the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca—before admitting the Tuscarora in 1722. name: Jambi Sultanate
description: The Jambi Sultanate was an autonomous Malay maritime state situated along the Batang Hari River basin in eastern Sumatra. Emerging in the mid-fifteenth century following the decline of Majapahit authority, the realm established its royal capital at Tanah Pilih, modern Jambi. The sultanate grew wealthy through the export of black pepper, gold and timber, maintaining bustling commercial ties with Chinese, Arab and European merchants. Sovereign independence persisted across centuries until Dutch colonial forces invaded the interior, killing Sultan Thaha Syaifuddin and dissolving the realm in 1904. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Tanah Pilih; Common languages: Jambi Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jambi royal line; Historical era: Early modern to late modern; Established: 1460; Disestablished: 1904; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies; Ruler title: Sultan

name: Jobat State
description: Jobat State was a small Rajput principality located in the rugged tribal uplands of western Madhya Pradesh. Founded in the mid-fifteenth century by Rana Kesar Deo, a prince of the Rathore dynasty, the realm was governed from its central hill town at Jobat. The state held jurisdiction over Bhil and Bhilala tribal populations, maintaining order through kinship alliances and collecting dues on cattle trade and forest produce. name: Kingdom of 'Uvea
description: The Kingdom of 'Uvea was an autonomous Polynesian island kingdom located on the island of Wallis in the South Pacific Ocean. Established in the mid-fifteenth century following the expulsion of Tongan imperial garrisons, the kingdom was governed by a paramount monarch titled the Lavelua from the central settlement of Mata-Utu. name: Kingdom of Butua
description: The Kingdom of Butua was a prominent Kalanga realm situated across the south-western plateau of modern Zimbabwe. Governed by the Torwa dynasty from their impressive terraced stone citadel at Khami, the kingdom rose to prominence following the decline of Great Zimbabwe by controlling the rich goldfields of the southwest. The rulers, styled mambos, exchanged refined gold and ivory with Arab and Portuguese merchants along the Zambezi and Indian Ocean trade corridors. Butua maintained formidable political power until the mid-seventeenth century, when dynastic civil wars culminated in the realm's absorption into the emerging Rozvi Empire. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Khami; Common languages: Kalanga and Shona; Religion: Traditional Shona religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Torwa dynasty; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1450; Disestablished: 1661; Succeeded by: Rozvi Empire; Ruler title: Mambo

name: Kingdom of Karagwe
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Karagwe was an influential Great Lakes Bantu monarchy located in north-western Tanzania between Rwanda and Lake Victoria. Founded in the mid-fifteenth century by King Ruhinda I, who claimed descent from the semi-mythical Bachwezi dynasty, the state was administered from its royal capital at Bweranyange. The kingdom flourished through pastoral cattle culture, advanced iron-smelting technologies and strategic oversight of long-distance caravan routes carrying ivory, salt and copper across eastern Africa. Karagwe retained sovereign authority under its hereditary monarchs until 1 July 1890, when the Anglo-German Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty incorporated the region into German East Africa. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Bweranyange; Common languages: Nyambo and Swahili; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ruhinda dynasty; Historical era: Precolonial to late modern; Established: 1450; Disestablished: 1 July 1890; Succeeded by: German East Africa; Ruler title: Omukama

name: Kingdom of Koya

Governed by a paramount king titled the Bai from royal headquarters at Port Loko, the polity maintained tributary authority over regional subordinate chiefs styled gbana. Koya participated actively in Atlantic maritime trade, exchanging ivory, timber and rice with Portuguese, British and French merchants while defending its river frontiers. The kingdom preserved its sovereign jurisdiction until 31 August 1896, when the British Empire declared a formal protectorate over the Sierra Leone hinterland. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Port Loko; Common languages: Temne; Religion: Traditional animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Paramount monarchy; Ruler title: Bai; Historical era: Early modern to late modern; Established: 1451; Disestablished: 31 August 1896; Succeeded by: Sierra Leone Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Tallo
description: The Kingdom of Tallo was an autonomous Makassar maritime principality situated at the mouth of the Tallo River in south-western Sulawesi. Established in the mid-fifteenth century after a dynastic partition within the House of Gowa, the realm was governed by hereditary rulers styled Karaeng from their coastal seat at Tallo. This initial sovereign period formed the foundation for Tallo's subsequent dual federation with Gowa into the united Makassar kingdom. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Tallo; Common languages: Makassarese; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Karaeng; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1451; Reorganised: 1502; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Gowa-Tallo

name: Kotoko Kingdom
description: The Kotoko Kingdom was a sophisticated precolonial urban civilisation established in the Lake Chad basin across modern-day Cameroon, Chad and north-eastern Nigeria. Descended from the ancient Sao culture, the polity flourished as an autonomous confederation of fortified city-states governed from walled brick capitals including Makari and Logone-Birni. The Kotoko people excelled in metal casting, riverine navigation, intensive fishing along the Logone and Chari rivers and irrigated flood-retreat farming. name: Lordship of Schramberg

name: Muisca Confederation

Divided into regional confederacies led principally by the Zipa of Bacatá and the Zaque of Hunza, the polity governed densely populated highland plateaus without a single centralised monarch. The Muisca developed sophisticated raised-field agriculture, mined rock salt at Zipaquirá, extracted emeralds and crafted exquisite tumbaga gold alloys that inspired European legends of El Dorado. name: Nogai Horde

Descended from the Manghud clan under the military commander Edigu following the fracture of the Golden Horde, the state established its winter administrative headquarters at Saray-Jük. The Nogai beys commanded mobile horse cavalry, regulated vast pastoral grasslands and conducted lucrative livestock trade and slave-raiding expeditions across Eastern Europe and Central Asia. name: Nojpetén Kingdom

Established in the mid-fifteenth century following migrations from northern Yucatán, the monarchy was governed by hereditary kings titled Kan Ek' from the island capital of Nojpetén. The kingdom preserved Maya hieroglyphic writing, astronomical calendars and ancestral temple rituals while maintaining defensive water palisades against neighbouring groups. name: Poqomam Kingdom

description: The Poqomam Kingdom was an autonomous Postclassic Maya highland state situated in the mountainous valleys of central Guatemala. Governed from heavily fortified plateau citadels such as Mixco Viejo and Chinautla Viejo, the kingdom commanded strategic mountain passes and fertile agricultural basins. The Poqomam people cultivated maize, beans and cacao, maintained elaborate ceramic workshops and defended their hilltop plazas with steep ravines and stone ramparts against encroaching K'iche' and Kaqchikel rivals. The kingdom's sovereign independence was crushed in 1526 following a protracted siege and assault conducted by Spanish conquistadores under Pedro de Alvarado. \n\n Status: Indigenous kingdom; Capital: Mixco Viejo; Common languages: Poqomam; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 1451; Disestablished: 1526; Succeeded by: New Spain; Ruler title: Ajaw

name: Principality of Kondia

description: The Principality of Kondia was an autonomous indigenous Ugric realm situated along the Konda River basin in western Siberia. Governed by hereditary Mansi princes from their fortified wooden settlement at Kondinskoe, the polity encompassed expansive taiga hunting territories and river networks. The inhabitants engaged in seasonal sturgeon fishing, elk hunting and sable trapping, with princely families maintaining traditional shamanic shrines and collecting pelts for regional trade. Muscovite military expeditions pushed east of the Urals during the late sixteenth century, decisively defeating local warrior bands and incorporating Kondia into the Tsardom of Russia in 1595. \n\n Status: Indigenous principality; Capital: Kondinskoe; Common languages: Mansi and Khanty; Religion: Shamanism; Government: Principality; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1451; Disestablished: 1595; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia; Ruler title: Prince

name: Principality of Lyapin

Governed by Mansi and Khanty chieftains from their fortified settlement at Saranpaul, the realm existed as a tributary vassal subordinate to the Siberian Khanate during the late fifteenth century. The principality delivered annual tributes of sable pelts and ermine skins to Tatar collectors in exchange for trade access and regional security. name: Principality of Pelym

Centred at the fortified stronghold of Pelym, the state was ruled by martial princes, notably Prince Asyka, who united several Ugric clans into a formidable coalition. Pelym warriors defended their boreal forests against foreign encroachment and conducted daring raids across the Urals into Russian Perm. The sovereign principality was systematically subjugated in the 1590s by Russian expeditionary forces, who erected a Muscovite ostrog upon the captured site. \n\n Status: Indigenous principality; Capital: Pelym; Common languages: Mansi; Religion: Shamanism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Asyka dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1451; Disestablished: 1596; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia; Ruler title: Prince

name: Principality of Ruza

description: The Principality of Ruza was an autonomous Rus appanage principality situated along the Ruza River west of Moscow. Created through a division of the Volotsk princely patrimony, the realm was governed by Prince Ivan Borisovich from his wooden fortress overlooking the river bend. The prince administered local agrarian estates, levied tolls on river traffic and maintained an elite bodyguard while honouring agreements with neighbouring Rus lords. name: Sultanate of Multan
description: The Sultanate of Multan was an independent late medieval Islamic monarchy based in the southern Punjab region of the Indus basin. Established around 1450 by Sultan Qutbu'd-Din Mahmud of the Langah dynasty following the collapse of central Delhi Sultanate authority, the realm was governed from the ancient fortified city of Multan. The sultanate controlled agricultural irrigated tracts along the Chenab and Ravi rivers, patronised revered Sufi shrines and flourished through overland merchant caravans linking India with Persia and Kandahar. Independent Langah rule ended in 1526 when invading Arghun forces from Sindh besieged and captured Multan. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Multan; Common languages: Saraiki, Punjabi and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Langah dynasty; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1445; Disestablished: 1526; Succeeded by: Arghun dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan

name: Sultanate of Tidore
description: The Sultanate of Tidore was an influential maritime spice empire centred on the volcanic island of Tidore in the northern Maluku archipelago. Governed by monarchs styled Kië ma-kolano and later Sultan from their capital at Soasio, the state commanded an extensive sphere of influence extending into the Raja Ampat islands and western New Guinea. Tidore derived wealth from native clove cultivation, conducting fierce trade rivalries with neighbouring Ternate. The sultanate maintained sovereign independence through maritime diplomacy until expanding Dutch East India Company interventions curtailed its autonomy in 1781. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Soasio; Common languages: Tidore and North Moluccan Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tidore royal line; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1450; Ruler title: Sultan; Currency: Clove barter and silver reals

name: Tunjur Kingdom

Displacing the earlier Daju dynasty, the Tunjur rulers established their capital at Uri in northern Jebel Marra, where they constructed monumental stone palaces, mosques and circular stone enclosures. The kingdom controlled trans-Saharan caravan routes linking Lake Chad with the Nile Valley, facilitating trade in horses, salt and copper while introducing Islamic administrative customs. Internal fragmentation and the rise of the Keira dynasty led to the kingdom's dissolution around 1650. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Uri; Common languages: Tunjur and Arabic; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern; Established: 1451; Disestablished: 1651; Preceded by: Daju kingdom; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Darfur and Wadai Empire

name: Duchy of Modena and Reggio

description: The Duchy of Modena and Reggio was a sovereign imperial principality situated in the fertile Emilia-Romagna plain of northern Italy. Created in 1452 when Holy Roman Emperor Frederick III elevated Borso d'Este to the ducal dignity, the state had its capital at Modena. The House of Este governed the realm with administrative sophistication, commissioning Renaissance palaces, sponsoring literary masters and expanding hydraulic irrigation networks across the Po drainage. The duchy maintained its sovereign status as an imperial fief through complex diplomatic alliances with Spain, France and the Papacy across four centuries of European conflicts. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Modena; Common languages: Emilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Este; Historical era: Renaissance to Early modern; Established: 1452; Ruler title: Duke

name: Qasim Khanate

Established in 1452 when Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow granted the town of Gorodets Meshchersky to Prince Qasim Khan of Kazan, the capital was renamed Kasimov. The khanate served as a crucial diplomatic bridge and military buffer between Muscovy and the steppe khanates, fielding skilled Tatar cavalry regiments that campaigned alongside Russian forces. The realm preserved Islamic court customs, mosques and autonomous royal succession under the patronage of the Moscow grand princes. \n\n Status: Autonomous khanate; Capital: Kasimov; Common languages: Volga Turki and Old East Slavic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jochid dynasty; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1452; Ruler title: Khan; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia

name: Despotate of the Morea
label: frankokratia
description: The Despotate of the Morea functioned as the final sovereign remnant of the Byzantine imperial realm following the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in May 1453. Spanning the Peloponnese peninsula with its court at the fortified hilltop city of Mystras, the state was ruled jointly by despots Demetrios and Thomas Palaiologos. The realm was severely crippled by bitter fratricidal discord between the co-rulers alongside widespread domestic insurrections. Sultan Mehmed II invaded the peninsula in May 1460, capturing Mystras and extinguishing the last vestige of independent Byzantine statehood. \n\n Status: Sovereign despotate; Capital: Mystras; Common languages: Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Palaiologos; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 29 May 1453; Disestablished: 31 May 1460; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire; Ruler title: Despot

name: Sublime Ottoman State
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Sublime Ottoman State was a transcontinental Islamic empire established as an imperial power following Sultan Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople on 29 May 1453. Making the newly renamed city of Istanbul its grand capital, the Ottoman dynasty unified southeastern Europe, Western Asia and North Africa under centralised bureaucratic administration.
